title: Spectral phase transitions and trainability in neural network learning dynamics
summary: The emergence of low-dimensional structures in the spectra of neural network weight matrices is a common empirical feature of trained models, but the dynamical origin of this phenomenon during learning remains an open problem. We formulate neural network training as the stochastic evolution of an initially random matrix ensemble, driven by stochastic gradient descent (SGD) updates that reshape the spectral bulk while amplifying signal strength. This induces a Baik-Ben Arous-Péché (BBP) transition during training, where isolated eigenvalues detach from the random bulk distribution, providing a dynamical framework for representation formation in high-dimensional learning dynamics. We demonstrate this in a solvable linear teacher-student model, where spectral evolution is analytically tractable and a phase diagram of trainability governed by the step size (or learning rate) and initial weight variance is obtained, and subsequently extend our formalism beyond the linear regime to nonlinear and stochastic settings. Numerical simulations in realistic settings support this picture, showing robust emergence of spectral alignment during training. Our results suggest that spectral analysis may provide a unified perspective of stochastic learning dynamics, linking trainability, optimisation hyperparameters, spectral phase transitions, and representation learning in neural networks.

AI.tldr: Training neural networks induces a Baik-Ben Arous-Péché (BBP) phase transition in the weight matrix spectrum, where isolated eigenvalues detach from the random bulk, providing a dynamical framework for representation learning. This is analytically shown in a linear teacher-student model and extended to nonlinear settings, with numerical validation.
AI.motivation: Low-dimensional spectral structures in trained neural network weights are empirically common, but their dynamical origin during SGD training is not understood. The paper aims to explain how spectral phase transitions emerge during learning.
AI.method: Models training as stochastic evolution of random matrix ensembles driven by SGD, analytically analyzes spectral evolution in a solvable linear teacher-student model, derives a phase diagram governed by learning rate and initial weight variance, and extends to nonlinear/stochastic settings with numerical simulations.
AI.result: Shows that a BBP transition occurs during training where isolated eigenvalues separate from the spectral bulk, providing a phase diagram of trainability. Numerical simulations confirm robust spectral alignment in realistic settings.
AI.conclusion: Spectral analysis offers a unified perspective linking trainability, hyperparameters, spectral phase transitions, and representation learning in neural networks.

title: Geometric Approach to Zero-Memory Quantum Dot Reservoir Computing
summary: Physical reservoir computing offers an energy-efficient alternative to conventional neural networks, where the intrinsic memory capacity in the physical system plays a central role. We demonstrate that memory capacity can be engineered extrinsically in memoryless systems by exploiting the computational space-time tradeoff, substituting temporal memory with spatial degrees of freedom. Our approach utilizes multidimensional input nodes to function as a spatial memory axis, thereby removing the dependency on intrinsic history-dependent dynamics in the reservoir. We validate this framework through numerical simulations of a generalized quantum dot, whose discrete energy levels provide strong nonlinearity crucial for reservoir computing as well. By coupling this inherent nonlinearity with our extrinsic memory, we show that memoryless quantum reservoir can achieve high performance on both chaotic Mackey-Glass future prediction and nonlinear transformation tasks. Furthermore, by analyzing the geometry of the quantum state trajectories, we identify the physical mechanism underlying this memory emergence: extrinsic memory constructs a hysteresis loop within the quantum Hilbert space, and this loop becomes topologically stable when the evolution of the system state synchronizes with the input signal's frequency. Our work decouples reservoir computing from material-specific memory properties, significantly expanding the range of candidate systems for quantum neuromorphic computing.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates that memory capacity in physical reservoir computing can be engineered extrinsically in memoryless systems by using spatial degrees of freedom instead of temporal memory, validated through quantum dot simulations where topological hysteresis loops in Hilbert space enable high-performance chaotic time-series prediction and nonlinear transformation tasks.
AI.motivation: To overcome the dependency of physical reservoir computing on intrinsic memory properties of specific materials, thereby expanding the range of candidate systems for quantum neuromorphic computing.
AI.method: Extrinsic memory is implemented via multidimensional input nodes serving as a spatial memory axis, substituting temporal memory with spatial degrees of freedom. The framework is validated through numerical simulations of a generalized quantum dot with discrete energy levels providing strong nonlinearity.
AI.result: Memoryless quantum reservoirs achieve high performance on chaotic Mackey-Glass future prediction and nonlinear transformation tasks. The physical mechanism is identified as a hysteresis loop in quantum Hilbert space that becomes topologically stable when system state evolution synchronizes with input signal frequency.
AI.conclusion: Reservoir computing is decoupled from material-specific memory properties, significantly expanding candidate systems for quantum neuromorphic computing by exploiting the computational space-time tradeoff.

title: Provable random-matrix spectral ramp in a static, geometrically local Hamiltonian
summary: Quantum chaos is commonly associated with the emergence of random-matrix statistics in the spectra of quantum systems. A useful diagnostic is provided by the spectral form factor (SFF), which for random matrix ensembles displays a universal linear-growth regime (`ramp'). In the last decade, a landmark result by Bertini, Kos and Prosen (BKP) identified for the first time a class of geometrically local quantum dynamics of finite-dimensional particles where the SFF provably exhibits a random-matrix ramp: periodically driven (Floquet) qudit chains whose evolution is described by `dual-unitary' circuits. Here, building on the BKP result and on a recently proposed variant of the Feynman-Kitaev clock construction, we obtain a spectral ramp in a class of static, geometrically local Hamiltonians. Our strategy is to embed the Floquet quasienergy spectrum of a dual-unitary circuit into the energy spectrum of a static local Hamiltonian, and to prove that the latter's connected SFF inherits the BKP ramp within a symmetry sector. This is to our knowledge the first proof of a spectral ramp in a time-independent, geometrically local many-body system with finite local Hilbert space dimension.

AI.tldr: This paper proves the existence of a random-matrix spectral ramp in a class of static, geometrically local Hamiltonians by embedding the Floquet spectrum of dual-unitary circuits via a Feynman-Kitaev clock construction.
AI.motivation: To establish the first rigorous proof of a spectral form factor ramp (indicative of quantum chaos) in time-independent, geometrically local many-body Hamiltonians with finite local Hilbert space dimension.
AI.method: The authors embed the Floquet quasienergy spectrum of a dual-unitary circuit (which provably exhibits a BKP ramp) into the energy spectrum of a static local Hamiltonian using a variant of the Feynman-Kitaev clock construction, and then prove that the connected spectral form factor of the static Hamiltonian inherits the ramp within a symmetry sector.
AI.result: The static Hamiltonian's connected SFF reproduces the universal linear ramp characteristic of random-matrix statistics, inherited from the dual-unitary Floquet system.
AI.conclusion: This provides the first proof of a spectral ramp in a static, geometrically local many-body system with finite local Hilbert space dimension, extending the BKP result from Floquet to Hamiltonian dynamics.

title: Beyond Worst-Case Branching: Quantum Tree Search via Amplitude Amplification
summary: In this work, we investigate quantum tree search via amplitude amplification. Amplitude amplification generalizes Grover's algorithm by replacing the Hadamard initialization with an arbitrary unitary $A$, with Grover's algorithm recovered as the special case of uniform initialization. We demonstrate the construction of a dynamic search tree of depth $m$ with query complexity $\sqrt{\left(b_{avg}\right)^m}$ where $b_{avg}$ denotes the average branching factor, improving upon the commonly assumed $\sqrt{\left(b_{max}\right)^m}$, where $b_{max}$ is the maximum branching factor. We further challenge the widespread assumption that amplitude amplification is inferior to quantum backtracking. In fact, quantum backtracking is unsuitable for problems that do not naturally admit a backtracking structure; in such cases, amplitude amplification yields improved query complexity. We observe that amplitude amplification constructs the search tree dynamically, rendering its internal structure inaccessible, a constraint that applies equally to quantum backtracking. To address this, we propose sampling-based methods to estimate the tree structure, under the assumption that it approximates a normal distribution with increasing depth. Finally, we introduce a quantum greedy search based on a lookahead heuristic inspired by the classical cognitive architecture Soar, which models human-like problem-solving strategies.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a quantum tree search method using amplitude amplification, achieving query complexity √((b_avg)^m), improving over the standard √((b_max)^m). It challenges the superiority of quantum backtracking, introduces sampling-based tree structure estimation under a normality assumption, and presents a quantum greedy search with lookahead heuristics inspired by cognitive architectures.
AI.motivation: To improve quantum tree search efficiency by replacing the worst-case branching factor with the average branching factor, and to challenge the prevailing assumption that amplitude amplification is inferior to quantum backtracking for tree-structured problems.
AI.method: The authors construct a dynamic search tree of depth m using amplitude amplification with query complexity √((b_avg)^m). They compare amplitude amplification against quantum backtracking, propose sampling-based methods to estimate tree structure under a normal distribution approximation, and introduce a quantum greedy search with a lookahead heuristic inspired by the Soar cognitive architecture.
AI.result: Achieves query complexity √((b_avg)^m), improving over √((b_max)^m). Shows that amplitude amplification outperforms quantum backtracking on problems without natural backtracking structure. Provides sampling-based estimation of tree structure and introduces a novel quantum greedy search method.
AI.conclusion: Amplitude amplification is a competitive and often superior alternative to quantum backtracking for quantum tree search, especially when average branching factor is significantly smaller than the maximum, and when problems lack backtracking-friendly structure.

title: Quantum Fourier Generative Models Trainable at Large Scale
comment: 12 pages, 6 figures; supplementary material 21 pages, 12 figures
summary: We propose an algorithmic framework for building and training quantum generative models corresponding to multivariate probability distributions. Our model uses parallel Fourier feature maps for embedding continuous-valued variables combined with a forrelation-type quantum circuit for tuning Fourier coefficients of the quantum model. Crucially, we develop a distinct training strategy where training is enabled at large scale by log-likelihood loss with unbiased Monte Carlo estimator based on Parseval's identity. Unlike prior work that relied on maximal mean discrepancy (MMD) loss, our approach goes beyond matching just low frequency moments, while enabling efficient classical training. Once the model is trained, we use inverse quantum Fourier transforms to map it into a separate sampling circuit in the computational basis. We demonstrate the efficiency of the suggested framework by validating loss estimation at the scale of over 1000 qubits on a single GPU. We show that univariate and bivariate models with highly non-trivial structure can be trained to low total variation distance, while fine-tuned IQP models with MMD loss show poor performance. Comparing to classical baselines represented by normalizing flow and diffusion models, we show that our approach avoids oversmoothing and preserves multi-modal structure of the target. Finally, we have deployed the trained models on superconducting quantum devices, successfully sampling distributions with per-sample execution times of approximately $300\,μ\mathrm{s}$. Our work shows that quantum generative models with the train-on-classical deploy-on-quantum approach can provide both high-quality structure at increased scale and fast sampling access needed for inference.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a framework for quantum generative models using parallel Fourier feature maps and forrelation-type circuits, trained via log-likelihood loss with Monte Carlo estimation (Parseval's identity), enabling efficient classical training at over 1000 qubits on a GPU. The approach outperforms MMD-based quantum models and classical baselines (normalizing flows, diffusion models), preserves multi-modal structure, and achieves fast (~300μs) sampling on superconducting quantum devices.
AI.motivation: To develop quantum generative models that can be trained efficiently at large scale on classical hardware while providing fast sampling on quantum devices, overcoming limitations of prior quantum models that relied on MMD loss (which matches only low-frequency moments) and struggled with training scale and distribution quality.
AI.method: The model uses parallel Fourier feature maps for embedding continuous variables, a forrelation-type quantum circuit to tune Fourier coefficients, and training via log-likelihood loss with an unbiased Monte Carlo estimator derived from Parseval's identity. After training, inverse quantum Fourier transforms map the model into a sampling circuit in the computational basis.
AI.result: Loss estimation validated at over 1000 qubits on a single GPU; univariate and bivariate models trained to low total variation distance; fine-tuned IQP models with MMD loss showed poor performance; the approach avoids oversmoothing and preserves multi-modal structure compared to normalizing flow and diffusion models; deployed on superconducting devices achieving ~300μs per-sample sampling.
AI.conclusion: The train-on-classical deploy-on-quantum approach for quantum generative models can provide high-quality distribution modeling at increased scale and fast sampling for inference, outperforming both prior quantum and classical generative approaches.

title: The subthreshold issue of fusion-based quantum computing
summary: Fusion-based quantum architectures are the leading approach to photonic quantum computing. However, the sub-threshold regime, where logical error rates must reach the levels required by useful applications, has received little attention. We show that in this regime, fusion failure imposes a noise floor on the logical error rate that prevents all-linear-optics architectures from reaching the required rates at low overhead. For fusion-based architectures using quantum emitter spins, we show that the noise floor is reduced by orders of magnitude at a lower overhead.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes fusion-based quantum architectures in the sub-threshold regime, finding that fusion failure causes a noise floor preventing all-linear-optics approaches from reaching required logical error rates at low overhead, while quantum emitter spin-based architectures reduce this noise floor by orders of magnitude with lower overhead.
AI.motivation: The sub-threshold regime of fusion-based quantum architectures, where logical error rates must reach levels required by useful applications, has received little attention despite its critical importance for practical quantum computing.
AI.method: The authors analyze the sub-threshold regime of fusion-based quantum architectures, comparing all-linear-optics approaches against quantum emitter spin-based approaches, examining how fusion failure impacts logical error rates.
AI.result: Fusion failure imposes a noise floor on the logical error rate that prevents all-linear-optics architectures from reaching required rates at low overhead. Quantum emitter spin-based architectures reduce this noise floor by orders of magnitude at a lower overhead.
AI.conclusion: Quantum emitter spin-based fusion architectures are significantly more viable than all-linear-optics approaches for achieving the logical error rates needed in the sub-threshold regime for practical quantum computing applications.

title: Dissipative Effects in Transmission Line Analogues of Hawking Radiation
summary: Hawking radiation is a fundamental result of quantum field theory in curved spacetime, yet its direct observation remains beyond current experimental capabilities. Circuit quantum electrodynamics provides a practical platform for realizing analogue systems where Hawking-like radiation may be studied under controlled laboratory conditions. In this work, we analyze two superconducting-circuit analogues of Schwarzschild black holes: a tunable dc-SQUID transmission line and a SNAIL-based transmission line supporting solitonic solutions of the KdV equation. We investigate the conditions under which these architectures can generate an observable Hawking temperature and study the impact of dissipation and thermal noise using an open quantum systems approach. To assess the observability of the Hawking signal, we propose complementing particle number measurements with estimates of the Hilbert-Schmidt distance to the thermal bath. Our analysis establishes practical detectability thresholds and shows that Hawking temperatures above approximately 73 mK remain distinguishable under realistic experimental conditions. While the tunable transmission line architecture can reach temperatures of about 113 mK and therefore appears more viable, the solitonic model requires further optimization and more demanding experimental conditions.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes two superconducting-circuit analogues of Schwarzschild black holes (dc-SQUID and SNAIL-based transmission lines) for generating observable Hawking radiation. Using an open quantum systems approach, it establishes that Hawking temperatures above ~73 mK are distinguishable under realistic conditions, with the tunable dc-SQUID architecture reaching ~113 mK and appearing more viable than the solitonic KdV model.
AI.motivation: Hawking radiation is a fundamental prediction of quantum field theory in curved spacetime but remains unobservable in astrophysical black holes. The authors aim to bridge this gap by designing laboratory analogue systems using circuit quantum electrodynamics where Hawking-like radiation can be generated and detected under controlled conditions.
AI.method: The authors analyze two superconducting-circuit architectures: (1) a tunable dc-SQUID transmission line and (2) a SNAIL-based transmission line supporting KdV solitons. They employ an open quantum systems approach to model dissipation and thermal noise, and propose Hilbert-Schmidt distance as a metric complementary to particle number measurements for assessing signal distinguishability from the thermal bath.
AI.result: Hawking temperatures above approximately 73 mK remain distinguishable under realistic experimental conditions. The tunable dc-SQUID transmission line can reach ~113 mK, while the solitonic SNAIL-based model requires more demanding conditions and further optimization.
AI.conclusion: The dc-SQUID architecture is more viable for realizing observable analogue Hawking radiation, whereas the solitonic model needs additional optimization. The Hilbert-Schmidt distance provides a useful metric for detectability assessment.

title: Borrowed Identities: Malleable Distillation Factories and a Unified Numerical Search
summary: Magic-state distillation is one of the leading overheads in fault-tolerant quantum computation. Existing methods for finding distillation factories require a transversal gate to act correctly on the entire codespace, a constraint that limits both generality and search efficiency. We introduce a strictly weaker borrowed-identity condition, requiring only that the distillation circuit act as the identity on a single input state. It applies uniformly across all levels of the Clifford hierarchy and unifies, within a single level, factories that distill different magic states -- for example, the $|T\rangle$, $|CS\rangle$, and $|CCZ\rangle$ factories. A brute-force search over borrowed-identity circuits with two-group symmetry recovers, within the search range, all distance-2 factories known from code-construction approaches, including entangled-output and multi-output factories previously outside the scope of any single numerical search. This unification yields parent circuits that encode multiple factories, so the output magic-state type can be chosen at compile time rather than fixed by a hard-coded design. The framework also extends beyond CSS codes, unifying constructions, including synthillation and non-CSS catalytic factories, previously obtained by disparate approaches.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a borrowed-identity condition for magic-state distillation, which is weaker than the transversal gate condition, unifying various distillation factories across Clifford hierarchy levels. A brute-force search under this condition recovers all known distance-2 factories, including entangled-output and multi-output ones, and enables compile-time selection of output magic-state type.
AI.motivation: Magic-state distillation is a major overhead in fault-tolerant quantum computation. Existing methods require a transversal gate constraint that limits generality and search efficiency.
AI.method: The authors introduce a borrowed-identity condition requiring only that the distillation circuit acts as identity on a single input state, weaker than the transversal gate condition. They perform a brute-force search over borrowed-identity circuits with two-group symmetry.
AI.result: The search recovers all distance-2 factories known from code-construction approaches, including entangled-output and multi-output factories. The framework unifies factories distilling different magic states (|T⟩, |CS⟩, |CCZ⟩) within a single level and extends beyond CSS codes.
AI.conclusion: The borrowed-identity condition enables unification and search of distillation factories previously obtained by disparate approaches, allowing output magic-state type to be chosen at compile time rather than fixed by design.

title: High yield creation of germanium vacancy centers in diamond by focused ion beam implantation and high temperature annealing
summary: Negatively charged germanium vacancy centers (GeV) in diamond are a promising platform for quantum computing and quantum communication. However, these applications require the precise incorporation of GeV centers with good optical properties inside of nanophotonic structures. In this work, we demonstrate the highly efficient local creation of GeV centers in diamond via focused-ion-beam implantation, followed by high-temperature annealing. We report the successful creation of GeV centers over the depth range of 5.5 - 30 nm. Implantation at low fluence enables the creation of single GeV centers. The formation yield strongly depends on implantation energy and fluence, reaching up to 33% at energies of 35 and 70 keV. This method, therefore, enables the efficient creation of GeV centers within a small, well-defined local sample volume and offers a potential means of incorporating them into photonic structures.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates efficient local creation of negatively charged germanium vacancy (GeV) centers in diamond via focused-ion-beam implantation and high-temperature annealing, achieving up to 33% formation yield at 35-70 keV energies over 5.5-30 nm depth, enabling integration into nanophotonic structures for quantum applications.
AI.motivation: GeV centers in diamond are promising for quantum computing and quantum communication, but require precise incorporation with good optical properties inside nanophotonic structures.
AI.method: Focused-ion-beam implantation of germanium into diamond followed by high-temperature annealing to create GeV centers.
AI.result: Successful creation of GeV centers over 5.5-30 nm depth range; single GeV centers at low fluence; formation yield up to 33% at 35 and 70 keV energies.
AI.conclusion: The method enables efficient creation of GeV centers within a small, well-defined local sample volume, offering a potential means for incorporating them into photonic structures.

title: Dynamical decoupling of a quantum dot spin in a micropillar cavity for spin-multiphoton entanglement
summary: Graph states of mutually entangled photons are key resources for quantum computation and communication and can be generated by leveraging the entanglement between a single resident spin and emitted photons from a charged semiconductor quantum dot (QD). This approach is intrinsically limited by the decoherence of the spin. We study how to mitigate this decoherence with dynamical decoupling of an electron spin in the weak transverse magnetic field regime using spin echo and Carr-Purcell-Meiboom-Gill (CPMG) techniques. Application of these techniques allows us to extend the coherence time of a spin by more than two orders of magnitude, extracting a $T_2^{CPMG}$ of $298\pm53$ ns. We further demonstrate that this technique is compatible with the generation of a spin-photon-photon entangled state at a high rate enabled by a micropillar cavity, with a 20% improvement in simulated state fidelity when using dynamical decoupling. These results pave the way for generating larger and more complex entangled states with QDs.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that dynamical decoupling techniques (spin echo and CPMG) can mitigate electron spin decoherence in charged semiconductor quantum dots, extending coherence time by over two orders of magnitude to 298±53 ns, and improving simulated spin-photon-photon entangled state fidelity by 20% in a micropillar cavity setup.
AI.motivation: Graph states of entangled photons are crucial for quantum computation and communication. Generating them via entanglement between a single resident spin and emitted photons from a charged semiconductor quantum dot is intrinsically limited by spin decoherence. The study aims to mitigate this decoherence to enable generation of larger and more complex entangled states.
AI.method: The authors apply dynamical decoupling techniques—specifically spin echo and Carr-Purcell-Meiboom-Gill (CPMG) sequences—to an electron spin in a charged semiconductor quantum dot under a weak transverse magnetic field regime. They measure coherence times and simulate the fidelity of spin-photon-photon entangled state generation in a micropillar cavity with and without dynamical decoupling.
AI.result: Dynamical decoupling extends spin coherence time by over two orders of magnitude, achieving a CPMG-extracted T₂ of 298±53 ns. The technique is compatible with high-rate entanglement generation in a micropillar cavity, yielding a 20% improvement in simulated state fidelity when dynamical decoupling is applied.
AI.conclusion: Dynamical decoupling effectively mitigates spin decoherence in quantum dot systems, significantly extending coherence times and improving entanglement fidelity. These results enable the generation of larger and more complex entangled states with quantum dots, advancing quantum communication and computation applications.

title: Pauli-Sparse regularised Counterdiabatic Shortcuts for Linear-Ramp QAOA
summary:
Combinatorial optimization is a leading target for quantum algorithms, but finite-depth QAOA can suffer from strong diabatic errors when the interpolation Hamiltonian has small, or exponentially small, spectral gaps. We propose a Pauli-sparse counterdiabatic extension of linear-ramp QAOA based on the regularised adiabatic gauge potential \[
  \bigl(\mathcal L_H^2+ηI\bigr)A_λ^{(η)}
  =
  -\mathrm{i}\mathcal L_H(\partial_λH),
  \qquad
  \mathcal L_H(X)=[H,X]. \] Instead of computing a dense AGP, we solve this equation approximately by an inexact conjugate-gradient method in Pauli coordinates, truncating the Pauli expansion during the iteration to obtain a gate-budget-aware set of implementable rotations. The selected support is then improved by a Galerkin refit and certified by an a posteriori residual bound. The regularization parameter \(η\) acts as an energy-resolution scale: it suppresses transitions below \(\sqrtη\) while retaining larger-gap transitions. Thus, the method can avoid resolving exponentially small splittings inside a low-energy solution manifold while reducing leakage away from it. Numerical experiments on Ferromagnetic Chain (FC) and perturbed FC--MaxCut/MarketSplit instances show that the resulting LR-CD-QAOA ansatz improves approximation ratios over the uncorrected linear ramp, especially in regimes where LR-QAOA remains far from the optimum. Overall, the proposed regularized LR-CD-QAOA framework substantially broadens the practical applicability of QAOA to QUBO optimization by improving its robustness across heterogeneous problem landscapes, including instances with near-degenerate low-energy structures and small spectral gaps.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a Pauli-sparse counterdiabatic extension of linear-ramp QAOA (LR-CD-QAOA) using a regularized adiabatic gauge potential, solved via an inexact conjugate-gradient method in Pauli coordinates with truncation, Galerkin refit, and a posteriori residual certification. The method suppresses diabatic errors from small spectral gaps by introducing a regularization parameter η that acts as an energy-resolution scale, improving approximation ratios on Ferromagnetic Chain and perturbed FC–MaxCut/MarketSplit instances, particularly where standard LR-QAOA underperforms.
AI.motivation: Combinatorial optimization is a key target for quantum algorithms, but finite-depth QAOA suffers from strong diabatic errors when the interpolation Hamiltonian has small or exponentially small spectral gaps, limiting its practical applicability.
AI.method: The authors propose a regularized counterdiabatic extension of linear-ramp QAOA based on solving the regularized adiabatic gauge potential equation (L_H^2 + ηI)A_λ^{(η)} = -i L_H(∂_λ H) using an inexact conjugate-gradient method in Pauli coordinates. The Pauli expansion is truncated during iteration to obtain gate-budget-aware implementable rotations, followed by a Galerkin refit and a posteriori residual bound certification. The regularization parameter η suppresses transitions below √η while retaining larger-gap transitions.
AI.result: Numerical experiments on Ferromagnetic Chain (FC) and perturbed FC–MaxCut/MarketSplit instances demonstrate that LR-CD-QAOA improves approximation ratios over the uncorrected linear ramp, especially in regimes where LR-QAOA remains far from the optimum.
AI.conclusion: The proposed regularized LR-CD-QAOA framework substantially broadens the practical applicability of QAOA to QUBO optimization by improving its robustness across heterogeneous problem landscapes, including instances with near-degenerate low-energy structures and small spectral gaps.

title: Enhancing Initial-State Sensitivity through Time-Dependent Hamiltonian Readout in Ising Spin Chains
summary: Local observables can lose sensitivity to an initial state during strongly interacting many-body evolution even though the global dynamics remain unitary. We show that this sensitivity can be enhanced through a time-dependent Hamiltonian readout. Two orthogonal product states are first evolved under a slanted-field Ising Hamiltonian, where their distinction becomes strongly suppressed as observed through several local observables, including subsystem magnetizations and correlation functions, and are then quenched to the transverse-field Ising model at a tunable time. Exact simulations of chains up to $N=12$ show that the optimized time-averaged separation after the switch exceeds the residual slanted-field baseline for every observable and system size tested. In the strongest channels, the standardized readout separation remains robust over the accessible size range, with no clear systematic suppression at larger $N$. The enhancement recurs in widely separated late-time windows and persists qualitatively for open boundaries. These results establish Hamiltonian switching as an observable-selective mechanism for enhancing initial-state sensitivity without time reversal or implying recovery of the full reduced state.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that switching from a slanted-field Ising Hamiltonian to a transverse-field Ising model can enhance the sensitivity of local observables to initial orthogonal product states, even though the global dynamics remain unitary. The optimized readout separation after the switch consistently exceeds the baseline across all observables and system sizes tested (up to N=12), with no systematic suppression at larger N.
AI.motivation: Local observables can lose sensitivity to an initial state during strongly interacting many-body evolution, and the authors aim to find a mechanism to recover or enhance this sensitivity without time reversal or full state reconstruction.
AI.method: Exact simulations of chains up to N=12, evolving two orthogonal product states under a slanted-field Ising Hamiltonian, then quenching to the transverse-field Ising model at a tunable time. The time-averaged separation after the switch is optimized and compared to the residual slanted-field baseline across multiple local observables.
AI.result: The optimized time-averaged separation after the Hamiltonian switch exceeds the residual slanted-field baseline for every observable and system size tested. The standardized readout separation remains robust over the accessible size range with no clear systematic suppression at larger N, and the enhancement recurs in widely separated late-time windows.
AI.conclusion: Hamiltonian switching is an observable-selective mechanism for enhancing initial-state sensitivity without requiring time reversal or implying recovery of the full reduced state.

title: The Prepare and Broadcast Scenario
summary: We introduce the dimension-restricted prepare and broadcast (PAB) scenario, which generalizes standard prepare-and-measure frameworks. Here, the system prepared by a sender undergoes a broadcasting transformation before being locally measured by multiple receivers. We develop a hierarchy of classical, quantum, and nonsignalling models describing this scenario, characterize their corresponding correlation sets, and derive new families of Bell-like inequalities together with linear and semidefinite programming methods for their certification. First, assuming shared randomness, we prove that the hierarchy collapses into a single set whenever we consider only one measurement per party. Then, considering multiple possible measurements, we show that PAB scenarios allow the activation of nonclassicality, revealing genuinely nonclassical features in resources that admit classical descriptions in standard prepare-and-measure or Bell settings.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the dimension-restricted prepare-and-broadcast (PAB) scenario, which extends standard prepare-and-measure frameworks by adding a broadcasting step. It develops a hierarchy of classical, quantum, and nonsignalling models, derives Bell-like inequalities and certification methods, and shows that PAB scenarios can activate nonclassicality in resources that appear classical under standard settings.
AI.motivation: To generalize standard prepare-and-measure frameworks by introducing a broadcasting transformation, enabling the study of correlations and nonclassicality beyond what is possible in traditional settings.
AI.method: The authors develop a hierarchy of classical, quantum, and nonsignalling models for the PAB scenario, characterize correlation sets, and derive Bell-like inequalities along with linear and semidefinite programming methods for certification. They analyze the case of single vs. multiple measurements per party.
AI.result: For a single measurement per party, the hierarchy collapses into a single set under shared randomness. For multiple possible measurements, PAB scenarios activate nonclassicality, revealing genuinely nonclassical features in resources that admit classical descriptions in standard prepare-and-measure or Bell settings.
AI.conclusion: The PAB scenario is a powerful generalization that can expose nonclassicality hidden in standard frameworks, with practical certification tools provided.

title: The Schrödinger equation in the complex plane and quantum entanglement
summary: We formulate a continuity equation for the Schrödinger equation in the complex space. We define a complex momentum by normalizing the complex current by the particle density. This momentum is a quantum analog of the classical, kinematic momentum analytically continued into the complex plane. The kinematic momentum and the gradient of the wavefunction's phase each represent a fluid-like flow in the complex plane; the phase-gradient flow is incompressible. The zeros of the wavefunction give rise to simple poles in the momentum. The poles manifest as irrotational vortexes in the phase-gradient flow, while critical points of the wavefunction present as rigid body-like rotational flows of the kinematic momentum. A discrete nature of elementary excitations comes about inherently because the quantity of the poles is automatically integer. An exact quantization condition is subsequently formulated, which reduces to the Bohr-Sommerfeld condition in the semiclassical limit. We establish a priori that the Bohr-Sommerfeld condition must be exact for the Harmonic Oscillator. We show that the kinetic energy is a sum of contributions of the average value and fluctuations, respectively, of the kinematic momentum. The zero-point vibrations within bound states are solely due to the fluctuations of the momentum and manifest as rigid-body flows at infinity. The momentum poles -- and hence the wavefunction's zeros -- can be viewed as emergent, consistent with the remarkable property of quantum entanglement exhibited by standing wave solutions of the Schrödinger equation.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a complex momentum derived from a continuity equation in complex space for the Schrödinger equation, linking wavefunction zeros to momentum poles, irrotational vortices, and rigid-body rotational flows, leading to an exact quantization condition that reduces to Bohr-Sommerfeld semiclassically.
AI.motivation: To formulate a continuity equation for the Schrödinger equation in complex space, define a complex quantum momentum, and derive an exact quantization condition that bridges quantum mechanics and semiclassical approximations.
AI.method: Derives a complex momentum by normalizing complex current by particle density; analyzes phase-gradient flow (incompressible) and kinematic momentum flow; identifies wavefunction zeros as simple poles in momentum manifesting as irrotational vortexes, and critical points as rigid-body rotational flows.
AI.result: An exact quantization condition is formulated that reduces to Bohr-Sommerfeld semiclassically; Bohr-Sommerfeld is shown to be exact for the Harmonic Oscillator a priori; kinetic energy decomposes into average and fluctuation contributions; zero-point vibrations arise solely from momentum fluctuations manifesting as rigid-body flows at infinity.
AI.conclusion: Momentum poles (wavefunction zeros) are emergent and consistent with quantum entanglement in standing wave solutions; the discrete nature of elementary excitations arises inherently from integer-valued pole quantities.

title: Exploring the Effects of Entanglement on Quantum Machine Learning of Pathogen Epitope-Receptor Binding
summary: Parameterized quantum circuits (PQCs) provide a flexible substrate for hybrid quantum machine learning (QML), but their practical value on Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) devices remains an empirical question, especially because training depth and scale can introduce optimization challenges such as barren plateaus. Here we study how the number and topology of two-qubit entangling gates in the feature-map stage influence a fixed hybrid QNN workflow for classifying strong versus weak epitope-receptor binding in Porcine Reproductive and Respiratory Syndrome (PRRS) vaccine design. The dataset consists of docking-derived binding affinities for N=80 9-mer epitopes, labeled as Strong or Weak binding, and partitioned into training, validation, and test subsets using a 40:30:30 split. We compare a classical CNN benchmark with a hybrid Embedding-QNN architecture under four feature-map configurations: a non-entangling Z feature map, an all-to-all high-entanglement ZZ feature map, and two interleaved nearest-neighbour entanglement patterns of low and high depth. Among the configurations tested, the high-entanglement ZZ feature map is seen to provide the strongest evidence of reduced training-set overfit, with a lower training area under the accuracy curve (AUAC) and the highest test/training AUAC ratio, while preserving competitive test-set accuracy. These results do not establish a general QML advantage, but they suggest that feature-map entanglement topology is a meaningful design variable for sparse biological screening tasks and warrants further evaluation with additional metrics, larger datasets, and noise-aware or hardware-based experiments.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how the topology and number of two-qubit entangling gates in the feature-map stage of a hybrid quantum neural network affect classification performance on a small biological dataset (N=80 epitope-receptor binding affinities for PRRS vaccine design). Among four configurations tested, the high-entanglement ZZ feature map reduces training overfit and achieves the best test/training AUAC ratio, though no general QML advantage is established.
AI.motivation: To determine whether feature-map entanglement topology is a meaningful design variable for improving hybrid quantum machine learning on small, sparse biological screening tasks, specifically for classifying epitope-receptor binding strengths in PRRS vaccine design.
AI.method: A fixed hybrid Embedding-QNN architecture is compared against a classical CNN baseline on a dataset of N=80 docking-derived epitope-receptor binding affinities (Strong vs. Weak labels). Four feature-map configurations are tested: (1) non-entangling Z feature map, (2) all-to-all high-entanglement ZZ feature map, (3-4) two interleaved nearest-neighbour entanglement patterns of low and high depth. Performance is evaluated using training AUAC, test/training AUAC ratio, and test-set accuracy under a 40:30:30 train/validation/test split.
AI.result: The high-entanglement ZZ feature map shows the strongest reduction in training-set overfitting (lowest training AUAC, highest test/training AUAC ratio) while maintaining competitive test-set accuracy compared to other configurations and the classical CNN baseline.
AI.conclusion: Feature-map entanglement topology is a meaningful design variable for small-scale biological screening tasks, but no general QML advantage is demonstrated; further evaluation with larger datasets, additional metrics, and noise-aware or hardware-based experiments is warranted.

title: Emergence of Thermodynamics from Equilibration in Isolated Quantum Systems
summary: Understanding how macroscopic thermodynamic behavior emerges from microscopic quantum dynamics remains an open problem. While equilibration of quantum observables is well established, thermodynamics also relies on variables not directly associated with linear operators, but which are defined instead as functions of expectation values. Whether and how such derived quantities inherit equilibration properties is an open question. Here, we establish that any continuously differentiable function of equilibrating expectation values also equilibrates. We apply this result to a bipartite isolated system, showing that the entropy and conjugate variables of each subsystem -- defined through Jaynes' maximum entropy principle -- equilibrate. Moreover, with the assumption that their equilibrium properties depend solely on local conserved quantities, we show the dynamical maximization of the total entropy, enforcing equality of conjugate variables across subsystems. These results provide a direct dynamical justification for entropy maximization and the emergence of thermodynamic equilibrium conditions, showing that fundamental principles of thermodynamics follow from the unitary evolution of quantum systems.

AI.tldr: This paper proves that any continuously differentiable function of equilibrating expectation values also equilibrates, and applies this to show that entropy and conjugate variables in bipartite quantum systems equilibrate, with total entropy maximization and equality of conjugate variables emerging from unitary dynamics.
AI.motivation: Understanding how macroscopic thermodynamic behavior emerges from microscopic quantum dynamics remains an open problem. Whether derived quantities (functions of expectation values) inherit equilibration properties is an open question.
AI.method: The authors prove that any continuously differentiable function of equilibrating expectation values also equilibrates. They apply this to a bipartite isolated system using Jaynes' maximum entropy principle to define entropy and conjugate variables.
AI.result: Entropy and conjugate variables of each subsystem equilibrate. Under the assumption that equilibrium properties depend solely on local conserved quantities, the total entropy is dynamically maximized, enforcing equality of conjugate variables across subsystems.
AI.conclusion: Fundamental principles of thermodynamics (entropy maximization and thermodynamic equilibrium conditions) follow from the unitary evolution of quantum systems, providing a direct dynamical justification.

title: Temporal Dynamical Quantum Phase Transition in Dicke Model with Trapped Ions
summary: Temporal non-analyticities in the rate function of the Loschmidt echo manifests a class of dynamical quantum phase transitions (DQPTs) that has emerged as a powerful framework for understanding far-from-equilibrium many-body dynamics. While such DQPT has been extensively studied theoretically in spin-boson systems such as the Dicke model, their experimental observation remains elusive. In particular, the dynamics of DQPT in asymmetric spin subspaces and under the influence of spin dissipation are largely unexplored. Here, we report an experimental study of temporal DQPT in a generalized Dicke model using a trapped-ion quantum simulator. By coupling a linear chain of $\rm{^{40}Ca^{+}}$ ions to a collective center-of-mass motional mode, we probe the quench dynamics starting from both symmetric and asymmetric initial states. We extract the rate function and identify temporal turn-around points that are in quantitative agreement with theoretical predictions. Additionally, we investigate the impact of spin dissipation on these dynamics. Our results establish an experimental platform for probing complex many-body out-of-equilibrium phenomena and advance the development of hybrid oscillator-spin quantum simulators.

AI.tldr: This paper reports the first experimental observation of dynamical quantum phase transitions (DQPTs) in a generalized Dicke model using a trapped-ion quantum simulator with $\rm{^{40}Ca^{+}}$ ions, studying quench dynamics from symmetric and asymmetric initial states and the effects of spin dissipation.
AI.motivation: While DQPTs have been extensively studied theoretically in spin-boson systems like the Dicke model, experimental observation remains elusive. Additionally, dynamics of DQPT in asymmetric spin subspaces and under spin dissipation are largely unexplored.
AI.method: The authors use a trapped-ion quantum simulator coupling a linear chain of $\rm{^{40}Ca^{+}}$ ions to a collective center-of-mass motional mode, performing quench dynamics from both symmetric and asymmetric initial states to probe temporal DQPTs in a generalized Dicke model.
AI.result: The rate function of the Loschmidt echo was extracted, identifying temporal turn-around points in quantitative agreement with theoretical predictions. The impact of spin dissipation on these dynamics was also characterized.
AI.conclusion: This work establishes an experimental platform for probing complex many-body out-of-equilibrium phenomena and advances the development of hybrid oscillator-spin quantum simulators.

title: A QUBO Formulation for Nowhere-Zero $k$-Flows
comment: 22 pages, 7 tables; published in Utilitas Mathematica; supporting code available in public GitHub repository alilotfi90/nzflow-qubo/ (link in manuscript)
summary: We consider the encoding of graph problems as Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) problems, which are solvable by either quantum or classical annealers. Yet, the class of problems encoded as QUBO problems has not previously included nowhere-zero flows. Nowhere-zero flows are related to Tutte's $5$-flow conjecture and appear in many contexts in graph theory. We provide an encoding of nowhere-zero flows as a QUBO Hamiltonian and prove the correctness of the construction. Our construction yields a Hamiltonian $H_{\mathrm{mod},k}$ whose ground state has zero energy if and only if the graph $G$ has a nowhere-zero $\mathbb Z_k$-flow. By Tutte's equivalence theorem, zero ground energy is equivalent to $\varphi(G)\le k$, and the zero-energy degeneracy is given by the flow polynomial $F(G;k)$. In particular, when the ground-state energy is zero, this is also the ground-state degeneracy. The construction uses one-hot variables to represent the edge flow residues modulo $k$ and auxiliary variables to represent the per-vertex modular quotient. We prove that the correctness of the construction is independent of the choice of orientation, root vertex, and positive penalty weights. We verify the construction on $59$ examples of graphs and values of $k$ that include both yes-instances and no-instances. We exhaustively sweep orientations and root choices on selected robustness instances and test a finite suite of positive penalty weights. The resulting Hamiltonian is implemented using the dimod.BinaryQuadraticModel class, which is compatible with the D-Wave Ocean SDK. Quantum-hardware runs and claims about potential speedup using these devices are left to follow-up work.

AI.tldr: The paper encodes nowhere-zero flows (related to Tutte's 5-flow conjecture) as QUBO Hamiltonians solvable by quantum/classical annealers, proving correctness and verifying on 59 graph instances. The ground-state energy is zero iff the graph has a nowhere-zero Z_k-flow, with degeneracy given by the flow polynomial.
AI.motivation: To extend the class of graph problems encodable as QUBO problems to include nowhere-zero flows, which are central to graph theory and Tutte's 5-flow conjecture, thereby enabling their solution via quantum or classical annealing.
AI.method: The authors construct a QUBO Hamiltonian H_mod,k using one-hot variables for edge flow residues modulo k and auxiliary variables for per-vertex modular quotients. They prove correctness independent of orientation, root vertex, and positive penalty weights, and implement it using the dimod.BinaryQuadraticModel class compatible with D-Wave Ocean SDK.
AI.result: The Hamiltonian's ground state has zero energy iff the graph G has a nowhere-zero Z_k-flow; zero-energy degeneracy equals the flow polynomial F(G;k). Verified on 59 graph/k-value instances (both yes and no instances), with exhaustive sweeps of orientations and root choices on robustness instances.
AI.conclusion: The QUBO encoding of nowhere-zero flows is correct and robust, enabling future quantum-hardware runs and potential speedup investigations. Quantum-hardware experiments and speedup claims are left to follow-up work.

title: High-Fidelity Hole Spin Qubits Reveal Quadrupolar Nuclear-Bath Dynamics in Isotopically Purified Planar Germanium
summary: Planar Germanium has emerged as a promising platform to build spin-based large scale quantum computers. By exploiting the anisotropic hyperfine interaction of holes in Ge, qubits with long T2* have been recently realized. While the performance of single qubits is still more or less limited by 73Ge nuclear spin fluctuations, the site-to-site variation of qubit sweet spot becomes obstacles to maintaining high fidelity of each qubit across the whole wafer. To achieve high performance Ge-based quantum circuit, it is therefore essential to eliminate the origin source of hyperfine noise. In its Silicon counterparts, reduction of 29Si abundance enables exceptional high-fidelity operation. In contrast, hole qubits based on isotopically purified Ge have not been demonstrated. Here, we report the synthesis of high quality 2-dimensional hole gas (2DHG) with enriched 70GeH4 precursor. Due to the suppression of nonzero spin nucleus, the qubits' T2* on the sweet spot is moderately extended beyond 20 us, surpassing the previous best reported Ge hole qubits. More importantly, the qubits' T2* off the sweet spot is enhanced to above 3 us, enabling single qubit gate fidelity exceeding 99.9% in both operating regimes. Hahn-echo spectroscopy further resolves a finite-frequency nuclear-noise channel that is distinct from the conventional Larmor-linked hyperfine response. We associate this channel with quadrupole-modified dynamics of residual 73Ge nuclei sampling local electric-field gradients near the Ge/SiGe interface. Its field scaling and angle-dependent visibility are consistent with a qubit-visible quadrupolar nuclear-noise component transduced through the anisotropic hyperfine interaction of Ge holes. These results establish isotopically purified planar Ge as a high-coherence scalable platform for hole spin qubits and provide a spectroscopic probe of interfacial quadrupolar nuclear dynamics.

AI.tldr: Isotopically purified planar Ge with enriched 70GeH4 precursor suppresses nuclear spin noise, extending qubit T2* beyond 20 µs (sweet spot) and above 3 µs (off sweet spot), enabling single-qubit gate fidelities exceeding 99.9% and revealing quadrupole-modified nuclear dynamics at the Ge/SiGe interface.
AI.motivation: 73Ge nuclear spin fluctuations limit qubit coherence and site-to-site variation of sweet spots hinders high-fidelity operation across wafers. Isotopic purification, already successful in Si, had not been demonstrated for Ge hole qubits.
AI.method: Synthesis of high-quality 2-dimensional hole gas (2DHG) using isotopically enriched 70GeH4 precursor to reduce nonzero-spin nuclei; characterization via T2* measurements, Hahn-echo spectroscopy, and analysis of quadrupolar nuclear dynamics.
AI.result: T2* at sweet spot extended beyond 20 µs; T2* off sweet spot enhanced to >3 µs; single-qubit gate fidelities >99.9% in both regimes; identification of a finite-frequency nuclear-noise channel attributed to quadrupole-modified dynamics of residual 73Ge nuclei at the interface.
AI.conclusion: Isotopically purified planar Ge is a high-coherence, scalable platform for hole spin qubits, and the observed quadrupolar nuclear noise provides a spectroscopic probe of interfacial nuclear dynamics.

title: Detecting entanglement of non-Gaussian continuous-variable states from single-copy homodyne measurements
summary: The entanglement of Gaussian continuous-variable (CV) states is fully determined by the state's second moments. In contrast, some entangled non-Gaussian states evade every second-moment criterion, and non-Gaussian entanglement detection remains an experimental challenge. The $p_3$-PPT criterion detects entanglement using moments of the partial transpose of the density matrix. This criterion was recently extended to CV systems using photon-number-resolving detectors and multi-copy interferometry; here we introduce a single-copy homodyne protocol that detects bipartite CV entanglement via the same criterion. Unbiased U-statistic estimators for the partial-transpose moments $p_2$ and $p_3$ are constructed directly from randomized homodyne data and used to evaluate the $p_3$-PPT entanglement witnesses: a linear one for detection, and a quadratic one whose violation yields a dimension-free lower bound on the entanglement negativity. The protocol estimates $p_2$ and $p_3$ up to additive error $\varepsilon$ at Fock cutoff $N$ from $O((N+1)^{14/3}/\varepsilon^2)$ measurements at fixed confidence. We demonstrate the protocol on six families of Gaussian and non-Gaussian states, reaching $95\%$ empirical one-sided detection probability from $\sim 10^3$ to $10^4$ homodyne measurements for states with $\bar{n} \approx 2$, placing non-Gaussian entanglement detection within reach of current homodyne experiments.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a single-copy homodyne protocol for detecting bipartite CV entanglement via the p3-PPT criterion, using unbiased U-statistic estimators for partial-transpose moments p2 and p3 from randomized homodyne data. The protocol achieves additive error ε at Fock cutoff N with O((N+1)^14/3/ε^2) measurements, and demonstrates ~95% detection probability from ~10^3-10^4 measurements on non-Gaussian states with n̄≈2.
AI.motivation: Non-Gaussian entangled states evade second-moment entanglement criteria, making their detection experimentally challenging. Existing p3-PPT criterion methods require either photon-number-resolving detectors or multi-copy interferometry; a more experimentally accessible single-copy homodyne protocol is needed.
AI.method: The authors develop unbiased U-statistic estimators for partial-transpose moments p2 and p3 directly from randomized homodyne measurement data, and use these to evaluate linear and quadratic p3-PPT entanglement witnesses.
AI.result: The protocol achieves additive error ε at Fock cutoff N with O((N+1)^14/3/ε^2) measurement complexity at fixed confidence. Demonstrated on six families of Gaussian and non-Gaussian states, achieving 95% empirical one-sided detection probability from ~10^3 to 10^4 homodyne measurements for states with mean photon number ≈ 2.
AI.conclusion: The single-copy homodyne protocol makes non-Gaussian entanglement detection feasible with current experimental technology, placing it within reach of existing homodyne setups.

title: Quantum Counterparty Credit Risk: A Study of Path-Dependent Derivatives
summary: Estimating potential future exposure (PFE) for path-dependent derivatives, such as FX Target Redemption Forwards (TARFs), represents a formidable computational challenge due to the demand of nested Monte Carlo simulations. We present a hybrid quantum-classical framework that leverages Iterative Quantum Amplitude Estimation (IQAE) to address this via a reduced-order counterparty credit risk model. Our methodology maps the non-linear TARF payoff -- including cumulative gains and knock-out features -- into a quantum circuit via a two-step formulation, whereby a first-step percentile is computed classically and then used to condition quantum evaluation of subsequent exposure. We employ discretisation of the FX process and a linearised additive approximation of dynamics to enable implementation on current quantum platforms. Developed via the Classiq platform and validated on NVIDIA CUDA-Q and Amazon Braket SV1, our approach achieves relative errors of 1%-8% against classical benchmarks at the 97.5% and 99% confidence levels. While discretisation constraints and approximate monotonicity assumption may introduce bias and limit recovery of the full exposure distribution, our framework offers a tractable testbed for quantum acceleration. Scaling analysis suggests that $\sim$300 logical qubits could enable full 52-week exposure estimation, reducing sample complexity for tail-risk estimation via amplitude estimation at the cost of increased circuit depth.

AI.tldr: A hybrid quantum-classical framework for computing Potential Future Exposure (PFE) of path-dependent FX Target Redemption Forwards (TARFs) using Iterative Quantum Amplitude Estimation (IQAE), achieving 1%-8% relative error at high confidence levels (97.5%, 99%) on quantum simulators (NVIDIA CUDA-Q, Amazon Braket SV1), with scaling analysis indicating ~300 logical qubits could enable full 52-week exposure estimation.
AI.motivation: Estimating PFE for path-dependent derivatives like FX TARFs requires computationally expensive nested Monte Carlo simulations, motivating the need for more efficient approaches. Quantum amplitude estimation offers theoretical quadratic speedup for Monte Carlo-based risk estimation.
AI.method: 1) Reduced-order counterparty credit risk model to simplify the problem. 2) Two-step formulation: classical computation of a first-step percentile conditions quantum evaluation of subsequent exposure. 3) TARF payoff (cumulative gains, knock-out features) encoded into quantum circuits via discretisation of FX process and linearised additive approximation of dynamics. 4) IQAE algorithm implemented on Classiq platform, validated on NVIDIA CUDA-Q and Amazon Braket SV1 simulators.
AI.result: Relative errors of 1%-8% against classical benchmarks at 97.5% and 99% confidence levels. Scaling analysis shows ~300 logical qubits could enable full 52-week exposure estimation, with reduced sample complexity for tail-risk estimation via amplitude estimation at the cost of increased circuit depth.
AI.conclusion: The hybrid quantum-classical framework provides a tractable testbed for quantum acceleration of PFE computation, though discretisation constraints and approximate monotonicity assumptions introduce bias and limit full exposure distribution recovery. The approach trades sample complexity reduction for increased circuit depth.

title: Dissipative phase decision without ground-state preparation
summary: We propose a dynamical approach to identifying ground-state quantum phases through short-time dissipative cooling. Rather than determining the phase by preparing highly accurate approximations to ground states, we prepare a representative state of a candidate phase and monitor the early-time response of phase-sensitive observables under cooling dynamics tailored to the target Hamiltonian. For a class of phase-decision problems in which the relevant observables can be inferred from the low-energy manifold, and with jump operators implementable using only short-time Hamiltonian simulation, the dissipative evolution rapidly suppresses high-energy components and drives the system into a low-energy manifold whose observables already reveal the underlying ground-state phase, well before mixing to the steady state. We demonstrate this strategy for the frustrated $J_1$--$J_2$ Heisenberg chain, the Kitaev honeycomb model, and the XXZ chain, including Berezinskii--Kosterlitz--Thouless and topological phase transitions. In particular, coarse filter resolutions and short evolution times suffice to recover phase-sensitive quantities such as the Luttinger parameter and topological diagnostics. We further provide theoretical justification that cooling dynamics with such jump operators can rigorously prepare low-energy manifolds for free-fermionic and free-bosonic systems, and investigate this mechanism for interacting fermionic systems. Our results suggest that phase decision is a plausible target for future utility-scale studies on early fault-tolerant quantum devices.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes using short-time dissipative cooling dynamics to identify ground-state quantum phases without needing highly accurate ground state preparation. By monitoring early-time responses of phase-sensitive observables under tailored cooling, the underlying phase can be revealed before steady-state mixing. Demonstrated on frustrated Heisenberg, Kitaev honeycomb, and XXZ models, this approach requires only coarse filter resolutions and short evolution times, making it plausible for early fault-tolerant quantum devices.
AI.motivation: To identify ground-state quantum phases without the expensive requirement of preparing highly accurate ground states, leveraging short-time cooling dynamics as a more practical alternative for near-term quantum devices.
AI.method: The method prepares a representative state of a candidate phase and monitors early-time responses of phase-sensitive observables under dissipative cooling dynamics (with jump operators implementable via short-time Hamiltonian simulation). The cooling rapidly suppresses high-energy components, driving the system into a low-energy manifold where observables reveal the ground-state phase before mixing to the steady state.
AI.result: Demonstrated successfully on the frustrated $J_1$-$J_2$ Heisenberg chain, Kitaev honeycomb model, and XXZ chain (including BKT and topological phase transitions). Coarse filter resolutions and short evolution times suffice to recover the Luttinger parameter and topological diagnostics. Theoretical justification provided for free-fermionic and free-bosonic systems, with investigation for interacting fermionic systems.
AI.conclusion: Phase decision via short-time dissipative cooling is a plausible target for utility-scale studies on early fault-tolerant quantum devices.

title: Linear and nonlinear optical torque in multi-level atomic systems driven by counter-rotating orbital angular momentum fields
summary: We investigate the generation of optical torque in coherently prepared multi-level atomic media driven by a vector vortex beam composed of two counter-rotating components carrying opposite orbital angular momenta, $+l\hbar$ and $-l\hbar$. We consider a three-level $Λ$ configuration and a four-level tripod configuration. Using a perturbative steady-state solution of the optical Bloch equations, we obtain analytical expressions for both linear and nonlinear contributions to the optical torque. The results show that the torque is strongly controlled by atomic coherence, including the initial population imbalance and the relative phase between the vortex components. Nonvanishing torque can arise even when the two components have equal amplitudes, due to coherence-induced asymmetry in the atomic response. In the tripod configuration, the presence of a strong control field leads to electromagnetically induced transparency, which suppresses the torque near resonance and shifts the dominant response to finite detunings. These results establish a route for controlling light-induced rotational dynamics in atomic media using vector vortex fields, with potential applications in coherent optical manipulation and angular-momentum-based control in quantum systems.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates optical torque generation in multi-level atomic media using vector vortex beams with counter-rotating orbital angular momenta. Analytical solutions for optical torque in Λ-type and tripod-type atomic configurations are derived, showing strong control by atomic coherence, initial population imbalance, and relative phase. In the tripod configuration, electromagnetically induced transparency suppresses resonant torque and shifts dominant response to finite detunings.
AI.motivation: To understand and control optical torque generation in multi-level atomic systems using vector vortex beams, enabling coherent optical manipulation and angular-momentum-based control in quantum systems.
AI.method: Perturbative steady-state solution of the optical Bloch equations for three-level Λ and four-level tripod atomic configurations, driven by a vector vortex beam with two counter-rotating components carrying opposite OAM (+lℏ and -lℏ). Analytical expressions for linear and nonlinear torque contributions are derived.
AI.result: Optical torque is strongly controlled by atomic coherence, initial population imbalance, and relative phase between vortex components. Nonvanishing torque arises even with equal-amplitude components due to coherence-induced asymmetry. In the tripod configuration, EIT suppresses resonant torque and shifts the dominant response to finite detunings.
AI.conclusion: The results establish a route for controlling light-induced rotational dynamics in atomic media using vector vortex fields, with potential applications in coherent optical manipulation and angular-momentum-based control in quantum systems.

title: Bipartite Gaussian Boson Sampling for Hamiltonian Cycles in Directed Graphs
summary: Bipartite Gaussian boson sampling (BipartiteGBS) produces output probabilities governed by squared permanents of submatrices of arbitrary complex matrices, matching the nonsymmetric structure of directed graphs. Most GBS-based graph algorithms, however, rely on symmetric hafnian structure and are formulated for undirected problems. Here we propose a BipartiteGBS-based framework for directed-graph heuristic optimization. We introduce Max-Perm as a canonical optimization task for BipartiteGBS and derive a closed-form sampling enhancement factor relative to uniform classical sampling in this idealized setting. We then use permanent-biased BipartiteGBS samples to guide a genetic algorithm for the celebrated directed Hamiltonian cycle problem. Numerical experiments on Erdős--Rényi random directed graphs show that the resulting BipartiteGBS-enhanced algorithms improve success rates over a standard genetic algorithm and yield longer valid paths when no Hamiltonian cycle is found, while ablation tests indicate that BipartiteGBS-guided initialization is the dominant contributor. These results show how permanent-based photonic sampling can provide useful algorithmic guidance for asymmetric combinatorial search.

AI.tldr: Bipartite Gaussian boson sampling (BipartiteGBS) is used to solve directed-graph optimization problems, specifically the Hamiltonian cycle problem, by leveraging permanent-biased samples to guide a genetic algorithm, achieving improved success rates and longer valid paths compared to a standard genetic algorithm on random directed graphs.
AI.motivation: Existing GBS-based graph algorithms rely on symmetric hafnian structures for undirected problems, but many real-world problems involve directed (asymmetric) graphs. The authors aim to extend GBS to directed-graph heuristic optimization using BipartiteGBS, which naturally captures the nonsymmetric structure of directed graphs via squared permanents of submatrices of arbitrary complex matrices.
AI.method: The authors propose Max-Perm as a canonical optimization task for BipartiteGBS and derive a closed-form sampling enhancement factor. They then integrate permanent-biased BipartiteGBS samples as initialization for a genetic algorithm targeting the directed Hamiltonian cycle problem.
AI.result: Experiments on Erdős–Rényi random directed graphs show that BipartiteGBS-enhanced genetic algorithms improve success rates over standard genetic algorithms and yield longer valid paths when no Hamiltonian cycle exists. Ablation tests confirm that BipartiteGBS-guided initialization is the dominant factor behind the improvement.
AI.conclusion: Permanent-based photonic sampling (BipartiteGBS) can provide useful algorithmic guidance for asymmetric combinatorial search problems, demonstrating a practical application of quantum-inspired sampling to directed graph optimization.

title: Properties of 2D Electron or Hole Gases at Tailored s-Si/SiGe Interfaces: A First-Principles Investigation
comment: Submitted to Advanced Functional Materials (Wiley). 17 pages 9 figures
summary: We have performed first-principles hybrid density functional theory calculations to study the formation and properties of two-dimensional electron or hole gases (2DEG or 2DHG) at s-Si/SiGe interfaces. For small Ge concentrations $x < 0.25$, we find a novel type of band alignment with no offset in the conduction bands, implying that a 2DEG cannot be formed, though a 2DHG can. In contrast, for $x > 0.25$ the band alignment suggests that either a 2DEG or 2DHG can be formed. The electronic band structure features two nearly degenerate 2DEG states at the bottom of the conduction bands, and two 2DHG states at the top of the valence band. These states can be accessed by appropriate doping and gating. Charge density plots of these states show that they feature carriers confined to the near vicinity (2--3 atomic layers) of the interface. Calculated effective masses are anisotropic, being markedly so for the 2DHG states, and in excellent agreement with experiment. This property can be exploited to create a 1D carrier gas. Our results are especially important for s-Si/SiGe-based semiconducting spin qubits for quantum computing applications.

AI.tldr: First-principles hybrid DFT calculations reveal that at s-Si/SiGe interfaces, a 2DEG cannot form for Ge concentration x < 0.25 due to no conduction band offset, while both 2DEG and 2DHG can form for x > 0.25. The confined carrier states are within 2-3 atomic layers of the interface with anisotropic effective masses, and can be exploited for 1D carrier gases, relevant for spin qubit quantum computing.
AI.motivation: To understand the formation and properties of 2DEG and 2DHG at s-Si/SiGe interfaces using first-principles hybrid DFT, to clarify conditions for carrier confinement and assess suitability for quantum computing applications.
AI.method: First-principles hybrid density functional theory calculations.
AI.result: For x < 0.25, no conduction band offset exists (2DEG impossible, 2DHG possible). For x > 0.25, both 2DEG and 2DHG can form. Two nearly degenerate 2DEG states at conduction band bottom and two 2DHG states at valence band top are found, with carriers confined to 2-3 atomic layers near the interface. Effective masses are anisotropic, especially for 2DHG, agreeing well with experiment.
AI.conclusion: The anisotropic effective masses and confined nature of carriers at s-Si/SiGe interfaces can be exploited to create 1D carrier gases, with important implications for semiconducting spin qubits in quantum computing.

title: A unified framework for determining transition dipole polarization in solid-state spin defects
summary: Spin-photon interfaces based on solid-state defects are key building blocks for scalable quantum networks and hybrid quantum platforms. Optimizing light-matter coupling in these systems requires precise knowledge of the optical transition dipole polarization, yet for many promising quantum emitters this quantity is hard to determine and therefore remains poorly characterized. Here, we develop a framework for reconstructing electric transition dipole polarization in spin-1/2 solid-state defects directly from ensemble spectroscopy. The approach combines the response of photoluminescence spectra to magnetic field, optical polarization, and strain. Applied to erbium ions in silicon, a particularly challenging system containing multiple crystallographic subsites, the framework identifies strain-induced shifts as the origin of asymmetric ensemble spectra and enables simultaneous determination of the optical dipole polarization and strain-orbital coupling tensor. The resulting model predicts how cavity-ion coupling depends on crystallographic orientation and magnetic-field direction, which we verify using single erbium ions coupled to a nanophotonic cavity. Together, these results establish a broadly applicable route for extracting microscopic properties of solid-state quantum emitters from ensemble spectroscopy and for engineering optimized spin-photon and spin-phonon interfaces.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a framework to reconstruct electric transition dipole polarization in spin-1/2 solid-state defects from ensemble spectroscopy, combining magnetic field, optical polarization, and strain responses. Applied to erbium ions in silicon, it identifies strain-induced shifts as the cause of asymmetric spectra and determines dipole polarization and strain-orbital coupling. Predictions are verified with single ions in nanophotonic cavities, enabling optimized spin-photon and spin-phonon interfaces.
AI.motivation: Optimizing light-matter coupling in solid-state defect-based spin-photon interfaces requires precise knowledge of optical transition dipole polarization, but this quantity is hard to determine and poorly characterized for many promising quantum emitters.
AI.method: A framework that reconstructs electric transition dipole polarization from ensemble spectroscopy by combining the response of photoluminescence spectra to magnetic field, optical polarization, and strain. Applied to erbium ions in silicon.
AI.result: The framework identifies strain-induced shifts as the origin of asymmetric ensemble spectra and enables simultaneous determination of optical dipole polarization and strain-orbital coupling tensor. Predictions of cavity-ion coupling dependence on crystallographic orientation and magnetic-field direction are verified using single erbium ions coupled to a nanophotonic cavity.
AI.conclusion: Establishes a broadly applicable route for extracting microscopic properties of solid-state quantum emitters from ensemble spectroscopy and for engineering optimized spin-photon and spin-phonon interfaces.

title: Quantum Variational Approaches to the Maximum Independent Set Problem at Utility Scale
summary: We study variational quantum algorithms for the Maximum Independent Set (MIS) problem on benchmark graphs of 64, 99, and 180 vertices. The Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) and Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) are compared across SPSA and COBYLA optimizers at multiple circuit depths. A preprocessing pipeline comprising spectral graph reordering (via the Fiedler vector) and distance-based sparsification reduces circuit depth while preserving energy fidelity. Classical post-processing via history-guided bitstring correction and stepwise maximality extension recovers the exact MIS across all instances. With CVaR optimization, VQE with SPSArecovers up to 6 distinct MIS per run for the 64-node instance and up to 10 distinct MIS per run for the 99-node instance, sampling broadly from the optimal solution population. Repeated runs with different SPSA trajectories collectively enumerate a larger fraction of all MIS for each instance. For the 180-node instance, where standard approaches stall at size 14 (MIS is 15), we introduce ancilla-assisted superposition initialization: ancilla qubits prepare a uniform superposition over classically-found near-optimal solutions, and an excitation-preserving ansatz evolves this state while conserving Hamming weight. This novel construction enables quantum-parallel variational search over multiple seeds simultaneously, discovering the exact MIS where single-seed methods fail. The 180-qubit simulation represents, to our knowledge, the largest scale at which gate-based variational algorithms have solved MIS to optimality.
