Hardware validation on IBM Quantum hardware ibm_marrakesh confirms that converged simulator parameters transfer effectively to noisy quantum execution.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that variational quantum algorithms (VQE and QAOA) with preprocessing (spectral graph reordering, distance-based sparsification), classical post-processing (history-guided bitstring correction, maximality extension), and ancilla-assisted superposition initialization can solve the Maximum Independent Set problem on graphs up to 180 vertices to optimality, representing the largest gate-based variational quantum MIS solution to date.
AI.motivation: To scale variational quantum algorithms for the Maximum Independent Set problem to larger graph instances (up to 180 vertices) where standard approaches fail, by combining classical preprocessing, post-processing, and novel quantum initialization techniques.
AI.method: Compared VQE and QAOA with SPSA and COBYLA optimizers at multiple circuit depths on graphs of 64, 99, and 180 vertices. Used spectral graph reordering (Fiedler vector) and distance-based sparsification as preprocessing. Applied history-guided bitstring correction and stepwise maximality extension as classical post-processing. Introduced ancilla-assisted superposition initialization with excitation-preserving ansatz for the 180-node instance to enable quantum-parallel variational search over multiple near-optimal seeds.
AI.result: VQE with SPSA and CVaR optimization recovers up to 6 distinct MIS per run for 64-node and up to 10 for 99-node graphs. The ancilla-assisted approach discovers the exact MIS (size 15) for the 180-node instance where single-seed methods stall at size 14. Hardware validation on IBM quantum hardware confirms simulator-to-hardware parameter transferability.
AI.conclusion: Variational quantum algorithms enhanced with classical preprocessing and post-processing, plus ancilla-assisted superposition initialization for hard instances, can solve MIS optimally on graphs up to 180 vertices, setting a new scale record for gate-based variational quantum optimization.

title: Kinetics of electron-phonon scattering in silicon resolved by Rydberg transitions of donors
summary: Rydberg states of atoms in vacuum are now well recognized as a resource for quantum technologies. Donors in semiconductors also display analogous states, which have been proposed for similar applications. While they benefit from permanent locations in their host crystals, electron-lattice coupling leads to much shorter excited-state lifetimes than for neutral atoms in vacuum. Here we provide a quantitative description of donor-phonon kinetics, creating a basis for engineering donor systems in realistic material stacks for quantum devices. Our theory incorporates both form factors for the Rydberg states, which given their large extents in real space provide strong selectivity in momentum space, and tabulated deformation potentials for all six phonon branches throughout the Brillouin zone. By confronting this framework with carefully controlled time-resolved free electron laser measurements, we show that the widely quoted position of the silicon conduction band minimum, $k_0$, is inconsistent with observed donor relaxation rates and that quantitative agreement is obtained for a value further from the X-point than commonly assumed. This stringent experiment-theory comparison establishes donor relaxation as a precision metrology for conduction band parameters and scattering processes in silicon, with consequences spanning from quantum devices to classical electronics.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a quantitative theory of donor-phonon kinetics in silicon, incorporating Rydberg state form factors and deformation potentials for all phonon branches. Combined with time-resolved free electron laser measurements, the study reveals that the commonly accepted conduction band minimum k0 is inconsistent with observed donor relaxation rates, and achieves agreement with a revised value. This establishes donor relaxation as a precision metrology tool for silicon conduction band parameters and scattering processes.
AI.motivation: To provide a quantitative description of donor-phonon kinetics in semiconductors, enabling engineering of donor systems in realistic material stacks for quantum devices, and to resolve inconsistencies between theoretical predictions and experimental observations of donor excited-state lifetimes.
AI.method: The theory incorporates form factors for Rydberg donor states (exploiting their large real-space extent for strong momentum-space selectivity) and tabulated deformation potentials for all six phonon branches across the Brillouin zone. The framework is tested against carefully controlled time-resolved free electron laser measurements of donor relaxation rates.
AI.result: The widely quoted position of the silicon conduction band minimum k0 is inconsistent with observed donor relaxation rates. Quantitative agreement is achieved with a value further from the X-point than commonly assumed.
AI.conclusion: This stringent experiment-theory comparison establishes donor relaxation as a precision metrology technique for conduction band parameters and scattering processes in silicon, with implications for both quantum devices and classical electronics.

title: A High-Performance Pauli-Algebra Framework for Large-Scale Quantum Simulations
summary: Efficient manipulation of Pauli-algebraic objects is a key bottleneck in the classical emulation and benchmarking of quantum algorithms for chemistry and many-body physics. This bottleneck appears in Hamiltonian construction, variational ansatz preparation, expectation-value and gradient evaluation, and real-time propagation, all of which require repeated Pauli-algebra operations. Here, we present a high-performance Pauli-algebra framework tailored to quantum many-body and quantum-chemical simulations. The framework combines compact binary symplectic encoding, canonical coefficient reduction, and grouped sparse operator representations that exploit shared bit-flip patterns among Pauli strings. The resulting Julia/C\texttt{++} implementation accelerates Pauli multiplication, Hamiltonian construction, and operator--state multiplication in sparse and symmetry-adapted many-electron spaces. Benchmarks demonstrate efficient Hamiltonian construction, large-active-space VQE and ADAPT-VQE calculations, and real-time variational dynamics on modern multicore CPU and GPU architectures. These results show that structure-aware Pauli-algebra engines provide a scalable classical backend for developing and benchmarking quantum algorithms in quantum chemistry and many-body simulation.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a high-performance Pauli-algebra framework using binary symplectic encoding, canonical coefficient reduction, and grouped sparse operator representations to accelerate quantum many-body and quantum-chemical simulations on classical hardware.
AI.motivation: Efficient manipulation of Pauli-algebraic objects is a key bottleneck in classical emulation and benchmarking of quantum algorithms for chemistry and many-body physics, particularly in Hamiltonian construction, variational ansatz preparation, expectation-value/gradient evaluation, and real-time propagation.
AI.method: The framework combines compact binary symplectic encoding, canonical coefficient reduction, and grouped sparse operator representations that exploit shared bit-flip patterns among Pauli strings, implemented in Julia/C++.
AI.result: Accelerates Pauli multiplication, Hamiltonian construction, and operator-state multiplication in sparse and symmetry-adapted many-electron spaces, with efficient performance on modern multicore CPU and GPU architectures for VQE, ADAPT-VQE, and real-time variational dynamics.
AI.conclusion: Structure-aware Pauli-algebra engines provide a scalable classical backend for developing and benchmarking quantum algorithms in quantum chemistry and many-body simulation.

title: Tracking Entanglement Transfer: Emergence of Thermodynamics from Quantum Information
summary: We study entanglement transfer in a minimal model of two qubits that are coupled with one another through an antiferromagnetic Heisenberg exchange ($\tilde{J}$), and where one of them is additionally coupled to a fermionic environment through another antiferromagnetic Heisenberg exchange ($J_{K}$). By tuning the coupling ratio $J_{K}/\tilde{J}$, the system undergoes a quantum phase transition at $T=0$, accompanied by a redistribution of entanglement from the $d'-d$ qubit-subsystem to the environment. Remarkably, the resulting physics exhibits properties that bear analogy with a quantum-information theoretic perspective of the physics of black hole thermodynamics. Carefully selected bipartite and tripartite mutual information measures displays behaviour analogous to the dynamical evolution of black hole entropy, Hawking entropy, and the Page curve expected during the process of evaporation. An effective temperature scale is obtained from the variation of the ground state energy with respect to changes in the bipartite mutual information between the subsystem and the bath. A steady growth of this temperature with the coupling ratio resembles that of the Hawking temperature with the inverse mass of the black hole. Concomitantly, the emergence of non-Fermi liquid behaviour observed near the quantum critical point and in the strong-coupling phase resembles strange-metal-like physics expected near the event horizon from a holographic duality perspective. Our results establish the minimal model as a platform for studying entanglement transfer and information scrambling within a fully unitary quantum framework, and offer new insights into a resolution of the black hole information paradox.

AI.tldr: A minimal two-qubit model coupled via antiferromagnetic Heisenberg exchange to each other and to a fermionic environment exhibits a quantum phase transition where entanglement redistributes from the qubit subsystem to the environment, showing analogies to black hole thermodynamics, Hawking radiation, Page curve behavior, and strange-metal physics, offering insights into the black hole information paradox.
AI.motivation: To study entanglement transfer and information scrambling in a minimal unitary quantum framework, and to explore analogies with black hole thermodynamics and the black hole information paradox.
AI.method: A minimal model of two qubits coupled via antiferromagnetic Heisenberg exchange (J̃), with one qubit additionally coupled to a fermionic environment (J_K). Bipartite and tripartite mutual information measures are used to analyze entanglement redistribution as a function of the coupling ratio J_K/J̃.
AI.result: A quantum phase transition occurs at T=0 as J_K/J̃ is tuned, redistributing entanglement from the qubit subsystem to the environment. Mutual information measures mimic black hole entropy, Hawking entropy, and the Page curve. An effective temperature scales similarly to Hawking temperature. Non-Fermi liquid behavior emerges near the quantum critical point, resembling strange-metal physics from holographic duality.
AI.conclusion: The minimal two-qubit model serves as a platform for studying entanglement transfer and information scrambling within a fully unitary framework, offering new insights toward resolving the black hole information paradox.

title: Quantum Primitive for Output-Hiding Function Sharing: QKD and Joint Computation Applications
summary: Applications of the proposed primitive: Quantum Primitive for Output-Hiding Function Sharing, are discussed for secure quantum communications and computation protocols. In particular, QKD applications provide notable enhanced security and efficiency properties relative to status-quo protocols. Additionally, we provide examples when parties may wish to encode joint functions, or decisions, which remain information-theoretically hidden from external parties and those internal to the quantum system, without additional private keys, hidden randomness, or classical communication. In particular these applications may be useful in domains such as; financial transactions, joint signaling or coordination decisions, and navigation systems, among others.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a quantum primitive for output-hiding function sharing, with applications in secure quantum communication and computation. It offers enhanced QKD security/efficiency and enables information-theoretically hidden joint functions without extra keys, randomness, or classical communication, applicable to finance, coordination, and navigation.
AI.motivation: To develop a quantum primitive that allows parties to share and hide output functions information-theoretically from both external and internal parties, without relying on additional private keys, hidden randomness, or classical communication.
AI.method: Proposes a quantum primitive for output-hiding function sharing, analyzed in the context of QKD and other secure quantum protocols.
AI.result: The primitive provides notably enhanced security and efficiency for QKD compared to status-quo protocols, and enables information-theoretically hidden joint function encoding without additional resources.
AI.conclusion: The proposed primitive is useful for secure quantum communications and computation, with applications in financial transactions, joint signaling/coordination decisions, and navigation systems.

title: Quantum Primitive for Output-Hiding Function Sharing: Strategic Settings
summary: Applications of the proposed primitive: Quantum Primitive for Output-Hiding Function Sharing are discussed for environments in which the parties may have strategic considerations over the generated function value, and therefore may not be mutually trusted. We show that in environments in which the measurement may not be reliably controlled by either party, the primitive permits the parties to generate private, unbiased coins.

AI.tldr: This paper discusses applications of a quantum primitive for output-hiding function sharing, enabling private, unbiased coin generation in environments with strategic parties and unreliable measurement control.
AI.motivation: To address scenarios where parties have strategic considerations over generated function values and may not be mutually trusted, requiring a primitive that ensures fairness and privacy.
AI.method: The proposed quantum primitive for output-hiding function sharing is applied to environments where measurement may not be reliably controlled by either party.
AI.result: The primitive permits parties to generate private, unbiased coins in distrustful environments.
AI.conclusion: The quantum primitive enables secure function sharing with output privacy, supporting unbiased randomness generation even when parties are mutually untrusted and measurement control is unreliable.

title: Quantifying Quantum Correlations in Annihilation Photon Pairs under Compton Scattering
summary: We present a theoretical study of the evolution of polarization entanglement and quantum coherence in 511 keV photon pairs produced by para-positronium decay during successive Compton scattering events. We start with a maximally entangled Bell state and employ the generalized Stokes-Mueller formalism to derive the two-photon density matrix following single-, double-, and triple-Compton scattering, explicitly considering both polar and azimuthal scattering geometries. Using this framework, we quantify the degradation of quantum correlations through concurrence (as a measure of entanglement) and the $l_1$-norm (as a measure of coherence). Our results demonstrate that entanglement is highly sensitive to the scattering geometry and disappears near right-angle scattering, while quantum coherence remains finite even in regimes where entanglement vanishes completely. These findings provide a unified description of polarization-dependent decoherence in annihilation photon pairs and clarify the distinct roles of entanglement and coherence in realistic two-photon interactions. These results are relevant for quantum-enhanced positron emission tomography and highlight the persistence of quantum resources in scattering-dominated media.

AI.tldr: This paper theoretically studies how polarization entanglement and quantum coherence degrade in 511 keV photon pairs from para-positronium decay through successive Compton scattering events, showing that entanglement is highly geometry-dependent and vanishes at right-angle scattering while coherence persists.
AI.motivation: To understand how realistic Compton scattering processes degrade quantum correlations (entanglement and coherence) in annihilation photon pairs, which is important for applications like quantum-enhanced positron emission tomography.
AI.method: The authors start with a maximally entangled Bell state from para-positronium decay, use the generalized Stokes-Mueller formalism to derive the two-photon density matrix after single-, double-, and triple-Compton scattering, and quantify degradation via concurrence (entanglement) and l₁-norm (coherence).
AI.result: Entanglement is highly sensitive to scattering geometry and disappears near right-angle scattering; quantum coherence remains finite even when entanglement is completely lost.
AI.conclusion: The findings provide a unified description of polarization-dependent decoherence in annihilation photon pairs, clarify the distinct roles of entanglement versus coherence, and highlight the persistence of quantum resources in scattering-dominated media relevant to quantum-enhanced PET.

title: Exact Hilbert-space ergodicity from continuous monitoring
summary: Quantum evolution is generally expected to drive a quantum many-body system toward equilibrium. This expectation is often justified by the Hilbert-space ergodicity of generic quantum dynamics, namely, the idea that pure-state evolution explores Hilbert space uniformly up to physical constraints. Such a statement can be made rigorous by requiring the associated state ensemble to form the Haar-random ensemble, or its more structured generalization, the Scrooge ensemble. In this Letter, we report the emergence of exact Hilbert-space ergodicity in a continuously monitored quantum many-body system. For any target density matrix $σ$, we construct a continuously monitored system for which we rigorously prove that the Scrooge ensemble of $σ$ is the unique late-time equilibrium distribution of quantum trajectories. Remarkably, this requires only that the jump operators in the monitoring form a deformed unitary 1-design, a seemingly much weaker condition than full ergodicity. We numerically demonstrate our predictions by simulating continuously monitored systems whose equilibrium states are thermal states. Our results establish a rigorous mechanism for the emergence of Hilbert-space ergodicity and provide a practical route for its investigation on quantum devices.

AI.tldr: This paper proves that continuously monitored quantum many-body systems can achieve exact Hilbert-space ergodicity, where the late-time equilibrium distribution of quantum trajectories converges to the Scrooge ensemble of any target density matrix σ, requiring only that the jump operators form a deformed unitary 1-design—a much weaker condition than full ergodicity. Numerical demonstrations with thermal equilibrium states confirm the predictions.
AI.motivation: To establish a rigorous mechanism for the emergence of Hilbert-space ergodicity in quantum many-body systems under continuous monitoring, and to show that full ergodicity (Haar-random or Scrooge ensemble) can arise from surprisingly weak conditions.
AI.method: The authors construct a continuously monitored system for any target density matrix σ and rigorously prove that the Scrooge ensemble of σ is the unique late-time equilibrium distribution of quantum trajectories, under the condition that the jump operators form a deformed unitary 1-design. Numerical simulations of thermal equilibrium states are used to support the analytical results.
AI.result: Exact Hilbert-space ergodicity (Scrooge ensemble) emerges at late times in continuously monitored systems, requiring only deformed unitary 1-design jump operators rather than full ergodicity conditions. Numerical simulations confirm the predictions for thermal equilibrium states.
AI.conclusion: The results establish a rigorous mechanism for Hilbert-space ergodicity in monitored quantum systems and offer a practical route for investigating ergodicity on quantum devices.

title: Localized Covariant Quantities Appear To Underlie Quantum Circuits
summary: Although entangled state vectors cannot be fully described in terms of variables localized in space and time, any given entanglement experiment can be built from basic quantum circuit components with well-defined locations. We analyze such quantum circuits and present evidence that the local weak values comprise a covariant tensor associated with each individual qubit. Even if the state is massively entangled, these tensors do not evolve or collapse when other qubits are measured or pass through distant circuit elements. They can therefore be viewed from different reference frames without contradiction. Furthermore, their evolution through any circuit always obeys covariant dynamical rules. Weak values are subject to both past and future constraints, so the covariant quantities can only be determined by considering the entire circuit "all-at-once", as in action principles, incorporating the future measurement basis to avoid the standard no-go theorems. Because these results hold for a set of universal quantum gates, this work lends support to the claim that any quantum circuit can be assigned a realistic, lower-level description compatible with our understanding of classical spacetime.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that local weak values form covariant tensors for individual qubits in quantum circuits, which do not collapse when other qubits are measured, and evolve via covariant dynamics determined by the entire circuit "all-at-once," suggesting a realistic lower-level description compatible with classical spacetime.
AI.motivation: To reconcile quantum entanglement (which resists local description) with classical spacetime intuition by showing that local weak values can provide a realistic, covariant description of individual qubits in any quantum circuit.
AI.method: Analysis of quantum circuits using weak values as covariant tensors associated with each qubit, considering the entire circuit "all-at-once" (action principle perspective) and incorporating future measurement bases to avoid no-go theorems.
AI.result: Local weak values behave as covariant tensors that do not collapse upon measurement of other qubits, obey covariant dynamical rules, and require knowledge of the full circuit (past and future) for determination, supporting a realistic spacetime-compatible description.
AI.conclusion: Any quantum circuit may admit a realistic, lower-level description compatible with classical spacetime, as evidenced by the covariant behavior of local weak values across universal quantum gates.

title: Shadow tomography for classical tensor network simulations
summary: Shadow tomography has appeared as a powerful tool for estimating observables on quantum computers from a small number of samples. We show that shadow-tomography-inspired ideas can offer similarly improved sample scaling for estimating observables on tensor network states on classical computers after proper adaptation. We develop strategies for both spin (bosonic) and fermionic systems, tailored to the contraction requirements of tensor networks, and generate scaling improvements of factors of $O(N)$ to $O(N^{3})$ (where $N$ is system size), depending on the specific task and system type. For the important and difficult task of evaluating the expectation value of long-range interacting Hamiltonians, we achieve the optimal $O(1)$ overall scaling (up to logarithmic factors) for an arbitrarily fixed relative Monte Carlo error in both spin and fermionic systems. Additionally, we show that shadow estimators offer more stable gradients of observables in variational optimization tasks than standard Monte Carlo estimators. We demonstrate practical advantage by simulating systems with long-range interactions, including the 2D long-range Heisenberg model and an ab-initio quantum chemistry Hamiltonian.

AI.tldr: Shadow tomography techniques adapted for classical tensor network simulations achieve O(N) to O(N³) sample scaling improvements for estimating observables, with optimal O(1) scaling for long-range Hamiltonians and more stable gradients in variational optimization.
AI.motivation: To improve sample efficiency of estimating observables on tensor network states on classical computers, inspired by shadow tomography methods originally developed for quantum computers.
AI.method: Adapt shadow-tomography-inspired estimators to tensor network contractions for both spin (bosonic) and fermionic systems, designing tailored sampling strategies.
AI.result: Achieves O(N) to O(N³) scaling improvements depending on task; optimal O(1) scaling (up to log factors) for long-range interacting Hamiltonians; more stable gradients in variational optimization; demonstrated on 2D long-range Heisenberg model and ab-initio quantum chemistry Hamiltonian.
AI.conclusion: Shadow tomography ideas can be effectively ported to classical tensor network simulations, yielding significant sample complexity improvements and practical advantage for challenging many-body systems.

title: Quantum scrambling of algebras of observables: the $\mathbb{Z}_2$-symmetric case
summary: We consider unitary quantum scrambling for an entire class of observable algebras $\mathcal A$ whose commutant ${\mathcal A}'=\mathbb{C}\mathbb{Z}_2$ is generated by a Hermitian involution $S$, i.e., a parity operator. We adopt two different, although related, scrambling measures: (a) the algebraic out-of-time-order correlator (A-OTOC) introduced in [Andreadakis, Anand, and Zanardi, Phys. Rev. A 107, 042217 (2023)], and (b) a Slater-determinant-type quantity, dubbed the Plücker fidelity, obtained by embedding operator algebras into a higher-dimensional projective operator space. Both measures admit a simple geometric interpretation in terms of distances between algebras and their dynamical images. Moreover, they can be expressed in terms of the norm of the $\mathbb{Z}_2$-symmetry-breaking component of the unitary, which is in turn controlled by the time autocorrelation function of the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ generator $S$. We derive exact expressions for the A-OTOC and the Plücker fidelity in the general case, as well as their values for a random unitary. For Hamiltonian-generated channels, we compute their long-time averages, as well as the typical values of these long-time averages for random generators $S$. Finally, we numerically explore the results of our formalism for interacting spin chains in different phases and for different physical parity operators.

AI.tldr: The paper studies unitary quantum scrambling for observable algebras with a $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetry (parity operator $S$), using two measures: algebraic out-of-time-order correlator (A-OTOC) and Plücker fidelity. Both measures geometrically represent distances between algebras and their dynamical images, and are governed by the $\mathbb{Z}_2$-symmetry-breaking component of the unitary, controlled by the autocorrelation of $S$. Exact expressions, random unitary values, long-time averages, and numerical simulations for interacting spin chains are provided.
AI.motivation: To develop a unified theoretical framework for quantum scrambling that applies to an entire class of observable algebras with $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetry, and to relate scrambling measures to symmetry-breaking dynamics.
AI.method: The authors adopt two scrambling measures: (a) the algebraic out-of-time-order correlator (A-OTOC) and (b) the Plücker fidelity, a Slater-determinant-type quantity from embedding operator algebras into projective operator space. Both are expressed in terms of the norm of the $\mathbb{Z}_2$-symmetry-breaking component of the unitary, linked to the autocorrelation function of $S$. Theoretical derivations are complemented by random unitary analysis, long-time averaging, and numerical simulations on interacting spin chains.
AI.result: Exact expressions for both scrambling measures are derived. Their values for random unitaries, long-time averages, and typical values for random generators $S$ are obtained. Numerical simulations on interacting spin chains in different phases with various parity operators illustrate the formalism.
AI.conclusion: The A-OTOC and Plücker fidelity provide complementary geometric perspectives on quantum scrambling under $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetry, and their dynamics are governed by the symmetry-breaking component of the unitary evolution.

title: Gaussian quantum steering of coupled three-mode squeezed vacuum in an expanding universe
summary: The coupled three-mode squeezed vacuum is a representative multimode squeezed Gaussian state featuring unique steerability. This work investigates Gaussian quantum steering distributions of the coupled three-mode squeezed vacuum under an expanding universe. Due to causal separation between the interior and exterior spacetime regions, quantum information behind the event horizon is inaccessible to Alice, Bob and Charlie. We separately analyze steering behaviors for physically accessible and inaccessible modes. Our analysis shows that greater total mean photon number and momentum, combined with reduced expansion volume and expansion rate, enhance quantum steering strength. Notably, Gaussian quantum steering for physically inaccessible modes undergoes the "sudden death" phenomenon when a critical threshold parameter $φ$ is exceeded. These results deliver novel insights into quantum correlations in curved spacetime.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates Gaussian quantum steering distributions of the coupled three-mode squeezed vacuum in an expanding universe, showing that higher mean photon number/momentum and lower expansion volume/rate enhance steering, with inaccessible modes experiencing "sudden death" beyond a critical threshold.
AI.motivation: To understand how quantum steering, a key non-classical correlation, behaves in curved spacetime (expanding universe) where event horizons causally separate regions, making some quantum information inaccessible.
AI.method: The authors analyze Gaussian quantum steering in a coupled three-mode squeezed vacuum state under an expanding universe background, separately treating physically accessible modes (Alice, Bob, Charlie) and inaccessible modes (behind the event horizon) using covariance matrix formalism.
AI.result: (1) Higher total mean photon number and momentum enhance steering strength; (2) Reduced expansion volume and expansion rate also enhance steering; (3) Steering of physically inaccessible modes undergoes "sudden death" when a critical parameter φ is exceeded.
AI.conclusion: The results provide novel insights into quantum correlations in curved spacetime, revealing how expansion parameters critically affect steering distributions and the loss of quantum coherence across event horizons.

title: Rodeo Filtering for Direct Steady-State Estimation in Open Quantum Systems
summary: Computing non-equilibrium steady states of open quantum systems is a challenging task on conventional computers, motivating quantum algorithms for direct steady-state estimation. A natural route is to regard the steady state as the zero mode of the Liouvillian and to isolate this sector spectrally. We formulate this task as a known-zero-sector projection problem and implement the corresponding filter using the Rodeo algorithm, which performs stochastic spectral filtering through repeated controlled evolutions and measurement-conditioned filtering steps. In the steady-state setting, the filter can be centered directly at the known zero eigenvalue, avoiding the spectral search required in generic eigenstate preparation. Compared with a phase-estimation-based implementation of the same projection, the Rodeo approach enables restart on failure and reduces the target-error dependence of the filtering cost and controlled-evolution depth from power-law to logarithmic. This advantage becomes more pronounced as the spectral separation of the Hermitian Liouvillian embedding increases, allowing Rodeo filtering to outperform phase-estimation filtering already at modest controlled-evolution depths. Our results identify Rodeo filtering as a resource-efficient primitive for estimating steady-state observables in open quantum systems.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes using the Rodeo algorithm for spectral filtering to compute non-equilibrium steady states of open quantum systems, achieving logarithmic scaling in target-error dependence and controlled-evolution depth compared to phase-estimation-based approaches, with the advantage growing as spectral separation increases.
AI.motivation: Computing non-equilibrium steady states of open quantum systems is challenging on classical computers, motivating the need for efficient quantum algorithms for direct steady-state estimation without spectral search.
AI.method: The steady state is treated as the zero mode of the Liouvillian and isolated via the Rodeo algorithm, which performs stochastic spectral filtering through repeated controlled evolutions and measurement-conditioned filtering steps, centered directly at the known zero eigenvalue.
AI.result: Compared to phase-estimation-based projection, Rodeo filtering enables restart on failure and reduces the target-error dependence of filtering cost and controlled-evolution depth from power-law to logarithmic, with advantages becoming more pronounced as spectral separation of the Hermitian Liouvillian embedding increases.
AI.conclusion: Rodeo filtering is identified as a resource-efficient primitive for estimating steady-state observables in open quantum systems, outperforming phase-estimation filtering already at modest controlled-evolution depths.

title: Imaginary pseudo entropy encodes temporal orientation
summary: Pseudo entropy between quantum states at different times is generally complex, yet its imaginary part has lacked a bounded operational meaning. We show that a calibrated replica interferometer converts the pseudo-Rényi phase into a directly measurable record of transition orientation. Together with replica visibility, it exactly determines the trace distance between forward and backward ancilla outputs and hence the Helstrom-optimal single-shot success probability. At short times, the symmetrized covariance of the modular and physical Hamiltonians sets the initial distinguishability response. Under any common quantum channel, the corresponding orientation information can only decrease, with equality characterized by Petz recovery. Imaginary pseudo entropy therefore records a reversible distinction between temporal orientations, while coarse graining can make the loss of that record irreversible.

AI.tldr: Imaginary pseudo entropy between quantum states at different times, once calibrated via replica interferometry, provides a measurable record of temporal orientation reversibility, bounded by Helstrom-optimal distinguishability and governed by Petz recovery conditions.
AI.motivation: To give the imaginary part of pseudo entropy a bounded operational meaning, as it was previously known to be complex but lacked such interpretation.
AI.method: A calibrated replica interferometer is introduced to convert the pseudo-Rényi phase into a measurable record of transition orientation, combined with replica visibility to compute trace distance and Helstrom success probability.
AI.result: The symmetrized covariance of modular and physical Hamiltonians governs short-time distinguishability; orientation information decreases under common quantum channels, with equality characterized by Petz recovery.
AI.conclusion: Imaginary pseudo entropy records a reversible distinction between temporal orientations; coarse graining can make the loss of that record irreversible.

title: QmDFT for Polycyclic Aromatics: Balancing Embedding Ground-State Fidelity and Experimental Gap Estimation
summary:
Quantum Embedding density functional theory (QmDFT) embedding offers a highly scalable approach to improve treatment for large highly correlated pi conjugated systems. However, estimating advanced electronic structure properties in polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) needs advanced exchange correlation functionals that frequently trigger convergence instabilities during the embedding cycle.
  In this work, we introduce an adaptive damping and direct inversion in the iterative subspace (DIIS) accelerated protocol that stabilizes the embedding procedure, enabling robust integration of hybrid functionals like B3LYP and CAM B3LYP. Using 10 selected PAHs (linear and fused) molecules as a benchmark. We demonstrate a clear functional-dependent ground-state energetics and frontier-orbital gap estimation. While LDA based approaches yield near-quantitative agreement with FCI in DFT reference energies and is further supported by thermochemical isomerization benchmarks, while B3LYP provide significantly improved agreement with experimental E0-0 transition values. This mapping allows us to bypass explicit excited-state calculations for E0 0 values, thereby significantly reducing computational overhead.
  Among the hybrid functionals screened, CAM B3LYP offers a balanced overall performance. Our results establish a stable QmDFT framework and provide useful guidance for functional selection for quantum embedding studies of PAHs and related low-dimensional pi-conjugated materials.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces an adaptive damping and DIIS-accelerated protocol to stabilize QmDFT embedding for PAHs, enabling robust use of hybrid functionals. It shows LDA matches FCI reference energetics, B3LYP excels for E0-0 transitions, and CAM-B3LYP offers balanced overall performance, bypassing expensive excited-state calculations.
AI.motivation: Estimating advanced electronic structure properties in PAHs requires hybrid exchange-correlation functionals, but these frequently cause convergence instabilities during the QmDFT embedding cycle, motivating a stabilized protocol.
AI.method: An adaptive damping and DIIS-accelerated protocol was introduced to stabilize the QmDFT embedding procedure, enabling robust integration of hybrid functionals (B3LYP, CAM-B3LYP). Benchmarked on 10 selected PAHs (linear and fused) for ground-state energetics and frontier-orbital gaps.
AI.result: LDA-based approaches yield near-quantitative agreement with FCI reference energies and thermochemical isomerization benchmarks. B3LYP provides significantly improved agreement with experimental E0-0 transition values, allowing bypass of explicit excited-state calculations. CAM-B3LYP offers balanced overall performance among hybrid functionals.
AI.conclusion: A stable QmDFT framework is established with useful guidance for functional selection in quantum embedding studies of PAHs and related low-dimensional pi-conjugated materials.

title: Quantum algorithm for the nonlinear Schrödinger equation via the Lax-pair scattering
summary: The nonlinear Schrödinger equation (NLSE) governs a broad class of wave phenomena, including deep-water waves, quantum turbulence, and solitons. The multiscale spatiotemporal coupling inherent in these systems imposes severe computational bottlenecks on classical high-fidelity numerical simulations. While quantum computing offers the potential for exponential speedup, its unitary dynamics pose a fundamental challenge to solve the NLSE. We propose a quantum framework based on the Lax-pair scattering for solving the 1D NLSE. Specifically, the physical field is first mapped into the spectral space via a quantum direct scattering circuit. Following a decoupled linear time evolution, the physical solution is reconstructed through an inverse scattering transform utilizing the quantum singular value transformation. Since the temporal evolution is performed analytically in the scattering domain, the framework bypasses iterative time stepping, rendering it highly advantageous for long-time simulations. To demonstrate the accuracy and noise resilience of this approach, we simulate a Gaussian wave packet under quantum noise, two-soliton collisions, breather dynamics, and modulational instability on a quantum emulator.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a quantum computing framework for solving the 1D nonlinear Schrödinger equation using Lax-pair scattering, which maps the physical field to spectral space via quantum direct scattering, evolves analytically in the scattering domain (bypassing iterative time stepping), and reconstructs solutions via inverse scattering transform using quantum singular value transformation. Simulations on a quantum emulator demonstrate accuracy and noise resilience for Gaussian wave packets, soliton collisions, breather dynamics, and modulational instability.
AI.motivation: Classical high-fidelity simulations of NLSE face severe computational bottlenecks due to multiscale spatiotemporal coupling, while quantum computing's unitary dynamics pose a fundamental challenge for solving this nonlinear equation.
AI.method: A quantum framework based on Lax-pair scattering: (1) map physical field to spectral space via quantum direct scattering circuit, (2) perform decoupled linear time evolution analytically in the scattering domain, (3) reconstruct physical solution via inverse scattering transform using quantum singular value transformation.
AI.result: The framework was validated on a quantum emulator for Gaussian wave packets under quantum noise, two-soliton collisions, breather dynamics, and modulational instability, demonstrating accuracy and noise resilience.
AI.conclusion: By performing temporal evolution analytically in the scattering domain, the framework bypasses iterative time stepping, making it highly advantageous for long-time simulations and noise-resilient quantum computation of nonlinear wave phenomena.

title: Private training in quantum machine learning
summary: With the emergence of machine learning (ML) models trained on large datasets containing potentially sensitive data, a major question in AI safety is how to make learning private with respect to the training data. Similar to classical machine learning, quantum machine learning (QML) models are not devoid of privacy vulnerabilities. Differential privacy (DP) is a standard tool for training ML models on sensitive data, but its impact in QML remains poorly understood. In this work we study private training in hybrid variational QML models using a classical private DP-SGD optimizer applied to pipelines with classical inputs and outputs. We analyze the interplay between gradient clipping and calibrated noise addition in DP-SGD, and its impact on optimization and accuracy for noisy and noiseless quantum models. We first explain why quantum noise does not provide a satisfactory replacement for the calibrated noise in DP-SGD for ensuring privacy. We then show how the deterministic bounds on gradient norms for a wide class of quantum models translate into explicit control of the detrimental clipping bias introduced by DP-SGD. Finally, we formulate a numerical comparison protocol under fixed clipping threshold and privacy budget and evaluate it on synthetic and image-classification tasks for equivalent quantum and classical models. Our results suggest that quantum models can retain higher accuracy in private-training regimes where the formal privacy guarantee is ensured by a classical DP-SGD mechanism.

AI.tldr: This paper studies private training in hybrid variational quantum machine learning models using the classical DP-SGD optimizer. It analyzes how quantum noise interacts with differential privacy mechanisms, shows that deterministic gradient norm bounds in quantum models help control clipping bias, and demonstrates that quantum models retain higher accuracy than classical models under formal DP guarantees.
AI.motivation: To understand how differential privacy (DP) mechanisms impact quantum machine learning (QML) models, and to investigate whether quantum noise or quantum model properties can provide advantages for private training compared to classical ML.
AI.method: Hybrid variational QML models trained with classical DP-SGD optimizer; analysis of gradient clipping and calibrated noise addition; comparison of quantum vs classical models on synthetic and image-classification tasks under fixed privacy budget and clipping threshold.
AI.result: Quantum noise does not replace calibrated DP noise; deterministic gradient norm bounds in quantum models reduce clipping bias; quantum models retain higher accuracy than classical counterparts under equivalent DP guarantees.
AI.conclusion: Quantum models can achieve better accuracy than classical models in private training regimes where formal privacy is enforced by classical DP-SGD, suggesting a practical advantage for QML in privacy-sensitive applications.

title: Volume Law and Universality of Entanglement Entropy in Random Graph Fermi Systems
summary: We study the ground-state entanglement entropy of free fermions on the Erdős--Rényi random graph, where each of the possible edges is present independently with some probability. Using random matrix theory and asymptotic freeness, we prove that the ground-state entanglement entropy obeys an exact volume law in the thermodynamic limit. The entanglement density, with a universal coefficient that is independent of the edge probability and the microscopic details of the graph. This coefficient is confirmed numerically to take the value approximately $0.386$ nats, strictly below the Page value. The volume law therefore reflects the absence of geometric locality in the random graph.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that ground-state entanglement entropy of free fermions on Erdős–Rényi random graphs follows an exact volume law with a universal coefficient ~0.386 nats (below the Page value), independent of edge probability and microscopic details.
AI.motivation: To understand entanglement entropy behavior in non-geometric, random graph systems lacking spatial locality, contrasting with area-law scaling typical in local geometries.
AI.method: Uses random matrix theory and asymptotic freeness to analytically derive the entanglement entropy scaling in the thermodynamic limit.
AI.result: Ground-state entanglement entropy obeys an exact volume law with universal coefficient ~0.386 nats, confirmed numerically, independent of edge probability.
AI.conclusion: The volume law reflects the absence of geometric locality; the universal coefficient is strictly below the Page value, indicating distinct entanglement structure in random graphs.

title: Intrinsic Indistinguishability of Identical Particles and How Particle Labels Affect It
comment: Main text of 5 pages; Appendices A-E of 15 pages in total; one figure is divided into two independent parts
summary: We investigate indistinguishability of identical bosons and fermions undergoing arbitrary particle-number-preserving evolutions of their visible degrees of freedom. For the projective indistinguishability measure, defined by the projection of the visible state onto the symmetric/anti-symmetric subspace, we derive an equivalent expression in terms of the dynamically invariant internal state. We further generalize the textbook symmetrization/anti-symmetrization framework for bosons and fermions to arbitrary partial distinguishability by deriving an explicit reconstruction formula for the multiparticle visible state in terms of the indistinguishability function encoding the dynamical invariants. We give complete characterization of the class-functions of indistinguishability by projective measures on generalized symmetries. Finally, we reveal a strikingly counterintuitive effect: introducing additional particle label states can increase the multiparticle indistinguishability of identical particles. The effect originates from the cancellation of collective multiparticle phases.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates indistinguishability of identical bosons and fermions under particle-number-preserving evolutions, derives an equivalent expression for the projective indistinguishability measure in terms of internal state, generalizes symmetrization framework to partial distinguishability, characterizes class-functions of indistinguishability, and reveals a counterintuitive effect where adding particle label states can increase multiparticle indistinguishability due to cancellation of collective phases.
AI.motivation: To understand and characterize indistinguishability of identical particles (bosons and fermions) undergoing arbitrary particle-number-preserving evolutions of their visible degrees of freedom, and to resolve the gap between textbook symmetrization and realistic partial distinguishability scenarios.
AI.method: Derivation of an equivalent expression linking projective indistinguishability measure to dynamically invariant internal state; generalization of symmetrization/anti-symmetrization framework to partial distinguishability via explicit reconstruction formula using indistinguishability function; characterization of class-functions via projective measures on generalized symmetries.
AI.result: A complete characterization of class-functions of indistinguishability by projective measures on generalized symmetries; discovery that introducing additional particle label states can increase multiparticle indistinguishability, attributed to cancellation of collective multiparticle phases.
AI.conclusion: The work extends the theoretical understanding of partial distinguishability in identical particles, provides a reconstruction formula linking visible state to dynamical invariants, and reveals a counterintuitive phenomenon where more label complexity can paradoxically enhance indistinguishability through collective phase cancellation.

title: Generic Number-of-Copies Amplification for Pseudorandom States
summary: We show that any quantum pseudorandom state that is secure against single-copy distinguishers, i.e. a $1$-PRS, can be amplified to $t$-copy security, i.e. to a $t$-PRS, without additional assumptions, for any polynomial $t$ in the security parameter. Prior work (Ananth and Goldin, arXiv 2025) was only able to show this for a restricted class of $1$-PRS constructions, namely ones whose generators only use a small number of ancilla qubits. Technically, we show that by carefully accounting for the randomness that is used in the construction, and using quantum extractors, it is possible to eliminate an ancilla register of any length and obtain a meaningful $t$-PRS outcome.

AI.tldr: This paper proves that any single-copy secure quantum pseudorandom state (1-PRS) can be amplified to t-copy security (t-PRS) for any polynomial t, eliminating prior restrictions on ancilla qubits, using quantum extractors and careful randomness accounting.
AI.motivation: Prior work could only amplify 1-PRS to t-PRS for constructions with a limited number of ancilla qubits. This paper aims to remove that restriction and show the amplification holds for all 1-PRS constructions without additional assumptions.
AI.method: The authors use quantum extractors and careful accounting of the randomness used in the construction to eliminate ancilla registers of any length, enabling a meaningful t-PRS outcome from any 1-PRS.
AI.result: The paper shows that any 1-PRS (secure against single-copy distinguishers) can be amplified to a t-PRS (secure against t-copy distinguishers) for any polynomial t, without any additional assumptions or restrictions on the original construction.
AI.conclusion: The restriction on ancilla qubits in prior work is unnecessary; universal amplification from 1-PRS to t-PRS is possible for all constructions.

title: Squeezing-enhanced Pairwise Fusion of Photonic Qudits
summary: Pairwise fusion gates are linear-optical measurements that herald Bell projections onto two-rail subspaces of two \(d\)-rail single-photon qudits. Without ancillary input photons, these passive measurements succeed with probability \(1-d^{-1}\), with all failures confined to the diagonal logical subspace. We show that identical single-mode squeezers applied to the \(2d\) interferometer outputs before photon-number-resolving detection recover part of this structured failure sector. Photon-number parity preserves the successful off-diagonal fusion signatures, while selected all-even patterns yield POVM elements proportional to definite pairwise Bell projectors. We derive the exact logical-space POVM and prove that a diagonal pattern is accepted if and only if its photon-number-imbalance vector has exactly two nonzero components of equal magnitude. The resulting closed elliptic-integral expression increases the ideal success probability, for instance, from \(75\%\) to \(79.62\%\) for \(d=4\), and from \(83.33\%\) to \(87.15\%\) for \(d=6\). With a representative finite detector saturation threshold, \(n_{\rm sat}=7\), the respective certified values remain \(78.84\%\) and \(86.71\%\). These results establish active Gaussian processing as a method for recycling structured measurement failures without ancillary input photons, at the cost of \(2d\) squeezing operations and a larger photon-number range at detection.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that applying single-mode squeezers to the outputs of pairwise fusion gates before photon-number-resolving detection can recover part of the structured failure sector in linear-optical Bell projections for d-rail single-photon qudits. This increases the success probability (e.g., from 75% to 79.62% for d=4, and from 83.33% to 87.15% for d=6) without ancillary input photons.
AI.motivation: To improve the success probability of pairwise fusion gates (linear-optical measurements that herald Bell projections) beyond the inherent 1-d^{-1} limit without requiring ancillary input photons, by recycling the structured failure sector through active Gaussian processing.
AI.method: Identical single-mode squeezers are applied to the 2d interferometer outputs before photon-number-resolving detection. The logical-space POVM is derived, showing that diagonal patterns are accepted iff the photon-number-imbalance vector has exactly two nonzero components of equal magnitude. Photon-number parity preserves successful off-diagonal fusion signatures while selected all-even patterns yield POVM elements proportional to definite pairwise Bell projectors.
AI.result: The ideal success probability increases from 75% to 79.62% for d=4, and from 83.33% to 87.15% for d=6. With a representative finite detector saturation threshold (n_sat=7), certified values remain at 78.84% and 86.71% respectively.
AI.conclusion: Active Gaussian processing via single-mode squeezing can recycle structured measurement failures without ancillary input photons, at the cost of 2d squeezing operations and a larger photon-number range at detection.

title: Steady-state Bell nonlocality in an autonomous quantum thermal machine
summary: A quantum thermal machine is presented that is able to autonomously generate steady-state Bell nonlocality. A Lindblad equation is derived for two qubits that are incoherently coupled to a pair of thermal baths and the resulting Liouvillian is found to have a strong symmetry. This out-of-equilibrium system can generate Bell-nonlocal steady states across a range of parameters and at arbitrarily high temperatures for certain initial conditions. To analyse how the machine operates in a more realistic setting, experimental imperfections are then included via a stochastic perturbation to the system Hamiltonian. This breaks the strong symmetry and results in collective and local dephasing noise. It is found that if the sole source of noise is local noise, then the steady state is Bell local. The co-presence of collective noise is then shown to be advantageous, with the ability to increase the degree of Bell-inequality violation and transform a steady state from Bell local to Bell nonlocal.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a quantum thermal machine that autonomously generates steady-state Bell nonlocality using two qubits coupled to thermal baths, exploiting a strong symmetry in the Lindblad equation. It shows that Bell-nonlocal steady states are achievable across various parameters and at high temperatures, and that collective noise can enhance Bell-inequality violation, while local noise alone destroys nonlocality.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate that a quantum thermal machine can autonomously generate steady-state Bell nonlocality without external control, and to understand how experimental imperfections (local and collective noise) affect the generation and persistence of nonlocality.
AI.method: A Lindblad master equation is derived for two qubits incoherently coupled to two thermal baths. The strong symmetry of the Liouvillian is identified and exploited. Experimental imperfections are modeled as stochastic perturbations to the Hamiltonian, introducing local and collective dephasing noise.
AI.result: Bell-nonlocal steady states can be generated across a range of parameters and at arbitrarily high temperatures for certain initial conditions. Local noise alone renders the steady state Bell local. Collective noise, when present alongside local noise, can increase Bell-inequality violation and transform a local state into a nonlocal one.
AI.conclusion: The proposed thermal machine can autonomously generate Bell nonlocality, and collective noise is beneficial (rather than detrimental) for nonlocality, offering a pathway to robust nonlocal state generation in realistic noisy environments.

title: Stabilizer entropy is trustworthy for mixed states
summary: Quantifying non-stabilizerness in mixed states is provably intractable, as any strict monotone requires superexponential time. We propose a linear Stabilizer Entropy that acts as a proper non-stabilizerness monotone with overwhelming probability when restricted to non-adaptive Clifford channels acting on flat mixed stabilizer states. Analytical and numerical results for Haar-random states, Clifford orbits, and random matrix product states show that monotonicity violation probabilities decay as $\exp-ηN$. We also prove the validity of Stabilizer Entropy in specific many-body systems undergoing partial measurements, where the amount of resource never increases for each measurement outcome as well as when averaged over outcome probabilities. Given the hardness of strict alternatives, Stabilizer Entropy emerges as a practical and theoretically justified resource measure.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a linear Stabilizer Entropy as a practical non-stabilizerness (magic) monotone for mixed states, which avoids the intractability of strict monotones while providing exponentially decaying violation probabilities and proven validity in many-body systems under partial measurements.
AI.motivation: Quantifying non-stabilizerness (magic) in mixed states is provably intractable, as any strict monotone requires superexponential time, motivating the need for a practical and theoretically justified resource measure.
AI.method: The authors propose a linear Stabilizer Entropy that acts as a proper non-stabilizerness monotone with overwhelming probability when restricted to non-adaptive Clifford channels acting on flat mixed stabilizer states. They provide analytical and numerical results for Haar-random states, Clifford orbits, and random matrix product states, showing monotonicity violation probabilities decay as exp(-ηN). They also prove validity in many-body systems undergoing partial measurements.
AI.result: Monotonicity violation probabilities decay exponentially as exp(-ηN). The Stabilizer Entropy is validated as a non-increasing resource measure for each measurement outcome and when averaged over outcome probabilities in many-body systems under partial measurements.
AI.conclusion: Given the hardness of strict alternatives, Stabilizer Entropy emerges as a practical and theoretically justified resource measure for non-stabilizerness in mixed states.

title: A superconducting qutrit link beyond the qubit limit
summary: Superconducting microwave links have enabled deterministic state transfer and remote entanglement between qubits, but deterministic links have so far operated with an effectively two-dimensional transmitted Hilbert space. Here we demonstrate a superconducting qutrit link between two independently packaged nodes connected by a microwave channel. Each node combines a transmon qutrit, a transmission resonator, and a tunable Purcell-filter interface, allowing the two remote microwave-photon interfaces to be matched in both frequency and bandwidth. We implement two transition-selective photon-mediated operations that transfer the $|e\rangle$ and $|f\rangle$ qutrit components in distinct temporal modes of the same channel. We tomographically characterize arbitrary qutrit-state transfer, obtaining a mean transferred-state fidelity of 83.68% and a qutrit process fidelity of 77.12%, exceeding both the classical qutrit-transfer benchmark and the best possible average fidelity of an effective qubit channel used to transmit an arbitrary qutrit. Using partial-transfer operations, we reconstruct a remote two-qutrit state with negativity 0.730, a tomography-inferred dense-coding capacity of 2.273 bits, and a tomography-inferred Collins-Gisin-Linden-Massar-Popescu (CGLMP) parameter $I_3=2.332$, all beyond the corresponding qubit or local bounds. These results demonstrate a superconducting microwave link that uses the native three-level structure of transmons as a genuine high-dimensional communication resource.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates a superconducting microwave link using qutrits (three-level systems) for high-dimensional quantum communication, achieving qutrit state transfer with 83.68% fidelity and demonstrating remote entanglement with negativity 0.730, exceeding qubit-based bounds.
AI.motivation: Previous deterministic superconducting microwave links have operated with an effectively two-dimensional (qubit) transmitted Hilbert space. The authors aim to exploit the native three-level structure of transmons to achieve genuine high-dimensional quantum communication.
AI.method: Two independently packaged nodes, each with a transmon qutrit, a transmission resonator, and a tunable Purcell-filter interface, are connected by a microwave channel. The interfaces are matched in frequency and bandwidth. Two transition-selective photon-mediated operations transfer |e⟩ and |f⟩ qutrit components in distinct temporal modes of the same channel.
AI.result: Mean transferred-state fidelity of 83.68%, qutrit process fidelity of 77.12%, remote two-qutrit state negativity of 0.730, tomography-inferred dense-coding capacity of 2.273 bits, and CGLMP parameter I₃=2.332, all exceeding corresponding qubit or local bounds.
AI.conclusion: These results demonstrate a superconducting microwave link that uses the native three-level structure of transmons as a genuine high-dimensional communication resource, going beyond effective qubit channels.

title: Concentration of Measure Phenomena for Quantum States on a Higher Dimensional Equator
summary: We revisit Lévy's lemma, a widely used analytical tool in quantum information theory. Concentration inequalities quantify the phenomenon in which Lipschitz observables concentrate around a median or mean, and serve as fundamental analytical tools across information theory, statistical physics, and learning theory. In particular, Lévy's lemma provides a crucial framework for describing functionals on pure quantum states, with applications in quantum entanglement and quantum statistical query learning. In this work, we isolate the hyper-equatorial part of the standard spherical concentration argument. The resulting estimate is a Lévy-type bound for Lipschitz functions on a fixed hyperequator, with the natural dimension parameter $d-1$. We also formulate the accompanying geometric localization in terms of neighborhoods of the boundary, hyperequator, and a codimension-two antipodal great subsphere. This viewpoint clarifies the structure of the usual proof and points to the measure-theoretic formulation needed for sharper constant-level statements.

AI.tldr: This paper refines Lévy's lemma by isolating the hyper-equatorial component of spherical concentration, yielding a dimension-(d-1) bound for Lipschitz functions on a hyperequator, and provides geometric localization in terms of boundary, hyperequator, and antipodal subspheres.
AI.motivation: To improve and clarify the analytical structure of Lévy's lemma, a key concentration inequality used in quantum information theory, by isolating its hyper-equatorial component and providing sharper geometric and measure-theoretic formulations.
AI.method: The authors isolate the hyper-equatorial part of the standard spherical concentration argument and formulate accompanying geometric localization using neighborhoods of the boundary, hyperequator, and a codimension-two antipodal great subsphere.
AI.result: A Lévy-type bound for Lipschitz functions on a fixed hyperequator with natural dimension parameter d-1, along with a clarified geometric structure and measure-theoretic formulation.
AI.conclusion: The hyper-equatorial perspective clarifies the proof structure of Lévy's lemma and points toward sharper constant-level concentration statements.

title: Quantum simulation of molecular excited-state manifolds and energies using the TEPID-ADAPT-VQE algorithm
summary: The simulation of molecular excited states is a key challenge in quantum chemistry and a promising application for quantum computing. In this work, we investigate the efficacy of the truncated eigenvalue parametrized initial density adaptive variational algorithm (TEPID-ADAPT-VQE) for computing low-lying excited states and potential energy surfaces. TEPID-ADAPT variationally diagonalizes a truncated low-temperature Gibbs state, enabling the simultaneous preparation of multiple excited states within a single optimization. We apply the method to H$_2$, LiH, and linear H$_4$ across bond lengths spanning weakly and strongly correlated regimes. The adaptive derivative-assembled problem-tailored (ADAPT) ansatz construction yields compact circuits suitable for near-term hardware. We also implement a modified version of the MORE-ADAPT-VQE algorithm for comparison with TEPID-ADAPT. We find that both algorithms accurately reproduce excited-state spectra and potential energy curves within chemical accuracy for all the molecules and geometries studied. However, TEPID-ADAPT has the advantage of utilizing only a single, physically motivated hyperparameter (temperature) that controls the energy scale at which excited states are targeted, while MORE-ADAPT utilizes multiple hyperparameters whose optimal values depend sensitively on the target problem. These results demonstrate that combining adaptive ansatz construction with density-matrix-based formulations provides an efficient framework for excited-state quantum chemistry on near-term devices.

AI.tldr: TEPID-ADAPT-VQE variationally diagonalizes a truncated low-temperature Gibbs state to simultaneously compute multiple molecular excited states using compact, adaptive ansatz circuits, achieving chemical accuracy across H₂, LiH, and H₄ with a single physically motivated hyperparameter (temperature).
AI.motivation: Simulating molecular excited states is a key challenge in quantum chemistry and a promising application for quantum computing, motivating the development of efficient variational algorithms suitable for near-term quantum devices.
AI.method: TEPID-ADAPT-VQE variationally diagonalizes a truncated low-temperature Gibbs state to simultaneously prepare multiple excited states in a single optimization, using ADAPT ansatz construction for compact circuits. A modified MORE-ADAPT-VQE is implemented for comparison.
AI.result: Both TEPID-ADAPT and MORE-ADAPT accurately reproduce excited-state spectra and potential energy curves within chemical accuracy for H₂, LiH, and linear H₄ across weakly and strongly correlated regimes.
AI.conclusion: Combining adaptive ansatz construction with density-matrix-based formulations provides an efficient framework for excited-state quantum chemistry on near-term devices; TEPID-ADAPT offers the advantage of a single physically motivated hyperparameter (temperature) versus multiple sensitive hyperparameters in MORE-ADAPT.

title: The QAOA on the ring of disagrees
summary: We study the performance of symmetric local algorithms finding large cuts on the cycle graph. Such algorithms that cannot see the whole graph at depth p cut at most a (2p+1)/(2p+2) fraction of edges in expectation. We prove that the QAOA achieves this value, a long-standing conjecture of Farhi, Goldstone, and Gutmann. Curiously we do this without finding the optimal parameters. Instead we show it is equivalent to find an optimal pair of Laurent polynomials of degree at most 2p-1. This is made possible by recasting the QAOA on one qubit in the language of quantum signal processing.

AI.tldr: This paper proves that the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) achieves the optimal cut fraction (2p+1)/(2p+2) for local algorithms on cycle graphs, confirming a long-standing conjecture. The proof avoids finding optimal parameters by reframing the problem as finding optimal Laurent polynomials of degree at most 2p-1, enabled by connecting QAOA on one qubit to quantum signal processing.
AI.motivation: To resolve a long-standing conjecture by Farhi, Goldstone, and Gutmann regarding whether QAOA achieves the optimal cut fraction for local algorithms on cycle graphs.
AI.method: The paper reframes QAOA on one qubit using quantum signal processing, showing that achieving the optimal cut fraction is equivalent to finding an optimal pair of Laurent polynomials of degree at most 2p-1, bypassing the need to find optimal variational parameters.
AI.result: QAOA achieves the optimal cut fraction (2p+1)/(2p+2) for symmetric local algorithms at depth p on cycle graphs.
AI.conclusion: The conjecture is confirmed, and the connection to quantum signal processing provides a new approach for analyzing QAOA performance without explicit parameter optimization.

title: Physics-Informed Neural Quantum Control for Extended Rovibrational Photoassociation in a Morse Molecular System
summary: We present a Physics-Informed Neural Quantum Control (PINQC) framework for rovibrational photoassociation in a Morse molecular system. The proposed method combines neural-network-based laser-field generation with differentiable quantum propagation, allowing optimized laser pulses to be obtained directly from the underlying quantum dynamics without requiring external training data. The optimized control fields efficiently transfer an initially continuum-like Gaussian wave packet into the vibrational ground-state level, promoting continuum-to-bound population transfer through coherent rovibrational dynamics. The resulting photoassociation process involves both vibrational stabilization and rotational redistribution arising naturally from dipole-induced couplings between neighboring rotational channels. A central result of the present work is the successful application of the PINQC framework to extended rovibrational models containing larger rotational levels than those previously accessible in our conventional photoassociation calculations. The optimization remains numerically stable despite the increased complexity of the molecular system, demonstrating that differentiable optimization provides an effective strategy for treating rovibrational models of increased dimensionality. These results establish the PINQC framework as a promising computational tool for molecular photoassociation and motivate future investigations of increasingly complex rovibrational quantum-control problems.

AI.tldr: PINQC combines neural-network-based laser-field generation with differentiable quantum propagation to optimize laser pulses for rovibrational photoassociation in Morse molecular systems, achieving stable continuum-to-bound population transfer and scaling to larger rotational models than previously possible.
AI.motivation: To develop a data-free, differentiable optimization framework for controlling rovibrational photoassociation dynamics in Morse molecules, particularly enabling extension to larger rotational-level models that were previously computationally inaccessible.
AI.method: Physically-Informed Neural Quantum Control (PINQC) framework combining neural-network-generated laser fields with differentiable quantum propagation to directly optimize pulses from underlying quantum dynamics without external training data.
AI.result: Successful continuum-to-bound population transfer via optimized laser pulses; vibrational stabilization and rotational redistribution through dipole-induced couplings; numerically stable optimization for larger rovibrational models beyond conventional reach.
AI.conclusion: PINQC is a promising computational tool for molecular photoassociation, enabling effective treatment of higher-dimensional rovibrational quantum-control problems via differentiable optimization.

title: Gaussian Quantum Metrology with Realistic Linear Sensors
summary: Quantum sensing promises enhanced precision, but the usual quantum Cramer Rao bound can be too optimistic for realistic linear sensors, where squeezing, filtering, and loss reshape quantum noise. We derive the tight Holevo Cramer Rao bound and show that realistic degradation yields a hierarchy with the usual bound and homodyne readout. This hierarchy already exists in gravitational-wave detectors. We propose a hardware-efficient readout that reaches the Holevo bound without extra signal loss, increasing compact-binary detection rates by up to 25% over the present LIGO homodyne readout.

AI.tldr: This paper derives the tight Holevo Cramér-Rao bound for realistic linear quantum sensors (e.g., gravitational-wave detectors) under squeezing, filtering, and loss, revealing a hierarchy with the usual quantum Cramér-Rao bound and homodyne readout, and proposes a hardware-efficient readout that achieves the Holevo bound without extra loss, boosting compact-binary detection rates by up to 25% over LIGO's current homodyne readout.
AI.motivation: The standard quantum Cramér-Rao bound is often too optimistic for realistic linear sensors because it ignores degradation effects such as squeezing, filtering, and loss that reshape quantum noise. A tighter bound is needed to accurately characterize and optimize practical quantum sensors.
AI.method: The authors derive the tight Holevo Cramér-Rao bound for realistic linear sensors and compare it with the usual quantum bound and homodyne readout performance. They propose a hardware-efficient readout scheme designed to reach the Holevo bound without introducing additional signal loss.
AI.result: A hierarchy is established between the Holevo bound, the usual quantum bound, and homodyne readout, already present in gravitational-wave detectors. The proposed readout reaches the Holevo bound with no extra loss, increasing compact-binary detection rates by up to 25% over current LIGO homodyne readout.
AI.conclusion: The Holevo bound provides a realistic benchmark for linear quantum sensors. The proposed readout offers a practical path to achieving this bound in current detectors like LIGO, with substantial improvements in detection rates.

title: Dynamics of quantum entanglement in two time-dependent coupled harmonic oscillators
summary: We investigate the quantum entanglement dynamics of two coupled harmonic oscillators with a time-dependent interaction. Using the Lewis-Riesenfeld invariant method, we derive the exact analytical wave functions without any perturbative or adiabatic approximations and combine this with a phase-space analysis using the Wigner function to provide a complete description of the system's quantum state evolution. We obtain general expression form for the purity and the linear entropy $S_L=1-\mathcal{P}$ for arbitrary excitation numbers $(n,m)$, allows a systematic study of entanglement for a large class of quantum states. We show that the entanglement dynamics is very sensitive to the interplay between the detuning parameters $θ$ and $\vartheta_2$, the frequency parameter $β_0$ and the coupling strength $ε$: the increase of detuning takes the system from slow irregular oscillations to fast and regular periodic behavior, and the stronger coupling systematically enhances both the amplitude and the average value of the linear entropy. Most importantly, for the resonance case $ω_1=ω_2=1$ and strong couplings $ε\approx 0.99$, the system shows robust undamped synchronized periodic oscillations of the linear entropy for all quantum states considered, indicating preserved quantum coherence without saturation. Our findings demonstrate that linear entropy is a sensitive and practical entanglement witness, and we establish explicit analytical relations between the coupling parameters of the system and its entanglement properties, which are directly relevant to quantum information processing and the control of quantum correlations in continuous-variable systems.

AI.tldr: This paper analytically studies entanglement dynamics in two coupled harmonic oscillators with time-dependent interaction using the Lewis-Riesenfeld invariant method and Wigner function analysis, showing that linear entropy is a sensitive entanglement witness, with resonance and strong coupling producing robust undamped periodic entanglement oscillations.
AI.motivation: To understand quantum entanglement dynamics in continuous-variable systems (coupled harmonic oscillators) with time-dependent interactions, without relying on perturbative or adiabatic approximations.
AI.method: Lewis-Riesenfeld invariant method for exact analytical wave functions; Wigner function phase-space analysis; linear entropy $S_L=1-\mathcal{P}$ as entanglement measure.
AI.result: Entanglement sensitivity to detuning, frequency, and coupling strength; at resonance ($\omega_1=\omega_2=1$) and strong coupling ($\epsilon\approx 0.99$), robust undamped synchronized periodic linear entropy oscillations occur for all quantum states, indicating preserved quantum coherence without saturation.
AI.conclusion: Linear entropy is a sensitive and practical entanglement witness; explicit analytical relations are established between coupling parameters and entanglement properties, relevant to quantum information processing and control of quantum correlations in continuous-variable systems.

title: Bright-mode parity synthesis for bosonic state transfer through a single ancilla
summary: Bosonic modes provide hardware-efficient quantum memories and logical registers, including highly non-Gaussian encoded states, but transferring finite-dimensional bosonic states through a restricted ancilla interface requires identifying which collective mode is actually controlled. We study a restricted setting in which two oscillators couple with opposite signs to a single two-level ancilla. In the normal-mode basis, the symmetric mode is dark, while transfer between the physical modes is equivalent to synthesizing parity on the antisymmetric bright mode.
