This reduction gives exact finite-sum transfer formulas for Fock states, Fock-state qubits, and finite Fock superpositions, and explains why resonant single-ancilla transfer is recurrence-limited beyond the single-photon sector. We then show that detuned Jaynes--Cummings evolution provides a native two-parameter route to high-fidelity finite-cutoff parity synthesis, with residual ancilla excitation, calibration sensitivity, and a minimal Markovian noise estimate quantified separately. Bosonic-code examples illustrate how transfer sensitivity is governed by photon-number support and residual bright-mode phase errors. The result provides a practical benchmark and organizing principle for constrained ancilla-mediated bosonic transfer when direct exchange is unavailable or undesirable.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes bosonic state transfer between two oscillators coupled with opposite signs to a single two-level ancilla. It shows that symmetric mode is dark while transfer reduces to synthesizing parity on the antisymmetric bright mode, providing exact formulas for Fock states and qubits. Detuned Jaynes-Cummings evolution enables high-fidelity parity synthesis. Transfer sensitivity is governed by photon-number support and residual phase errors.
AI.motivation: To understand how to transfer finite-dimensional bosonic states through a restricted ancilla interface when direct exchange between oscillators is unavailable or undesirable, and to identify which collective mode is actually controlled.
AI.method: The authors study two oscillators coupling with opposite signs to a single two-level ancilla. They transform to normal-mode basis, derive exact finite-sum transfer formulas for Fock states, Fock-state qubits, and finite Fock superpositions. They analyze detuned Jaynes-Cummings evolution for two-parameter high-fidelity parity synthesis, and quantify residual ancilla excitation, calibration sensitivity, and Markovian noise.
AI.result: Transfer between physical modes is equivalent to synthesizing parity on the antisymmetric bright mode. Resonant single-ancilla transfer is recurrence-limited beyond the single-photon sector. Detuned Jaynes-Cummings evolution provides native high-fidelity finite-cutoff parity synthesis. Transfer sensitivity is governed by photon-number support and residual bright-mode phase errors.
AI.conclusion: The result provides a practical benchmark and organizing principle for constrained ancilla-mediated bosonic transfer when direct exchange is unavailable or undesirable, with implications for bosonic-code examples.

title: Squeezing as a catalyst for non-Gaussian advantage in characterization of nonlinear media
summary: We address the precise characterization of coupling strength of nonlinear media in continuous-variable (CV) quantum systems using coherent and squeezed vacuum states as Gaussian probes, together with their photon-added and photon-subtracted counterparts as non-Gaussian probes. We consider three main classes of nonlinear Hamiltonians, namely quadrature nonlinearities, generalized squeezing and Kerr-type interactions. By analytically evaluating the quantum Fisher information (QFI), we compare the performance of Gaussian and non-Gaussian probes and assess the optimal probe based on the probe parameters, energy resource and non-Gaussianity. Our results are twofold as follows: first, for coherent-state family, the improvement provided by photon addition at fixed coherent amplitude originates mainly from the extra energy carried by the probe and does not provide a genuine metrological resource, since the same precision can be achieved by a Gaussian coherent-state signal of a larger energy, which can be more easily produced. Second, in contrast, photon addition and subtraction become effective resources when applied to already nonclassical states such as squeezed vacuum states. In this case, they lead to a significant enhancement of the QFI, particularly for higher-order interactions. Although Gaussian squeezed states remain optimal at equal energy constraint, photon-added and photon-subtracted squeezed states achieve comparable sensitives with significantly lower squeezing requirements. Since large squeezing level remains experimentally challenging, these non-Gaussian probes offer a practical route towards enhanced estimation of the nonlinear coupling strength within currently accessible squeezing regimes.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes how non-Gaussian probes (photon-added/subtracted states) compare to Gaussian probes (coherent and squeezed vacuum states) for estimating nonlinear coupling strengths in CV quantum systems. Photon addition only helps coherent states by adding energy (no genuine metrological advantage), but for squeezed states, photon addition/subtraction significantly enhances quantum Fisher information, enabling comparable sensitivity with much lower squeezing requirements.
AI.motivation: To precisely characterize coupling strength of nonlinear media in CV quantum systems and determine whether non-Gaussian probes offer genuine metrological advantages over Gaussian probes for estimating nonlinear interactions.
AI.method: Analytically evaluated quantum Fisher information for Gaussian probes (coherent and squeezed vacuum states) and non-Gaussian probes (photon-added/subtracted counterparts) across three nonlinear Hamiltonians: quadrature nonlinearities, generalized squeezing, and Kerr-type interactions.
AI.result: (1) For coherent-state family, photon addition improvement is due to extra energy, providing no genuine metrological advantage over higher-energy coherent states. (2) For squeezed vacuum family, photon addition/subtraction significantly enhances QFI, especially for higher-order interactions, achieving comparable sensitivity with much lower squeezing requirements.
AI.conclusion: Gaussian squeezed states remain optimal under equal energy constraints, but photon-added/subtracted squeezed states offer a practical route to enhanced nonlinear coupling estimation using experimentally accessible low-squeezing regimes.

title: Lie Group Diffusion Models for Hardware-Aware Quantum Circuit Synthesis
summary: An important task in quantum computing is unitary circuit synthesis compatible with physical hardware constraints. This problem has a natural hybrid structure as local single-qubit gates are continuous variables on the Lie group $SU(2)$ while the entangling circuit structure is discrete and hardware-dependent. In this work, we use generative models to perform quantum circuit synthesis incorporating both the natural $SU(2)$ manifold geometry of quantum gates and hardware constraints that determine the overall circuit structure. Our model comprises two components: a circuit skeleton selector that chooses an entangling circuit and a diffusion model that generates quantum gates on the given circuit template by performing diffusion on the curved manifold $\mathrm{SU(2)} \simeq S^3$ itself. We demonstrate this approach with unitary compilation of physically motivated three-qubit Hamiltonian simulation targets such as the Transverse Field Ising Model and the Heisenberg-XXZ Model and show that Lie group diffusion outperforms comparable baselines. The synthesised circuits can also be customised subject to constraints, which we demonstrate by producing circuits with large and small gate rotation angles for the same target unitary evolution. We also investigate the fidelity-complexity frontier of the synthesised gates to demonstrate that the circuit selector learns to select circuits that balance fidelity with complexity rather than collapsing onto the most expansive entangling template. These results demonstrate that Lie group diffusion provides a natural generative framework for hardware-aware quantum circuit synthesis.

AI.tldr: This paper uses generative models (a circuit skeleton selector + a diffusion model on the SU(2) manifold) to perform hardware-aware quantum circuit synthesis, demonstrating improved unitary compilation for Hamiltonian simulation targets.
AI.motivation: Quantum circuit synthesis must balance continuous single-qubit gates (SU(2) Lie group) with discrete, hardware-dependent entangling circuit structures, but existing approaches lack a natural generative framework that respects both the curved geometry of quantum gates and hardware constraints simultaneously.
AI.method: A two-component generative model: (1) a circuit skeleton selector that chooses the discrete entangling circuit structure, and (2) a diffusion model that generates continuous SU(2) gate parameters by performing diffusion directly on the curved manifold SU(2) ≃ S³, rather than in Euclidean space.
AI.result: Lie group diffusion outperforms comparable baselines on unitary compilation of three-qubit Hamiltonian simulation targets (Transverse Field Ising Model, Heisenberg-XXZ Model). The model produces customizable circuits (e.g., large vs. small rotation angles) and learns to balance fidelity with circuit complexity rather than always picking the most expansive entangling template.
AI.conclusion: Lie group diffusion provides a natural generative framework for hardware-aware quantum circuit synthesis, effectively integrating the continuous geometry of quantum gates with discrete hardware constraints.

title: Characterization of Unlearnable Noise with Mid-Circuit-Measurement-Based Cycle Benchmarking
summary: Noise characterization of multi-qubit entangling Clifford operations is a key practical bottleneck for quantum error mitigation and for the calibration, validation, and optimization of quantum error-correction protocols, especially in the presence of state preparation and measurement (SPAM) errors. Although cycle benchmarking can isolate some Pauli error components, it cannot resolve the problem of coupled error parameters, which leads to unlearnable degrees of freedom even in simple noisy gates, not to mention general $n$-qubit Clifford gates. Here we introduce mid-circuit-measurement-based generalized cycle benchmarking, a framework that makes otherwise unidentifiable Pauli fidelities and non-Markovian noise learnable via repeated measurements and classical post-processing. Applying the deferred feed-forward principle to generalized cycle benchmarking, we show that an insertion of mid-circuit measurements can reverse Pauli cycles induced by a general Clifford gate. This fact enables us to reveal a Pauli-noise learnability condition for Clifford gates. Assuming sufficient state preparation quality, we numerically demonstrate the feasibility of characterizing the previously unlearnable noise components. We implement the protocol on superconducting quantum processing units and validate its effectiveness in disambiguating the coupled noise components, benchmarked against conventional tomography. Finally, we observe consistent measurement-induced bit-flip bias and non-Markovian correlations, which define a range of applicability for the Pauli noise model and the proposed noise-characterization protocol.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces mid-circuit-measurement-based generalized cycle benchmarking to resolve unidentifiable Pauli fidelities and non-Markovian noise in multi-qubit Clifford operations, overcoming limitations of standard cycle benchmarking through repeated measurements and classical post-processing.
AI.motivation: Noise characterization of multi-qubit entangling Clifford operations is a key bottleneck for quantum error mitigation and error-correction protocols, especially due to coupled error parameters that create unlearnable degrees of freedom even in simple noisy gates.
AI.method: The authors propose mid-circuit-measurement-based generalized cycle benchmarking, which applies the deferred feed-forward principle to insert mid-circuit measurements that reverse Pauli cycles induced by general Clifford gates, enabling learnability of previously unidentifiable noise components.
AI.result: Numerical demonstrations confirm feasibility of characterizing previously unlearnable noise components. Implementation on superconducting quantum processing units validates effectiveness in disambiguating coupled noise components, benchmarked against conventional tomography.
AI.conclusion: The protocol identifies consistent measurement-induced bit-flip bias and non-Markovian correlations, which define the applicability range for the Pauli noise model and the proposed characterization protocol.

title: Hybrid Quantum Neighborhood Selection: NISQ-Compatible Combinatorial Optimization via Stochastic Frontier Decomposition
comment: 10 pages, 8 figures, 8 tables. Preprint submitted to arXiv
summary: Large-scale combinatorial optimization is a challenge for near-term quantum computing because dense Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) formulations yield interaction graphs that exceed the limits of NISQ processors. This work introduces Hybrid Quantum Neighborhood Selection (HQNS), a hybrid framework mitigating this via stochastic frontier decomposition. Instead of encoding all N variables into a monolithic circuit, HQNS selects a compact frontier of F << N active variables per stage, freezing the rest into reduced QUBO coefficients. A multi-stage crawling procedure rotates these frontiers, letting local quantum subproblems refine a global solution. We evaluate HQNS on the Maximum Diversity Subset Selection Problem (MDSSP) across six scales, N up to 1000. Circuit burden is reduced from the dense QAOA requirement of O(N^2) two-qubit terms per layer to O(F^2) per stage, with total complexity governed by the number of stages and classical overhead. Benchmarks show that HQNS achieves competitive solution quality relative to parallel simulated annealing (SA) while maintaining bounded circuit width and stable QPU time. In the N=1000 benchmark over ten executions, HQNS preserves 99.9908% of the mean diversity score of an 11-restart parallel SA baseline, while reducing wall-clock time by 65.03%, peak CPU usage by 55.97%, and peak memory by 35.21%. Ablation shows performance depends on frontier size, warm-starts, CVaR filtering, and stochastic rotation. These results demonstrate that structured frontier decomposition makes variational optimization executable for dense QUBO instances unsuitable for direct QAOA on present hardware.

AI.tldr: HQNS is a hybrid quantum-classical framework that decomposes dense QUBO problems into compact subproblems using stochastic frontier decomposition, enabling NISQ-era quantum optimization on large-scale instances (up to N=1000) while achieving competitive quality to simulated annealing with significant reductions in circuit width, time, CPU, and memory usage.
AI.motivation: Large-scale combinatorial optimization is challenging for near-term quantum computing because dense QUBO formulations produce interaction graphs that exceed NISQ processor limits, making direct encoding of all N variables infeasible.
AI.method: HQNS selects a compact frontier of F << N active variables per stage via stochastic frontier decomposition, freezes the rest into reduced QUBO coefficients, and uses a multi-stage crawling procedure that rotates frontiers to let local quantum subproblems refine a global solution.
AI.result: On MDSSP benchmarks (N up to 1000), HQNS reduces circuit burden from O(N²) to O(F²) per stage. It preserves 99.9908% of the mean diversity score of an 11-restart parallel SA baseline while reducing wall-clock time by 65.03%, peak CPU by 55.97%, and peak memory by 35.21%.
AI.conclusion: Structured frontier decomposition makes variational optimization executable for dense QUBO instances that are unsuitable for direct QAOA on present hardware, with performance depending on frontier size, warm-starts, CVaR filtering, and stochastic rotation.

title: A Machine-Verified Proof of a Quantum-Optimization Conjecture
summary: We report a machine-verified resolution of a problem open for over a decade in quantum optimization: the Farhi, Goldstone and Gutmann (FGG) conjecture that depth-$p$ Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) on the ring of disagrees attains approximation ratio $(2p+1)/(2p+2)$ exactly. We found the proof using a large language model, Claude Fable 5, and verified its correctness end-to-end by the Lean 4 proof assistant. Our methodology includes several ingredients: building on a substantial Lean library of quantum information, we formalized the QAOA components and the known parts of the problem, and reduced the conjecture to a single open mathematical statement. The model was then handed the library and our agentic toolkit, and tasked with closing that gap by constructing a proof in Lean. The resulting process is a feedback loop between the model's natural-language reasoning and Lean's mechanical verification, which converged to a machine-verified proof. Human verification is required only for the structural scaffolding - that the formal statement faithfully encodes the intended claim - while the proof itself is supplied by the model and certified mechanically by Lean. The proof is nevertheless striking - the model uncovered a hidden dynamical symmetry of the problem and exploited it, borrowing tools and machinery from an adjacent field to turn a hard existence problem into an explicit construction. This work paves the way for resolving open conjectures in quantum information science and beyond.

AI.tldr: A large language model (Claude Fable 5) proved the Farhi-Goldstone-Gutmann conjecture about QAOA approximation ratios on the ring of disagrees, with the proof machine-verified by the Lean 4 proof assistant. The model discovered a hidden dynamical symmetry and used tools from an adjacent field to construct the proof through a human-scaffolded, LLM-Lean feedback loop.
AI.motivation: To resolve a decade-old open problem in quantum optimization — the FGG conjecture regarding the exact approximation ratio of depth-p QAOA on the ring of disagrees — and to demonstrate that LLMs combined with formal verification can close long-standing mathematical gaps.
AI.method: Built a substantial Lean 4 library formalizing QAOA components and known results; reduced the conjecture to a single open mathematical statement; deployed an LLM (Claude Fable 5) with an agentic toolkit to construct the missing proof via iterative natural-language reasoning and Lean's mechanical verification feedback loop; human involvement limited to structural scaffolding (ensuring the formal statement matched the intended claim).
AI.result: A machine-verified proof of the FGG conjecture, showing depth-p QAOA on the ring of disagrees achieves an approximation ratio of exactly (2p+1)/(2p+2). The LLM uncovered a hidden dynamical symmetry and imported techniques from an adjacent field to convert a hard existence problem into an explicit construction.
AI.conclusion: This work demonstrates that LLMs, when paired with formal proof assistants like Lean, can discover and verify non-trivial proofs for open problems in quantum information science, establishing a paradigm for human-scaffolded, machine-driven theorem proving.

title: Alleviating the Sparse Matrix Scaling Bottleneck in Adaptive VQE via High-Order Taylor State Evolution
comment: 7 pages, submitted to IEEE Transactions on Quantum Engineering
summary: The Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) is a leading algorithm for noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices, but its adaptive variants (e.g., ADAPT-VQE) suffer from severe classical simulation bottlenecks during the ansatz growth phase. Representing and exponentiating pool operators for multi-qubit systems constructs massive sparse matrices that quickly scale to millions of elements, choking classical memory bandwidth and CPU/GPU cycle capacity. In this work, we present a resource-efficient software-layer framework that completely bypasses dense matrix exponentiation by evaluating state updates through a deterministic fifth-order (O(5)) Taylor series expansion. This approach reframes the costly unitary evolution into a chained sequence of five lightweight, successive sparse matrix-vector multiplications scaling strictly as O(Nz), where Nz is the number of non-zero elements. We validate our framework using equilibrium BeH2 (14 qubits), equilibrium H2O (12 qubits), and strongly correlated asymmetrically stretched H2O molecular profiles under both Jordan-Wigner (JW) and Bravyi-Kitaev (BK) transformations. The simulation results demonstrate that the O(5) truncation maintains exceptional numerical fidelity, retaining a state fidelity > 0.999999 and matching absolute ground state energies down to subchemical accuracy, while effortlessly navigating matrix spaces exceeding 268 million structural elements. This framework provides a scalable, high-performance pathway for executing deep variational simulations on hardware platforms with constrained computational budgets.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a resource-efficient software framework that replaces dense matrix exponentiation in ADAPT-VQE with a deterministic fifth-order Taylor series expansion, enabling lightweight sparse matrix-vector multiplications that scale as O(Nz). Validated on BeH₂ (14 qubits) and H₂O (12 qubits) systems, it achieves state fidelity >0.999999 and subchemical accuracy while handling matrices with over 268 million elements.
AI.motivation: Adaptive VQE variants suffer from severe classical simulation bottlenecks during ansatz growth because representing and exponentiating pool operators for multi-qubit systems constructs massive sparse matrices that scale to millions of elements, choking classical memory bandwidth and CPU/GPU capacity.
AI.method: The framework bypasses dense matrix exponentiation by evaluating state updates through a deterministic fifth-order (O(5)) Taylor series expansion, reframing unitary evolution into a chained sequence of five lightweight successive sparse matrix-vector multiplications scaling as O(Nz), where Nz is the number of non-zero elements.
AI.result: Validation on equilibrium BeH₂ (14 qubits), equilibrium H₂O (12 qubits), and strongly correlated asymmetrically stretched H₂O under both Jordan-Wigner and Bravyi-Kitaev transformations shows the O(5) truncation maintains state fidelity >0.999999 and matches absolute ground state energies to subchemical accuracy, while navigating matrix spaces exceeding 268 million structural elements.
AI.conclusion: This framework provides a scalable, high-performance pathway for executing deep variational simulations on hardware platforms with constrained computational budgets.

title: Quantum complexity resource in Gaussian boson sampling: Core structure of the semidefinite program
summary: We present a rigorous analysis of the algebraic and geometric structure of the quantum complexity resource of a system of bosonic modes in Gaussian boson sampling. This resource underlies the quantum advantage of the system: its photon-counting statistics require the evaluation of a hafnian of the resource covariance matrix, and that computation is #P-hard. The resource covariance matrix is the solution of a semidefinite program that extracts the minimum-trace physical quantum part of the total covariance matrix; the complementary part is positive semidefinite and can therefore be simulated classically. Earlier work characterized this resource only through the trace of the quantum part, equal to its photon number. We characterize the optimizer itself, as a quantum state and as a geometric object, beyond the scalar given by its trace. We prove that it is a unique pure Gaussian state and construct an explicit oracle map, obeying an algebraic Riccati identity, that reconstructs the resource. We prove that the full problem compresses exactly onto the active symplectic sector that the dual program support generates. The passive-diagonalizable states are solved in closed form, the first explicit solvable class, and the whole program is shown to be equivalent to a minimization over the symplectic group, that is, over the Siegel upper half-space. Together these results establish that the program determines a canonical localized pure Gaussian component of the resource, and they provide the structural foundation for its detailed analysis.

AI.tldr: This paper provides a rigorous analysis of the algebraic and geometric structure of the quantum complexity resource in Gaussian boson sampling, showing the resource covariance matrix optimizer is a unique pure Gaussian state with an explicit oracle map, and compressing the problem onto the active symplectic sector.
AI.motivation: Earlier work characterized the quantum complexity resource in Gaussian boson sampling only through the trace (photon number) of the quantum part of the covariance matrix. This paper aims to characterize the optimizer itself—as a quantum state and geometric object—beyond the scalar trace.
AI.method: The authors prove the optimizer is a unique pure Gaussian state, construct an explicit oracle map obeying an algebraic Riccati identity, show the problem compresses onto the active symplectic sector, solve passive-diagonalizable states in closed form, and prove equivalence to minimization over the symplectic group (Siegel upper half-space).
AI.result: The program determines a canonical localized pure Gaussian component of the resource; the optimizer is fully characterized structurally; a first explicit solvable class (passive-diagonalizable states) is provided in closed form.
AI.conclusion: These results establish the structural foundation for detailed analysis of the quantum complexity resource in Gaussian boson sampling, revealing a canonical pure Gaussian decomposition of the resource.

title: Unbiased Hamiltonian Simulation by Reversing Trotter Error Dynamics
summary: Owing to their simplicity and low overhead, Suzuki--Trotter formulas remain the de facto Hamiltonian simulation methods on current quantum computing platforms. Systematic Trotter errors, however, will quickly become limiting when scaling to larger problems and aiming for higher accuracy. We present a mechanism that removes the systematic error of any $k$-th order Suzuki--Trotter simulation, at the cost of a constant sampling overhead. The key insight is that the Trotter error is itself a coherent dynamics to be reversed, rather than a deviation to be bounded. By identifying the structure of this error in a suitable form, we carry out that reversal through quasi-probabilistic decompositions. The resulting algorithm, called Probabilistic Trotter Error Reversal (PTER), is unbiased, improves the gate-count scaling compared to Suzuki--Trotter formulas, and still retains their simplicity. Numerical simulations of a Heisenberg spin chain support the predicted resource advantage already at modest system sizes.Keisuke Murota, Yuta Kikuchi, Enrico Rinaldi, Frédéric Sauvage, Synge Todo

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Probabilistic Trotter Error Reversal (PTER), a method that eliminates systematic errors in Suzuki-Trotter Hamiltonian simulations by using quasi-probabilistic decompositions to reverse coherent Trotter errors, requiring only constant sampling overhead while improving gate-count scaling.
AI.motivation: Suzuki-Trotter formulas, while simple and low-overhead, suffer from systematic Trotter errors that become limiting when scaling to larger problems and aiming for higher accuracy. Existing approaches treat Trotter error as a deviation to be bounded rather than corrected.
AI.method: The authors identify that Trotter error is a coherent dynamics that can be reversed. By structuring this error in a suitable form, they apply quasi-probabilistic decompositions to reverse it, resulting in the Probabilistic Trotter Error Reversal (PTER) algorithm—an unbiased method that uses constant sampling overhead.
AI.result: PTER improves gate-count scaling compared to standard Suzuki-Trotter formulas while retaining their simplicity. Numerical simulations of a Heisenberg spin chain validate the predicted resource advantage even at modest system sizes.
AI.conclusion: PTER offers a practical, unbiased mechanism to remove systematic Trotter errors with only constant sampling overhead, making it a promising approach for Hamiltonian simulation on near-term quantum platforms.

title: Coherent manipulation of the biphoton generation in cavity-QED system
summary: We theoretically investigate the coherent manipulation of biphoton generation via spontaneous four-wave mixing in a cavity-QED system with a single atom. The atom is driven by pumping, coupling, and driving fields, and the generation of the Stokes and anti-Stokes photons are enhanced by two cavities. By solving the master equation in the steady state, we analyze the spectral brightness, as well as the degree of the auto-correlation and cross-correlation. Our results show that when the pumping and driving fields are in two-photon resonance, the dark state established between the ground and Rydberg states. efficiently enhances the controllability of the driving field over the biphoton generation and the quantum statistics. In contrast, under large two-photon detuning, the control capability of the driving field is significantly reduced. The coupling field, which directly relates to the electromagnetically induced transparency, modifies the linewidth of the biphoton, while the atom-cavity coupling strength only changes the brightness without affecting the linewidth.

AI.tldr: This paper theoretically investigates coherent control of biphoton generation via spontaneous four-wave mixing in a cavity-QED system with a single atom, showing that two-photon resonance enables dark state control between ground and Rydberg states, while coupling field modifies biphoton linewidth via EIT and atom-cavity coupling affects brightness only.
AI.motivation: To theoretically understand and demonstrate coherent control over biphoton generation and its quantum statistical properties using a cavity-QED system with a single atom, leveraging dark states and electromagnetically induced transparency.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis using master equation in steady state for a cavity-QED system with a single atom driven by pumping, coupling, and driving fields, with Stokes and anti-Stokes photon generation enhanced by two cavities.
AI.result: Under two-photon resonance, the dark state between ground and Rydberg states enhances driving field controllability over biphoton generation and quantum statistics. Under large two-photon detuning, control capability is reduced. The coupling field modifies biphoton linewidth via EIT, while atom-cavity coupling only affects brightness without changing linewidth.
AI.conclusion: The system provides tunable control over biphoton generation properties, with dark-state mediated control at resonance and EIT-based linewidth modification, offering a pathway for engineering quantum light sources.

title: Quantum Circuit Realization of the PPT and CCNR Criteria
summary: The efficient detection of quantum entanglement is a central problem in quantum information processing. This paper systematically proposes a quantum circuit implementation scheme based on the Positive Partial Transpose (PPT) and the Computable Cross-Norm Realignment (CCNR) criteria, providing a complete quantum algorithmic pathway for efficient and computable entanglement detection. By encoding quantum states into specific forms and utilizing SWAP operations, complex matrix operations such as partial transpose and realignment are transformed into executable quantum circuits. Furthermore, by integrating an improved variational quantum singular value decomposition subroutine, the scheme enables the efficient estimation of the trace norm, thereby determining the existence of entanglement. Designed to operate within a hybrid quantum-classical framework, this scheme exhibits excellent scalability and practicality, offering a theoretical tool and methodological support for analyzing the entanglement structure of complex quantum systems on future intermediate-scale quantum devices.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a quantum circuit implementation for entanglement detection using PPT and CCNR criteria, with a variational quantum singular value decomposition subroutine for trace norm estimation, operating in a hybrid quantum-classical framework.
AI.motivation: Efficient detection of quantum entanglement is a central problem in quantum information processing, and existing methods lack practical quantum circuit implementations.
AI.method: The scheme encodes quantum states into specific forms, uses SWAP operations to implement partial transpose and realignment in quantum circuits, and integrates a variational quantum singular value decomposition subroutine to estimate the trace norm.
AI.result: Complex matrix operations (partial transpose, realignment) are transformed into executable quantum circuits, enabling efficient trace norm estimation for entanglement detection.
AI.conclusion: The hybrid quantum-classical scheme offers scalability and practicality, providing theoretical and methodological support for analyzing entanglement structures on near-term intermediate-scale quantum devices.

title: Krylov Complexity in Non-Inertial Quantum Systems
summary: In this work, we formulate the Krylov complexity in non-In an inertial quantum system, the direct emergence of the $SU(1,1)$ sector from the Klein-Gordon symplectic form dictates that the Rindler pair-number sector naturally forms the Krylov basis for uniformly accelerating observers. Under this construction, we generalize the Bogoliubov coefficients by exploiting the $SU(1,1)$ group-structured Hamiltonian. Within this framework, we explicitly derive that the Krylov complexity is exactly equal to the mean number of correlated Rindler pairs generated via Bogoliubov mixing. Furthermore, the competition between the detuning parameter and the pair-production parameter in the Hamiltonian separates the dynamics into three distinct regimes: hyperbolic Krylov spreading, critical growth, and bounded Krylov-space motion. Notably, in the detuning-dominated regime, the pair-number distribution remains exponentially confined to low Krylov levels, implying that the wave packet becomes trapped at low levels, which manifests as the localization of Krylov complexity. Ultimately, our work sheds new light on the structural construction of Krylov complexity in non-inertial quantum systems.

AI.tldr: The paper formulates Krylov complexity in non-inertial quantum systems by linking it to the SU(1,1) group structure of the Klein-Gordon symplectic form, showing it equals the mean number of correlated Rindler pairs from Bogoliubov mixing, and identifies three dynamical regimes: hyperbolic spreading, critical growth, and bounded motion, with detuning-dominated localization.
AI.motivation: To extend the concept of Krylov complexity to non-inertial quantum systems by exploiting the SU(1,1) symmetry naturally emerging from the Klein-Gordon symplectic structure for uniformly accelerating (Rindler) observers.
AI.method: The authors derive Krylov complexity from the SU(1,1) group-structured Hamiltonian, generalize Bogoliubov coefficients, and analyze the dynamics via competition between detuning and pair-production parameters.
AI.result: Krylov complexity equals the mean number of correlated Rindler pairs from Bogoliubov mixing; three regimes emerge: hyperbolic spreading (pair-production dominated), critical growth (balanced), and bounded motion (detuning dominated, leading to exponential confinement and localization).
AI.conclusion: This work provides a structural construction of Krylov complexity in non-inertial systems, revealing its equivalence to pair production and the role of parameter competition in dynamical localization.

title: Multipartite quantum resource distillation through local measurement programs
summary: Distributed quantum resources in practical multi-user quantum networks are inevitably degraded by environmental noise, channel loss, and device-induced imperfections. To address these issues, quantum resource distillation offers a fundamental approach to recovering stronger resources from imperfect states. However, conventional implementations often require additional copies, dedicated physical filtering elements, or restrict to bipartite systems, posing challenges for scalable multipartite networks. Here, we introduce the method of quantum resource distillation based on the local measurement program (LMP), which transfers completely positive maps into programmable measurement processes. We experimentally demonstrate the performance of resource distillation through LMP in both bipartite and tripartite photonic systems, including the activation and enhancement of multipartite steering configurations. To demonstrate the flexibility and extensibility of the LMP framework, we also show that virtual resource distillation can be naturally reformulated within it. Our results establish a programmable and experimentally economical approach for distilling quantum resources in multipartite and higher-dimensional systems, thereby providing a practical route toward scalable quantum networks.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a Local Measurement Program (LMP) framework for distilling quantum resources in multipartite networks, experimentally demonstrating its effectiveness in bipartite and tripartite photonic systems, including activation and enhancement of multipartite steering.
AI.motivation: Distributed quantum resources in multi-user quantum networks are degraded by noise, loss, and imperfections. Conventional resource distillation methods require additional copies, dedicated physical filters, or are restricted to bipartite systems, posing scalability challenges for multipartite networks.
AI.method: The method, Local Measurement Program (LMP), transfers completely positive maps into programmable measurement processes, enabling resource distillation without dedicated physical filtering elements.
AI.result: Experimental demonstration of resource distillation via LMP in both bipartite and tripartite photonic systems, including activation and enhancement of multipartite steering. Virtual resource distillation is also reformulated within the LMP framework.
AI.conclusion: The LMP framework provides a programmable, experimentally economical approach for distilling quantum resources in multipartite and higher-dimensional systems, offering a practical route toward scalable quantum networks.

title: Nonlocal effects via Local Quantum Fisher Information: Characterizations and Interpretations
summary: We introduce a quantum Fisher information based measurement-induced nonlocality (QFI-MIN), which quantifies the maximal statistical distinguishability induced by locally invariant unitary dynamics. The proposed measure inherits desirable properties including positivity, local unitary invariance, monotonicity under local operations, and immunity to the local ancilla problem. Analytical expressions are obtained for pure states, arbitrary two-qubit states, and two-qubit X states, revealing a direct connection with entanglement for pure systems. We further establish clear operational interpretations of QFI-MIN in quantum parameter estimation, local channel discrimination, and correlation-assisted communication. Its behavior under amplitude damping, depolarizing, and generalized amplitude damping channels demonstrates robustness against environmental noise. The proposed framework provides a physically consistent and operationally meaningful quantifier of quantum correlations, linking nonlocality, quantum metrology, and quantum information processing

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a quantum Fisher information based measurement-induced nonlocality (QFI-MIN) that quantifies correlations via locally invariant unitary dynamics, providing analytical solutions for various states and demonstrating operational interpretations in parameter estimation, channel discrimination, and communication, while showing robustness against noise.
AI.motivation: To develop a physically consistent and operationally meaningful quantifier of quantum correlations that overcomes issues like the local ancilla problem and links nonlocality with quantum metrology.
AI.method: The authors define QFI-MIN based on quantum Fisher information to measure maximal statistical distinguishability under locally invariant unitary dynamics; they derive analytical expressions for pure states, arbitrary two-qubit states, and two-qubit X states.
AI.result: QFI-MIN satisfies positivity, local unitary invariance, monotonicity under local operations, and immunity to the local ancilla problem. It shows a direct connection with entanglement for pure states and demonstrates robustness under amplitude damping, depolarizing, and generalized amplitude damping channels.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework unifies nonlocality, quantum metrology, and quantum information processing within a consistent operational interpretation.

title: Infrared Safety from ZX-Diagrams: A Categorical Proof of Soft-QED as Open Quantum System
summary: The discard ZX-calculus, a diagrammatic language for mixed-state quantum mechanics, is used to give a nonperturbative, categorical proof of the Bloch-Nordsieck cancellation of infrared divergences in QED. Soft photons are treated as an open quantum system: the resolved charged particles and hard photons form the system, while photons below a detector resolution form the environment. The reduced hard channel is a completely positive trace-preserving (CPTP) map, and the soft-photon theorem replaces the full S-matrix by a controlled displacement operator whose Feynman-Vernon influence functional satisfies the equal-history normalization ${\cal F}[J,J]=1 $. In the ZX-calculus, this normalization is a single diagrammatic identity: the doubled displacement diagram collapses to the bare wire under the unitarity, cyclicity, and discard rules. The proof therefore serves as a categorical consistency check on the open-system treatment of soft QED given in a companion paper; it confirms that the physical derivation is logically complete and free of hidden assumptions about the infrared limit. For off-diagonal hard-state elements, the same diagram yields the coherent-state overlap, giving a first-principles account of soft-cloud decoherence. The soft-shell coarse graining is then constructed as a CPTP Schur channel whose infinitesimal limit produces the exact Lindblad generator with jump operators determined by the eikonal emission amplitudes. Finally, a local CPTP-certification pipeline is developed for non-Markovian process tensors, enabling constant-time verification of trace preservation in open quantum simulations. The framework bridges categorical quantum semantics, non-equilibrium field theory, and practical open-system compilation.

AI.tldr: The discard ZX-calculus provides a categorical proof of the Bloch-Nordsieck cancellation of infrared divergences in QED by treating soft photons as an open quantum system, where the soft-photon theorem's influence functional normalization collapses to a diagrammatic identity. The framework yields soft-cloud decoherence, a CPTP Schur channel for coarse-graining, and a local certification pipeline for non-Markovian process tensors.
AI.motivation: To give a nonperturbative, categorical proof of the Bloch-Nordsieck cancellation of infrared divergences in QED, and to provide a logically complete, assumption-free derivation of soft QED as an open quantum system.
AI.method: Uses the discard ZX-calculus (a diagrammatic language for mixed-state quantum mechanics) to treat soft photons as an open quantum environment, with the reduced hard channel as a CPTP map. The soft-photon theorem is recast as a controlled displacement operator whose Feynman-Vernon influence functional satisfies normalization 𝒥[J,J]=1, which collapses diagrammatically via unitarity, cyclicity, and discard rules. The soft-shell coarse-graining is constructed as a CPTP Schur channel whose infinitesimal limit yields a Lindblad generator with eikonal emission amplitudes as jump operators.
AI.result: A nonperturbative categorical proof of infrared divergence cancellation; a first-principles derivation of soft-cloud decoherence from off-diagonal coherent-state overlaps; a CPTP Schur channel for soft-shell coarse-graining; and a local CPTP-certification pipeline for constant-time verification of trace preservation in non-Markovian open quantum simulations.
AI.conclusion: The framework bridges categorical quantum semantics, non-equilibrium field theory, and practical open-system compilation, confirming the logical completeness of the open-system treatment of soft QED.

title: Quantum Eigenvalue Transformation via Linear Combination of Hamiltonian Simulation: A Weyl Calculus Approach
summary: Linear combination of Hamiltonian simulation (LCHS) provides an efficient method for implementing matrix exponentials $e^{-tA}$ on quantum computers. In this paper, we develop LCHS formulas for computing general matrix functions $f(A)$ when $f$ is analytic on the numerical range of $A$, with $A$ possibly non-normal. The essential technical tool is Weyl calculus, which reduces the construction of LCHS formulas for noncommuting operators to scalar Fourier approximation problems. Our construction yields a quantum eigenvalue transformation algorithm with optimal $\mathcal{O}(\log\frac{1}ε)$ query complexity scaling. Furthermore, our Weyl-calculus-based theory gives rise to an ansatz-free convex optimization framework that directly produces discrete LCHS formulas. This circumvents the inefficiencies of traditional quadrature rules and yields formulas highly optimized for coherent implementation on quantum computers. In addition, both our theory and optimization framework apply to the simulation of time-dependent dissipative ODE $\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} t} ψ(t) = -A(t)ψ(t)$, for which we achieve a $2.1\times$ cost reduction over prior art.

AI.tldr: The paper extends Linear Combination of Hamiltonian Simulation (LCHS) to compute general analytic matrix functions $f(A)$ on quantum computers using Weyl calculus, achieving optimal $\mathcal{O}(\log\frac{1}{\varepsilon})$ query complexity and a convex optimization framework that outperforms traditional quadrature rules, with applications to time-dependent dissipative ODEs yielding a $2.1\times$ cost reduction.
AI.motivation: To extend LCHS beyond Hamiltonian simulation ($e^{-tA}$) to general analytic matrix functions $f(A)$ for possibly non-normal $A$, and to overcome inefficiencies of traditional quadrature-based LCHS formula construction.
AI.method: Uses Weyl calculus to reduce the noncommuting operator problem to scalar Fourier approximation; develops an ansatz-free convex optimization framework for directly producing discrete LCHS formulas optimized for coherent quantum implementation.
AI.result: Achieves optimal $\mathcal{O}(\log\frac{1}{\varepsilon})$ query complexity for quantum eigenvalue transformation; $2.1\times$ cost reduction over prior art for time-dependent dissipative ODE simulation.
AI.conclusion: Weyl-calculus-based LCHS provides optimal and efficient quantum algorithms for general matrix functions and time-dependent dissipative ODEs, with a practical optimization framework that eliminates quadrature inefficiencies.

title: Nonperturbative Leakage Elimination Operator-Based Quantum Control Pulse Design Beyond the High Frequency Driving Regime
summary: Precise quantum pulse design is central to achieving high precision quantum control, while level leakage induced by system environment coupling is the bottleneck limiting control precision. The leakage elimination operator (LEO) approach is highly effective at suppressing leakage from target subspace to other leakage spaces. The analytical control conditions under the high frequency driving limit have been derived via the Feshbach PQ partitioning technique. However, low frequency driving is experimentally more feasible, and the driving strength is subject to a fundamental physical bound. In this work, we overcome the high frequency driving limit in the pulse design by recasting the LEO protocol within the nonperturbative Floquet-Magnus framework. Applying the Magnus expansion to Floquet dynamical localization, we establish a generalized optimal control formalism that is applicable to the low frequency regime. We prove that the analytical control conditions derived via the Feshbach PQ partitioning technique are equivalent to the zero order Magnus expansion, and that higher order Magnus terms must be taken into account in the low frequency driving regime. We validate our nonperturbative framework using two examples: near perfect quantum state transfer in a one dimensional spin chain and adiabatic speedup in a two level system, corresponding to time independent and time dependent system Hamiltonians, respectively. Our results provide an effective route for designing control pulses in the low frequency regime, which is promising for practical quantum information processing tasks across diverse experimental platforms, including superconducting qubits and ion traps.

AI.tldr: The paper overcomes the high-frequency driving limit in quantum pulse design by recasting the leakage elimination operator (LEO) protocol within a nonperturbative Floquet-Magnus framework, establishing a generalized optimal control formalism valid for the low-frequency regime, and validating it with quantum state transfer and adiabatic speedup examples.
AI.motivation: Level leakage from system-environment coupling limits quantum control precision. Existing LEO approaches work under high-frequency driving, but low-frequency driving is experimentally more feasible and physically bounded. This work aims to generalize pulse design to the low-frequency regime.
AI.method: The authors recast the LEO protocol using the nonperturbative Floquet-Magnus framework, applying Magnus expansion to Floquet dynamical localization. They prove equivalence between Feshbach PQ-derived conditions and zero-order Magnus expansion, and incorporate higher-order Magnus terms for low-frequency driving.
AI.result: The framework is validated on two examples: near-perfect quantum state transfer in a 1D spin chain (time-independent Hamiltonian) and adiabatic speedup in a two-level system (time-dependent Hamiltonian).
AI.conclusion: The work provides an effective route for designing control pulses in the low-frequency regime, promising for practical quantum information processing across platforms like superconducting qubits and ion traps.

title: Preparation-Space Diagnostics and Logical Information Loss in a Driven Kerr-Cat Qubit
summary: A Kerr-cat qubit encodes a logical bit in the two wells of a parametrically driven nonlinear oscillator, and a logic gate is a transient change of the drive. In the phase plane the gate deforms the double well and can split its separatrix into a turnstile that carries trajectories across the dividing surface between the wells; the same pulse, acting on the quantum oscillator, can corrupt the encoded bit. We study this process over a disk of coherent-state preparations, comparing classical phase-space transport diagnostics with the open-system quantum outcome on a common domain so that the two can be compared point by point. The central finding is that the corruption depends on the full temporal protocol, not on pulse strength alone: a sudden quench erases the bit, whereas a smooth ramp of the same peak amplitude largely preserves it. A finite-time sensitivity field locates the classical transport boundary, and a Loschmidt echo evaluated near the end of the gate predicts the much later quantum outcome. Sweeps of pulse amplitude and width, of cat size, and of engineered two-photon dissipation map where the classical transport picture predicts the quantum loss of the bit and where it does not.

AI.tldr: A Kerr-cat qubit's logical bit can be corrupted by control pulses that deform its double-well potential, with the outcome depending not just on pulse strength but on the temporal protocol—sudden quenches erase the bit while smooth ramps preserve it. Quantum loss is predicted by a finite-time sensitivity field and Loschmidt echo near the gate end, and classical transport diagnostics partially but not fully align with the quantum behavior across parameter sweeps.
AI.motivation: To understand how control pulses intended to implement logic gates on a Kerr-cat qubit inadvertently corrupt the encoded quantum information, and to determine whether classical phase-space transport theory can predict the quantum bit-loss.
AI.method: The study compares classical phase-space transport diagnostics (finite-time sensitivity field, turnstile dynamics) with open-system quantum simulations on a common domain of coherent-state preparations. It examines the effects of pulse protocols (sudden quench vs. smooth ramp), pulse amplitude/width, cat size, and engineered two-photon dissipation. A Loschmidt echo near the gate end is used to predict the quantum outcome.
AI.result: The corruption of the Kerr-cat qubit depends on the full temporal protocol, not just pulse strength: sudden quenches erase the bit while smooth ramps preserve it. The classical transport boundary is located by a finite-time sensitivity field, and a Loschmidt echo evaluated near the end of the gate predicts the later quantum outcome. Parameter sweeps reveal where the classical transport picture accurately predicts quantum loss and where it fails.
AI.conclusion: Classical phase-space transport diagnostics provide partial predictive power for quantum bit corruption in Kerr-cat qubits, but the quantum outcome is governed by the full temporal protocol and requires quantum-specific measures (like the Loschmidt echo) for accurate prediction.

title: Finite-key security analysis of decoy-state QKD with source and detector imperfections
summary: Decoy-state quantum key distribution (QKD) is the most widely adopted approach for overcoming the limitations of imperfect single-photon sources. However, existing security proofs typically either neglect important device imperfections or rely on assumptions that are difficult to justify in realistic high-speed implementations, such as the independent and identically distributed nature of the emitted signals. In this work, we combine and extend several recent theoretical advances to provide a comprehensive analytical finite-key security proof for decoy-state QKD that simultaneously incorporates multiple practically relevant transmitter and receiver imperfections, including state-preparation flaws, bit and basis side-channel leakage and correlations, setting-independent intensity fluctuations, and detection-efficiency mismatches.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a comprehensive analytical finite-key security proof for decoy-state QKD that simultaneously incorporates multiple practical transmitter and receiver imperfections, including state-preparation flaws, side-channel leakage, intensity fluctuations, and detection-efficiency mismatches.
AI.motivation: Existing decoy-state QKD security proofs either neglect important device imperfections or rely on unrealistic assumptions (e.g., independent and identically distributed signals) for high-speed implementations, creating a gap between theory and practice.
AI.method: The authors combine and extend several recent theoretical advances to derive a unified analytical finite-key security proof that jointly accounts for state-preparation flaws, bit and basis side-channel leakage and correlations, setting-independent intensity fluctuations, and detection-efficiency mismatches.
AI.result: A comprehensive security proof that simultaneously addresses multiple practical imperfections in both the transmitter and receiver modules of decoy-state QKD systems.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework bridges the gap between theoretical security and practical high-speed decoy-state QKD implementations by providing a more realistic and rigorous security analysis.

title: BPBO: Blindness-Preserving Brickwork Optimization by Certified Region Resynthesis
comment: 22 pages, 4 figures, 10 tables; ancillary artifact package included
summary: Universal blind quantum computation (UBQC) hides a client's computation by using a computation-independent BFK09 brickwork graph and encoding the computation in measurement angles, which limits the use of graph-changing optimizations. We study blindness-preserving brickwork optimization (BPBO): certified local resynthesis of BFK09-compatible brickwork patterns below the blinding layer. BPBO detects one-, two-, and three-wire regions; for each candidate region it either proves a semantic floor or supplies an executable witness, and it accepts a replacement only after its branch-frame, output-frame, and blinding behavior have been checked. The optimized outputs remain standard brickwork patterns and are evaluated with a logical qubit-recycled UBQC execution stack that runs arbitrary-length patterns using n x 2 active logical qubits. The layer evidence includes a one-wire H-count floor, a two-wire CNOT-cost floor, a three-wire parity-ledger floor, a clean three-cell CCZ witness whose optimality claim is scoped to the CNOT+T phase-gadget family, and an endpoint-target three-cell CCX/Toffoli application witness; the fixed middle-target CCX case is retained as a four-cell fallback. The security statement is a compatibility result: BPBO preserves UBQC blindness at the declared optimized dimensions and remains compatible with inherited verification guarantees under explicit test-round conditions, without introducing a new trap-soundness theorem. On Bell/CX, Grover-2, endpoint-Toffoli, and Grover-3 evaluation cases, BPBO demonstrates certified local reductions; in the largest case, Grover-3, the materialized pattern is reduced from 3 x 725 to 3 x 98 while preserving the expected marked-state statistics up to sampling noise.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces BPBO (Blindness-Preserving Brickwork Optimization), a method to locally optimize BFK09 brickwork patterns used in Universal Blind Quantum Computing (UBQC) without breaking blindness. It detects one-, two-, and three-wire regions, provides certified replacements with semantic floors and executable witnesses, and demonstrates significant pattern reductions (e.g., 3×725 to 3×98 for Grover-3) while preserving blindness and verification guarantees.
AI.motivation: Standard UBQC uses fixed computation-independent brickwork graphs, encoding computation only in measurement angles. This limits graph-changing optimizations. The paper aims to enable local resynthesis of brickwork patterns below the blinding layer while preserving blindness, allowing resource reductions that were previously impossible without compromising security.
AI.method: BPBO performs certified local resynthesis of BFK09-compatible brickwork patterns by detecting one-, two-, and three-wire regions. For each region, it either proves a semantic floor (lower bound) or supplies an executable witness (replacement pattern). Replacements are accepted only after verifying branch-frame, output-frame, and blinding behavior. Optimized patterns are evaluated using a logical qubit-recycled UBQC stack with n×2 active logical qubits for arbitrary-length patterns.
AI.result: On four evaluation cases (Bell/CX, Grover-2, endpoint-Toffoli, Grover-3), BPBO demonstrates certified local reductions. The largest case, Grover-3, shows reduction from 3×725 to 3×98 (roughly 86.5% reduction) while preserving expected marked-state statistics up to sampling noise. Layer evidence includes H-count floor (1-wire), CNOT-cost floor (2-wire), parity-ledger floor (3-wire), and specific CCZ/CCX witnesses.
AI.conclusion: BPBO enables blindness-preserving optimization of brickwork patterns, achieving substantial resource reductions without compromising the UBQC security model. It remains compatible with existing verification guarantees under explicit test-round conditions, without requiring a new trap-soundness theorem.

title: RiverONE: Generating Knowledge-Intensive VLM by Simulated Quantum Machines
summary: Quantum computing provides a powerful paradigm for representing and transforming high-dimensional information through superposition, entanglement, and measurement-induced nonlinear features. While current quantum hardware is not yet practical for direct large-scale vision-language model (VLM) inference, simulated quantum computation can be used during model construction to generate structured parameters for compact classical AI systems. We build RiverONE, a lightweight vision-language model for quantum calibration plot understanding, using simulated quantum computation. It employs a specialized visual encoder and an InternVL-based language backbone. To compensate for compression-induced information loss, we introduce quantum-generated parameters, which are materialized as classical tensors after training. This allows RiverONE to run entirely on classical GPUs at inference time, with no quantum hardware or runtime quantum simulation. With approximately 1.9 billion parameters, RiverONE achieves at least 95\% of the performance of NVIDIA Ising Calibration 1 on quantum calibration plot understanding tasks while using less than 10\% of its parameter count. These results suggest that simulated quantum computation can serve as a practical construction-stage mechanism for building lightweight, knowledge-intensive scientific VLMs. Our code is available at https://github.com/THeWakeSystems/RiverOne.

AI.tldr: RiverONE is a lightweight 1.9B parameter vision-language model for quantum calibration plot understanding that uses simulated quantum computation during construction to generate classical tensor parameters, achieving ≥95% of NVIDIA Ising Calibration 1's performance with <10% of its parameters while running entirely on classical GPUs.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate that simulated quantum computation can be used during model construction (not runtime) to generate structured parameters that enable compact, knowledge-intensive scientific VLMs, addressing the impracticality of direct quantum hardware inference for large-scale VLM tasks.
AI.method: RiverONE employs a specialized visual encoder with an InternVL-based language backbone. It introduces quantum-generated parameters — materialized as classical tensors after training — to compensate for compression-induced information loss. Simulated quantum computation is used only during the construction/training stage.
AI.result: With ~1.9B parameters, RiverONE achieves at least 95% of the performance of NVIDIA Ising Calibration 1 on quantum calibration plot understanding while using less than 10% of its parameter count.
AI.conclusion: Simulated quantum computation can serve as a practical construction-stage mechanism for building lightweight, knowledge-intensive scientific VLMs that run entirely on classical hardware at inference.

title: Temporal modes of quantum states of light scattered by a two-level system
summary: Non-Gaussian quantum states of light are of paramount importance to quantum computing. Nevertheless, their deterministic generation is challenging problem due to the difficulty to control nonlinearities in physical systems. In this work, we characterize the light stemming from one of the most fundamental quantum optics configurations: the unidirectional scattering of multimode and multiphoton light by a two-level system. We provide an analytic and explicit description of the output light solely in terms of the corresponding input temporal modes which allows a straightforward physical interpretation and is computationally more effective compared to numerical methods. Then, we focus on the specific case of the scattering of two photons in a single mode. By numerically decomposing the output state in terms of its principal modes, we find that it is possible to map single-mode two-photon inputs to be into two-mode entangled output states, i.e., two-photon NOON states, to very good approximation. The latter states, in turn, are known to have more Wigner negativity compared to the associated input, which ultimately suggests a potential application of our considered setup in the deterministic generation of non-Gaussian states.

AI.tldr: This paper characterizes light from unidirectional scattering of multimode multiphoton light by a two-level system, showing that single-mode two-photon inputs can be mapped to two-mode entangled NOON states with high Wigner negativity, enabling deterministic generation of non-Gaussian quantum states.
AI.motivation: Non-Gaussian quantum states of light are essential for quantum computing, but their deterministic generation is challenging due to difficulties in controlling nonlinearities in physical systems.
AI.method: The authors provide an analytic description of output light from unidirectional scattering of multimode multiphoton light by a two-level system, expressed solely in terms of input temporal modes. They numerically decompose the output state for the specific case of single-mode two-photon scattering to identify principal modes.
AI.result: Single-mode two-photon inputs can be mapped to two-mode entangled output states (two-photon NOON states) to very good approximation. These NOON states exhibit more Wigner negativity than the input states.
AI.conclusion: The setup shows potential for deterministic generation of non-Gaussian states, as evidenced by the increased Wigner negativity in the output two-mode entangled states.

title: Equality Conditions for an Additive Three-Observable Uncertainty Relation
summary: Uncertainty relations play a fundamental role in quantum mechanics by quantifying the intrinsic limitations on the simultaneous sharpness of incompatible observables. Beyond the standard two-observable product form, additive uncertainty relations for triples of observables provide a natural framework for describing collective constraints among three noncommuting components. In this work, we study an additive uncertainty relation for three Hermitian observables from the viewpoint of rotational symmetry and covariance geometry. We give a short rotational derivation by rotating the observable triple and applying the Robertson uncertainty relation to the two transverse observables. This derivation makes the saturation mechanism transparent and leads to a necessary and sufficient condition for equality for general density operators. In the nontrivial equality case, the covariance ellipsoid of the observable triple degenerates into a disk perpendicular to the expectation value of the commutator vector. We also discuss an inverse construction based on finite-dimensional representations of the Lie algebra \(\mathfrak{su}(2)\), which provides a systematic way to construct observable triples with prescribed saturating states. These results clarify the geometric and representation-theoretic structure underlying the tightness of additive three-observable uncertainty relations.

AI.tldr: This paper derives an additive uncertainty relation for three Hermitian observables using rotational symmetry and covariance geometry, revealing that saturation occurs when the covariance ellipsoid degenerates into a disk perpendicular to the commutator vector expectation, and provides an inverse construction via su(2) Lie algebra representations.
AI.motivation: To understand additive uncertainty relations for triples of observables from a geometric and symmetry perspective, and to clarify the conditions under which such relations are tight.
AI.method: Rotational derivation by applying Robertson's uncertainty relation to transverse observables; analysis of covariance ellipsoid geometry; inverse construction using finite-dimensional representations of su(2).
AI.result: Necessary and sufficient condition for equality: covariance ellipsoid degenerates into a disk perpendicular to the expectation value of the commutator vector. Systematic construction of saturating observable triples via su(2) representations.
AI.conclusion: The tightness of additive three-observable uncertainty relations is governed by geometric (covariance ellipsoid disk degeneracy) and representation-theoretic (su(2) algebra) structures.

title: Deterministic nonlinear bunching of bosons
comment: 8 pages includes references and appendices; 4 + 2 figs
summary: The ability of bosonic energy quanta to bunch together in an energy-conserving interaction is a fundamental feature of quantum harmonic oscillators. Linear systems together with measurement allow for the conditional concentration of energy quanta and, subsequently, breeding of the quantum states, but only with an exponentially decreasing success rate. Deterministic, energy-conserving and unconditional bunching however, requires nonlinearity. We investigate which nonlinear energy-conserving interactions deterministically combine bosons into high number states at the same frequency. We show that in order to do so it is advantageous to use nonlinear interactions involving highly saturable systems, such as qubits, as they preserve the hierarchical quantum non-Gaussian features and are also sufficiently robust against pure loss. Nonlinear bunching therefore demonstrates the advantage of a {\it qubit-inside} nonlinearity and opens new directions in the deterministic preparation, processing, and detection of quantum non-Gaussian states.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates deterministic, energy-conserving, unconditional bunching of bosonic energy quanta into high number states using nonlinear interactions, particularly with highly saturable systems like qubits. The authors show that such nonlinear bunching preserves hierarchical quantum non-Gaussian features and is robust against loss, offering advantages over linear systems with measurement.
AI.motivation: While bosonic energy quanta can bunch together via linear systems with measurement, this approach yields exponentially decreasing success rates. The authors seek a deterministic, energy-conserving, and unconditional bunching mechanism, which requires nonlinearity.
AI.method: The authors investigate which nonlinear energy-conserving interactions can deterministically combine bosons into high number states at the same frequency, with a focus on highly saturable systems such as qubits.
AI.result: Nonlinear interactions involving highly saturable systems (e.g., qubits) are advantageous as they preserve hierarchical quantum non-Gaussian features and are robust against pure loss.
AI.conclusion: Nonlinear bunching demonstrates the advantage of qubit-inside nonlinearity and opens new directions in deterministic preparation, processing, and detection of quantum non-Gaussian states.

title: Coherent Control of Quantum and Classical Correlations in Photoionization
summary: The ability to control quantum correlations in strongly driven systems is a central challenge across quantum science, with implications for ultrafast dynamics, quantum control, and information processing. In photoionization, the emitted electron and residual ion may form an entangled system whose correlations encode the underlying light-matter interaction, yet control of their generation and observable manifestation in continuum systems remains largely unexplored. Here we demonstrate phase-resolved control of electron-ion correlations using phase-locked pulse sequences in the strong-coupling regime. We show that entanglement can be halted and reshaped with attosecond precision, and that phase-dependent correlations can be redistributed into population-based correlations, leading to entanglement that is directly reflected in joint observables. These results establish a route to coherently shape entanglement in photoionization and open new possibilities for accessing and controlling quantum correlations in systems where measurements are intrinsically basis constrained.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates phase-resolved control of electron-ion correlations using phase-locked pulse sequences in strong-coupling photoionization, showing that entanglement can be halted and reshaped with attosecond precision, and phase-dependent correlations can be redistributed into population-based correlations reflected in joint observables.
AI.motivation: Controlling quantum correlations in strongly driven systems is a central challenge across quantum science. In photoionization, electron-ion entanglement encodes the underlying light-matter interaction, yet control of their generation and observable manifestation in continuum systems remains largely unexplored.
AI.method: Using phase-locked pulse sequences in the strong-coupling regime to achieve phase-resolved control of electron-ion correlations, with attosecond precision shaping of entanglement.
AI.result: Entanglement can be halted and reshaped with attosecond precision; phase-dependent correlations can be redistributed into population-based correlations that are directly reflected in joint observables.
AI.conclusion: Establishes a route to coherently shape entanglement in photoionization and opens new possibilities for accessing and controlling quantum correlations in systems where measurements are intrinsically basis constrained.

title: Cooperative control and geometric amplification in dissipative quantum systems
summary: In the control of dissipative quantum systems, the slow relaxation modes usually set the ultimate manipulation timescale. Here we show that this apparent bottleneck can be bypassed: dissipation itself becomes a control resource when fast relaxation channels are deliberately exploited. We demonstrate this mechanism for a qubit subject to non-unital and anisotropic Bloch relaxation. A short coherent pulse first reorients the Bloch vector onto a fast dissipative eigendirection; the subsequent free relaxation then carries the state close to the target, with at most one final corrective pulse. The resulting bang-drift-bang strategy is cooperative: coherent control selects the dissipative channel, while the bath performs most of the transfer. For axial targets, we obtain a closed-form speedup over passive relaxation by a factor of order $κ=T_1/T_2\gg1$. For out-of-equilibrium non-axial targets, an additional off-axis interception mechanism provides a further geometric amplification, allowing the hitting-time speedup, still normalized to the axial passive-reset time, to exceed the axial $κξ$ benchmark by an extra factor of four to five. The mechanism therefore directly connects to standard Bloch-vector qubit platforms, including magnetic-resonance spins, nitrogen-vacancy centers, and superconducting circuits, with potential relevance for quantum-control and fast-reset protocols.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that fast dissipation channels can be exploited as a control resource to speed up quantum state manipulation beyond the slow relaxation bottleneck, using a bang-drift-bang strategy on a qubit with non-unital Bloch relaxation, achieving speedups up to ~$κ$ (axial) or ~$4\text{-}5\times κξ$ (non-axial) relative to passive reset.
AI.motivation: Slow relaxation modes are typically the bottleneck in controlling dissipative quantum systems; the authors aim to demonstrate that this limitation can be bypassed by deliberately using fast dissipation channels as a control resource rather than a hindrance.
AI.method: A qubit subject to non-unital and anisotropic Bloch relaxation is controlled using a "bang-drift-bang" strategy: a short coherent pulse reorients the Bloch vector onto a fast dissipative eigendirection, free relaxation carries the state toward the target, and at most one final corrective pulse is applied. Axial and non-axial (out-of-equilibrium) target scenarios are analyzed analytically and geometrically.
AI.result: For axial targets, a closed-form speedup factor of order $κ = T_1/T_2 \gg 1$ over passive relaxation is achieved. For non-axial targets, an off-axis interception mechanism yields a geometric amplification, giving an extra factor of four to five beyond the axial $κξ$ benchmark.
AI.conclusion: Dissipation can be turned into a control resource, offering significant speedups for quantum-state manipulation in standard qubit platforms such as magnetic-resonance spins, nitrogen-vacancy centers, and superconducting circuits, with relevance for quantum control and fast-reset protocols.

title: Programmable generation of flying cat-qubits
summary: We propose a framework for the direct generation of flying cat-qubit states from vacuum using time-dependent two-photon drives in nonlinear bosonic systems. We study both Kerr-based and two-photon-dissipation-based generation. By engineering Kerr nonlinearity, two-photon driving, and dissipation, we demonstrate logical control of a cat qubit during its generation and emission, while its quantum information is simultaneously shared between the nonlinear system and the propagating output field. We further analyze the effects of photon loss and pure dephasing, showing that both the state generation and logical control remain robust under realistic noise conditions. These results provide a route toward programmable bosonic quantum networks and future propagating error-correctable encodings.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a framework to directly generate flying cat-qubit states from vacuum using time-dependent two-photon drives in nonlinear bosonic systems, studying both Kerr-based and two-photon-dissipation-based approaches. It demonstrates robust logical control during generation and emission under realistic noise conditions, offering a path toward programmable bosonic quantum networks.
AI.motivation: To enable direct generation and logical control of flying cat qubits from vacuum, advancing the realization of programmable bosonic quantum networks and propagating error-correctable encodings.
AI.method: The authors engineer Kerr nonlinearity, two-photon driving, and dissipation in nonlinear bosonic systems to generate and control flying cat-qubit states via time-dependent two-photon drives, comparing Kerr-based and two-photon-dissipation-based generation schemes.
AI.result: Logical control of a cat qubit is achieved during generation and emission, with quantum information simultaneously shared between the nonlinear system and the propagating output field. The generation and control remain robust under realistic photon loss and pure dephasing noise.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a viable route toward programmable bosonic quantum networks and future propagating error-correctable encodings.

title: Enhanced Magnon Synchronization in Coupled WGM Optomagnonic Resonators with Phase-Dependent Photon Hopping
summary: We investigate quantum synchronization in a coupled cavity optomagnonic system which consists of two spatially separated optical whispering-gallery-mode (WGM) resonators and each resonator is also coupled to a yttrium iron garnet (YIG) sphere through the optomagnonic interaction. Phase-dependent single-photon hopping factor couples the two optical resonators and provides an indirect interaction between the two distant magnon modes. We then investigate complete synchronization, φ-synchronization, and quantum phase synchronization using the covariance-matrix formalism as well as also studying the effects of the hopping term on the overall synchronization dynamics of two distant magnon modes. It can be seen that the photon-hopping phase provides an efficient way to control the synchronization dynamics and when it is varied from 0 to π, the magnon trajectories gradually evolve from weakly correlated motion to a highly synchronized state, which is also accompanied by a significant reduction in the synchronization error.
