The influence of the photon-hopping strength and thermal fluctuations is also investigated, where it can be seen that stronger photon hopping enhances all synchronization measures, while thermal noise weakens the coherent correlations responsible for synchronized dynamics. Our results demonstrate that the phase of the hopping factor offers a simple and effective approach for controlling synchronization dynamics in WGM based coupled cavity optomagnonic systems and also provide a useful route towards coherent control of collective magnon dynamics in such quantum optomganonic devices.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates quantum synchronization in a coupled cavity optomagnonic system with two optical WGM resonators, each coupled to a YIG sphere. The phase-dependent photon-hopping factor enables control of synchronization between distant magnon modes, with the hopping phase providing an effective knob to transition from weakly correlated to highly synchronized states.
AI.motivation: To understand and control quantum synchronization dynamics in coupled cavity optomagnonic systems, specifically between distant magnon modes, and to demonstrate that the phase of the photon-hopping factor offers a simple control mechanism for synchronization.
AI.method: The authors model a system of two spatially separated optical WGM resonators, each coupled to a YIG sphere via optomagnonic interaction, with phase-dependent single-photon hopping between the resonators. They analyze complete synchronization, φ-synchronization, and quantum phase synchronization using the covariance-matrix formalism.
AI.result: Varying the photon-hopping phase from 0 to π transitions magnon trajectories from weakly correlated to highly synchronized motion with reduced synchronization error. Stronger photon hopping enhances all synchronization measures, while thermal noise weakens coherent correlations responsible for synchronized dynamics.
AI.conclusion: The phase of the hopping factor provides a simple and effective approach for controlling synchronization dynamics in WGM-based coupled cavity optomagnonic systems, offering a route towards coherent control of collective magnon dynamics in quantum optomagnonic devices.

title: A Modular Benchmark of Variational Quantum Attack Algorithms for S-DES
summary: Variational quantum algorithms (VQAs) have emerged as a promising approach to quantum cryptanalysis on noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices. Although numerous variational attack schemes have been proposed for symmetric cryptosystems, a systematic and modular benchmarking framework to evaluate their performance is still lacking. In this work, we present a comprehensive benchmark study of variational quantum attacks on the Simplified Data Encryption Standard (S-DES), focusing on the modular design choices that determine attack efficiency. We formulate variational quantum attacks within a unified framework consisting of four components: initial state preparation, parameterized circuit (Ansatz) design, cost function construction, and classical optimization. Through numerical simulations, we systematically compare representative design alternatives and evaluate their combinations in terms of convergence behavior, success probability, and effective time complexity. We further introduce standardized metrics for assessing variational quantum attack performance. Our results reveal clear performance hierarchies among different modular configurations and show that carefully optimized designs can significantly outperform naive quantum search. This work establishes a principled benchmark methodology for variational quantum cryptanalysis and positions S-DES as a practical testbed for evaluating quantum attacks on symmetric ciphers in the NISQ era.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a comprehensive benchmark framework for evaluating variational quantum attacks on the S-DES cipher, systematically comparing modular design choices (initial state, ansatz, cost function, optimizer) and showing that optimized designs outperform naive quantum search.
AI.motivation: While variational quantum algorithms show promise for cryptanalysis on NISQ devices, there is no systematic, modular benchmarking framework to evaluate their performance on symmetric cryptosystems.
AI.method: The authors formulate variational quantum attacks as a unified framework with four components: initial state preparation, parameterized circuit (ansatz) design, cost function construction, and classical optimization. They perform numerical simulations comparing representative design choices using metrics like convergence behavior, success probability, and effective time complexity.
AI.result: Clear performance hierarchies among different modular configurations are identified; carefully optimized designs significantly outperform naive quantum search. Standardized metrics for assessing variational quantum attack performance are introduced.
AI.conclusion: This work establishes a principled benchmark methodology for variational quantum cryptanalysis and positions S-DES as a practical testbed for evaluating quantum attacks on symmetric ciphers in the NISQ era.

title: Spin bath mediated long-lived coherent oscillations of NV centers in diamond
summary: Decoherence is the biggest bottleneck in all quantum technologies. For nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond, the loss of coherence is caused by the electron and nuclear spin bath of the diamond lattice. Here, we demonstrate that the spin bath - that typically causes decoherence - entangles the spin states of the NV electron and the host $^{14}$N nucleus. The many-body interaction between the $^{14}$N nucleus - electron - bath spins at an energy level anti-crossing occurring for an applied magnetic field orientation perpendicular to the NV axis is responsible for this effect. This is observed experimentally on NV ensembles via electron spin-echo measurements, where the echo envelope is modulated at the frequency of a $^{14}$N nuclear spin transition. Using numerical simulations, we show that the spin bath coupling to the NV centers is essential for observing this modulation. Due to the zero first-order Zeeman effect at the anti-crossing, the observed oscillations have long spin-echo coherence times, 2--3 times those at the parallel magnetic field orientation. The oscillation frequency is highly stable and robust against environmental fluctuations. These findings provide new opportunities for fundamental studies of many-body physics and quantum sensing.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates that the spin bath, typically causing decoherence in NV centers, actually entangles the NV electron with the host ¹⁴N nucleus at a specific energy-level anti-crossing (magnetic field perpendicular to NV axis). This produces long-lived echo modulations with coherence times 2-3 times longer than parallel fields, offering new quantum sensing and many-body physics opportunities.
AI.motivation: Decoherence is the primary bottleneck in quantum technologies, particularly for NV centers in diamond where the electron and nuclear spin baths cause coherence loss. The authors aim to understand and exploit the many-body interactions at an energy-level anti-crossing to potentially turn the decohering bath into a resource.
AI.method: Experimental electron spin-echo measurements on NV ensembles, combined with numerical simulations, performed at an energy-level anti-crossing with magnetic field orientation perpendicular to the NV axis.
AI.result: The echo envelope is modulated at the ¹⁴N nuclear spin transition frequency, with coherence times 2-3 times longer than at parallel magnetic field orientation. The oscillation frequency is highly stable and robust against environmental fluctuations. Simulations confirm the spin bath coupling is essential for this modulation.
AI.conclusion: The many-body interaction at the anti-crossing turns the decohering spin bath into an entangling resource, producing long-lived coherent oscillations. This provides new opportunities for studying many-body physics and advancing quantum sensing technologies.

title: Quantum percolation theory for dynamic propagation connectivity of transport networks
summary: Connectivity degradation in transport networks under structural disturbance is a central problem in network resilience research. Existing methods rely mainly on percolation theory and topological connectivity measures. They focus on whether paths exist and whether connected components fragment. These approaches cannot capture functional degradation where network topology remains intact but propagation ability has already declined substantially. This paper introduces quantum percolation theory into transport network connectivity analysis and proposes Dynamic Propagation Connectivity (DPC) as a new measure that characterises network propagation ability under disturbance. By mapping a transport network under disturbance into a propagation operator system, this paper establishes a spectral analysis framework for DPC and defines the time-averaged participation index as its core quantification. This paper provides a series of rigorous theoretical results. DPC remains constant under homogeneous disturbance and degrades under heterogeneous disturbance. This paper establishes a quantitative relationship between the degradation rate, the minimum eigenvalue spacing of the propagation operator, and heterogeneous deviation strength. This paper proves a separation theorem between DPC and algebraic connectivity. It derives an analytical expression for DPC and a second-order perturbation approximation on the ring graph. Numerical experiments on three transport benchmark networks verify all theoretical conclusions and confirm degradation monotonicity, separation from algebraic connectivity, and degradation amplification by network size. This paper provides a theoretical framework for transport network resilience assessment that goes beyond topological connectivity.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Dynamic Propagation Connectivity (DPC), a quantum percolation-based measure for transport network resilience that captures functional degradation beyond topological connectivity, with rigorous theoretical results on degradation behavior under heterogeneous disturbances.
AI.motivation: Existing network resilience methods rely on percolation theory and topological connectivity measures that only detect path existence or component fragmentation, failing to capture functional degradation where network topology remains intact but propagation ability declines.
AI.method: The paper maps a transport network under disturbance into a propagation operator system, establishes a spectral analysis framework for DPC, defines the time-averaged participation index as core quantification, and derives analytical expressions with second-order perturbation approximation on ring graphs.
AI.result: DPC remains constant under homogeneous disturbance and degrades under heterogeneous disturbance. A quantitative relationship is established between degradation rate, minimum eigenvalue spacing, and heterogeneous deviation strength. A separation theorem between DPC and algebraic connectivity is proved. Numerical experiments on three benchmark networks verify all theoretical conclusions.
AI.conclusion: This paper provides a theoretical framework for transport network resilience assessment that goes beyond topological connectivity, capturing functional propagation degradation under structural disturbances.

title: Quantum percolation based dynamic propagation connectivity for critical-area identification in transport networks
summary: Transport networks often lose functionality through gradual degradation in link operating conditions before topological disconnection occurs. Link-centred and binary percolation measures identify important facilities or connectivity failures, but they provide limited information on which spatial areas cause the largest loss of network-wide propagation capability. This paper develops a Dynamic Propagation Connectivity (DPC) metric based on quantum percolation for critical-area identification in transport networks. Time-varying link travel times are converted into continuous propagation strengths, which define a Hermitian propagation operator at each observation time. Candidate regions are then evaluated by a regional degradation experiment that measures the resulting loss of DPC. The method is applied to a benchmark Sioux Falls network and six Florida road networks during the post-Hurricane Irma disruption and recovery period, using 1,281 five-minute observation times. The benchmark confirms that the regional DPC score identifies a predefined structurally critical corridor. In the Florida networks, the identified critical areas differ from regions selected by link count, local degradation, edge betweenness, algebraic connectivity, and classical percolation. In Networks 1 to 4, DPC and classical percolation rankings have negative Spearman correlations, showing that continuous propagation degradation and binary fragmentation reveal different vulnerability patterns. Robustness tests under alternative travel time scaling, degradation strength, and grid size show stable results, with mean rank agreement between 0.84 and 0.96. The findings extend transport resilience analysis based on percolation from binary connectivity loss to continuous propagation degradation and provide a spatial diagnostic tool for regional monitoring, emergency planning, and recovery prioritisation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a Dynamic Propagation Connectivity (DPC) metric based on quantum percolation to identify critical spatial areas in transport networks experiencing gradual degradation, moving beyond traditional binary connectivity measures.
AI.motivation: Transport networks lose functionality through gradual degradation before topological disconnection, but existing link-centred and binary percolation measures cannot identify which spatial areas cause the largest loss of network-wide propagation capability.
AI.method: The DPC metric converts time-varying link travel times into continuous propagation strengths to define a Hermitian propagation operator. Candidate regions are evaluated via a regional degradation experiment measuring DPC loss. The method was tested on a Sioux Falls benchmark and six Florida road networks during post-Hurricane Irma disruption using 1,281 five-minute observations.
AI.result: The benchmark validated DPC's ability to identify a structurally critical corridor. In Florida networks, DPC identified areas differing from conventional metrics (link count, edge betweenness, algebraic connectivity, classical percolation). DPC and classical percolation rankings showed negative Spearman correlations in Networks 1-4. Robustness tests showed stable results (mean rank agreement 0.84-0.96).
AI.conclusion: The DPC metric extends percolation-based transport resilience analysis from binary connectivity loss to continuous propagation degradation, offering a spatial diagnostic tool for regional monitoring, emergency planning, and recovery prioritisation.

title: Photonic Violation of Wigner's Inequality
summary: Teaching quantum mechanics is challenging, not least because the theory often conflicts with our classical worldview. Quantum correlations in particular are notoriously counter-intuitive. Their non-classical behavior is typically revealed through Bell-type inequalities. Among these, Wigner's Inequality constitutes a particularly accessible test, as it relies on minimal set-theoretic assumptions. In this pedagogical paper, we derive Wigner's Inequality, describe a quantum-optical setup to experimentally violate it, and provide access to the raw data, enabling students and instructors to perform their own analyses. Our measured data shows clear violations of Wigner's Inequality, directly illustrating the non-classical nature of quantum correlations. By connecting theory, experiment, and data analysis, this paper equips educators with a resource for engaging students in authentic scientific practice and developing a deeper understanding of quantum systems.

AI.tldr: This pedagogical paper derives Wigner's Inequality, describes a quantum-optical experiment that violates it, and provides raw data for students to analyze, demonstrating the non-classical nature of quantum correlations.
AI.motivation: Teaching quantum mechanics is challenging due to conflicts with classical intuition, particularly regarding quantum correlations. The authors aim to provide an accessible, hands-on resource that connects theory, experiment, and data analysis for educators.
AI.method: The paper derives Wigner's Inequality (a Bell-type inequality based on set-theoretic assumptions), describes a quantum-optical experimental setup to test it, and provides access to raw experimental data for independent analysis.
AI.result: Measured data shows clear violations of Wigner's Inequality, directly illustrating the non-classical nature of quantum correlations.
AI.conclusion: This resource equips educators with a tool for engaging students in authentic scientific practice, helping them develop a deeper understanding of quantum systems through the combination of theoretical derivation, experimental demonstration, and hands-on data analysis.

title: Action on the Sphere: An Interfering Mean-Field Propagator for the Bose-Hubbard Dimer
summary: The Bose-Hubbard system has been studied extensively both theoretically and experimentally, in particular in the context of ultracold atomic gases in optical lattices. Even in the two-mode case the many-particle dynamics display complex interference effects resulting in revival and breakdown phenomena as well as tunnelling. The most basic theoretical description is the mean-field approximation, which can be derived from a time-dependent variational principle assuming the many-particle wave function is an SU(2) coherent state. Here we build on this to construct a simple initial-value coherent state propagator, summing over mean-field trajectories and keeping track of their phases, given by the corresponding mean-field actions. This yields an approximation to the full time-dependent many-particle state, and is able to reproduce breakdown and revival dynamics. Applying a time-slicing procedure on top of this, we are able to accurately capture many-particle tunnelling effects. While in this paper we focus our analysis on the Bose-Hubbard dimer, the methods developed can be applied to more general SU(2) Hamiltonians, and can be extended to SU(M) systems.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a coherent state propagator for the Bose-Hubbard dimer that sums over mean-field trajectories with phase information, capturing revival, breakdown, and tunneling dynamics beyond standard mean-field theory, with potential generalization to SU(M) systems.
AI.motivation: To construct a simple yet accurate approximation beyond mean-field theory for the Bose-Hubbard system that captures complex many-particle interference effects such as revival, breakdown, and tunneling, which the standard mean-field approximation fails to reproduce.
AI.method: The authors build a coherent state propagator from a time-dependent variational principle using SU(2) coherent states. They sum over mean-field trajectories while retaining phase information via mean-field actions, and apply a time-slicing procedure to capture tunneling effects.
AI.result: The propagator reproduces breakdown and revival dynamics, and with time-slicing, accurately captures many-particle tunneling effects in the Bose-Hubbard dimer.
AI.conclusion: The methods are applicable to general SU(2) Hamiltonians and extendable to SU(M) systems, offering a tractable semiclassical approach for many-body quantum dynamics.

title: Quantum Lazy Sampling and Path Recording for Any Group
summary:
A central challenge in quantum algorithms and cryptography is reasoning about algorithms with oracle access to a random group element (e.g. a random function, permutation, or unitary). Can we efficiently simulate such algorithms? Can we determine what they know after t queries? A classical tool for this is lazy sampling: the oracle does not commit to the full group element upfront, but rather samples partial information about it on the fly. We study a quantum analog of lazy sampling: compressed oracles (or recording oracles). These are quantum data structures that allow on-the-fly simulation for quantum queries, originally introduced by Zhandry (CRYPTO '19) for random functions, and generalized to unitaries by Ma-Huang (STOC '25) and permutations by Carolan (STOC '26), and used to great effect in security proofs and lower bounds due to their interpretability.
  We define and analyze a general-purpose and interpretable path-recording oracle, derived from first principles, that perfectly simulates random elements of any closed subgroup of $U(N)$. Our oracle stores, in superposition, t input-output pairs, with updates described in terms of the commutant of the group's tensor power representation. This transparently records the information the algorithm has learned. Our oracle builds on recent work of Grinko-Yoshida (QIP '26), who gave a different general-purpose compressed oracle without clear interpretability.
  One interesting application of our path-recording is allowing direct comparisons between compressed oracles of different groups, giving a new technique for proving pseudorandomness results. For example, comparing $S_N$ and $U(N)$ yields what is arguably the simplest construction to date of pseudorandom unitaries: the product PC of a pseudorandom permutation and a random Clifford, improving on the prior PFC construction (Metger-Poremba-Sinha-Yuen, FOCS '24; Ma-Huang, STOC '25).

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a general-purpose path-recording oracle that simulates random elements of any closed subgroup of U(N), storing t input-output pairs in superposition. This interpretable oracle enables direct comparisons between compressed oracles of different groups, yielding a simpler construction of pseudorandom unitaries (product of a pseudorandom permutation and a random Clifford).
AI.motivation: Efficiently simulating quantum algorithms that query random group elements (functions, permutations, unitaries) and determining what information they learn after t queries is a central challenge. While classical lazy sampling solves this, a quantum analog—compressed oracles—existed only for specific groups (functions, unitaries, permutations) without a general, interpretable framework.
AI.method: The authors construct a general-purpose path-recording oracle from first principles that works for any closed subgroup of U(N). The oracle stores t input-output pairs in superposition, with update rules derived from the commutant of the group's tensor power representation. This builds on Grinko-Yoshida's non-interpretable general compressed oracle but adds clear interpretability.
AI.result: The path-recording oracle allows direct comparisons between compressed oracles of different groups. Comparing S_N and U(N) yields a simplified construction of pseudorandom unitaries: the product PC of a pseudorandom permutation and a random Clifford, improving on the prior PFC construction.
AI.conclusion: The general interpretable compressed oracle provides a foundational tool for quantum algorithm analysis and cryptography, enabling new pseudorandomness results and simplifying prior constructions.

title: Thermometry with multilevel transmon probes
summary: Superconducting transmon systems are promising platforms for nanoscale thermometry due to their high sensitivity to environmental fluctuations. Their intrinsic anharmonicity, which is essential for qubit operations, gives rise to a non-equidistant energy spectrum that significantly affects the thermal populations and, consequently, the thermometric sensitivity. In this work, we investigate the ultimate quantum limits of temperature estimation with a transmon beyond the two-level approximation. We compare the thermometric performance of three complementary models: the qubit, a harmonic oscillator and a weakly anharmonic Duffing oscillator, evaluating their corresponding quantum Fisher information (QFI) as a function of the temperature. We show that the multilevel anharmonic structure of the transmon affects its thermometric precision. Indeed, including higher excited states enhances the maximum amount of information that can be extracted about the system temperature, compared to a qubit probe. Furthermore, we address a fundamental limitation of the standard quartic truncation, which yields a potential that is unbounded from below and supports only spurious metastable states. By introducing bounded anharmonic models, namely a confined quartic potential and a sextic correction term, we assess the robustness of the thermometric precision beyond the Duffing regime. Our results provide practical guidelines for transmon-based nanoscale thermometry and clarify the role of the anharmonic multilevel spectrum in quantum temperature estimation.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the ultimate quantum limits of temperature estimation using superconducting transmon systems beyond the two-level approximation. By comparing qubit, harmonic oscillator, and Duffing oscillator models, the authors show that the multilevel anharmonic structure of transmon enhances thermometric precision. They also address limitations of standard quartic truncation by introducing bounded anharmonic models (confined quartic and sextic potentials) to assess robustness of thermometric precision.
AI.motivation: To investigate the ultimate quantum limits of temperature estimation with a transmon beyond the two-level approximation, addressing how its intrinsic anharmonicity and multilevel structure affect thermometric sensitivity.
AI.method: The authors compare three complementary models: the qubit (two-level), a harmonic oscillator, and a weakly anharmonic Duffing oscillator, evaluating their quantum Fisher information (QFI) as a function of temperature. They also introduce bounded anharmonic models (confined quartic potential and sextic correction) to address the unbounded-from-below issue of the standard quartic truncation.
AI.result: Including higher excited states in the transmon enhances the maximum amount of information extractable about the system temperature compared to a qubit probe. The standard quartic truncation yields an unbounded potential with spurious metastable states; bounded anharmonic models provide more robust thermometric precision beyond the Duffing regime.
AI.conclusion: The multilevel anharmonic structure of transmon significantly affects thermometric precision, and bounded anharmonic models offer practical guidelines for transmon-based nanoscale thermometry, clarifying the role of the anharmonic multilevel spectrum in quantum temperature estimation.

title: All-optical switching of continuous-variable entanglement in an absorption-suppressed plasmonic nanodimer
summary: A subwavelength quantum-photonic circuit element should simultaneously generate nonclassical light, suppress plasmonic loss, and remain dynamically tunable. We show that an orthogonal plasmonic nanorod dimer can satisfy all three requirements. A phase-locked control polarization induces plasmonic refractive-index enhancement, driving the probe response toward a near-zero-extinction regime while simultaneously tuning the local second-harmonic parametric interaction. The resulting nonlinear plasmonic source operates in an absorption-suppressed regime and enables all-optical control of quantum correlations. We demonstrate switchable logarithmic negativity and single-mode nonclassicality, establishing a route toward actively tunable quantum-plasmonic circuit elements operating well below the diffraction limit.

AI.tldr: An orthogonal plasmonic nanorod dimer enables subwavelength quantum-photonic circuitry with simultaneous nonclassical light generation, plasmonic loss suppression, and dynamic tunability via polarization-controlled refractive-index enhancement and second-harmonic parametric interaction.
AI.motivation: A subwavelength quantum-photonic circuit element should simultaneously generate nonclassical light, suppress plasmonic loss, and remain dynamically tunable—goals that are typically conflicting and unmet by existing designs.
AI.method: The authors use an orthogonal plasmonic nanorod dimer with phase-locked control polarization to induce plasmonic refractive-index enhancement, driving the probe response toward a near-zero-extinction regime while simultaneously tuning local second-harmonic parametric interaction.
AI.result: The nonlinear plasmonic source operates in an absorption-suppressed regime and demonstrates switchable logarithmic negativity and single-mode nonclassicality.
AI.conclusion: This establishes a route toward actively tunable quantum-plasmonic circuit elements operating well below the diffraction limit.

title: Phase-Altered Interleaved Randomized Benchmarking for Compiled Quantum Gates
summary:
Interleaved randomized benchmarking (IRB) provides a scalable estimate of a gate's error rate, but its standard guarantees require the interleaved gate to be Clifford~\cite{Magesan2012Interleaved,magesan2012characterizing}. In superconducting processors, many non-Clifford phase gates in compiled circuits are implemented virtually as software-defined frame updates rather than as additional control pulses~\cite{mckay2017efficient}. This raises the question of whether inserting or removing such virtual phases measurably changes IRB error estimates.
  We introduce \emph{phase-altered interleaved randomized benchmarking} (PA-IRB), a paired-IRB diagnostic protocol comparing phase-stripped and phase-dressed Clifford interleaving gates derived from the same compiled implementation. PA-IRB reports $Δr=r_d-r_s$ with combined uncertainty to test whether virtual phase gates affect the extracted IRB decay beyond statistical error.
  As a case study, we apply PA-IRB to a compiled Toffoli gate executed on IBM superconducting processors, where the constituent $T/T^\dagger$ gates are implemented as virtual $Z$ rotations. Across tested calibration runs, $Δr$ is consistent with zero within uncertainty, indicating that virtual phase addition or removal does not measurably alter the IRB-derived error estimate under the employed compilation and execution stack. More generally, PA-IRB provides a lightweight, abstraction-aware diagnostic for benchmarking workflows involving software-defined phase operations. The same paired comparison can also be used to place operational bounds on the contribution of non-Clifford components to the compiled gate error, even when those components are physically executed rather than implemented virtually.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces PA-IRB, a paired-IRB diagnostic protocol that compares phase-stripped and phase-dressed Clifford gates to test whether virtual phase gates (software-defined frame updates) measurably affect interleaved randomized benchmarking error estimates. Applied to a compiled Toffoli gate on IBM superconducting processors, Δr is consistent with zero, indicating virtual phases do not alter IRB error estimates.
AI.motivation: Standard IRB guarantees require interleaved gates to be Clifford, yet many non-Clifford phase gates in superconducting processors are implemented virtually as software-defined frame updates. It is unclear whether inserting or removing such virtual phases measurably changes IRB error estimates.
AI.method: PA-IRB (Phase-Altered Interleaved Randomized Benchmarking) is a paired-IRB diagnostic protocol that compares phase-stripped (r_s) and phase-dressed (r_d) Clifford interleaving gates derived from the same compiled implementation, reporting Δr = r_d - r_s with combined uncertainty.
AI.result: Applied to a compiled Toffoli gate on IBM superconducting processors, Δr is consistent with zero within uncertainty across tested calibration runs, indicating virtual phase addition/removal does not measurably alter IRB-derived error estimates.
AI.conclusion: PA-IRB provides a lightweight, abstraction-aware diagnostic for benchmarking workflows involving software-defined phase operations, and can also place operational bounds on the contribution of non-Clifford components to compiled gate error.

title: Learning the structure of open quantum systems
summary:
We design an algorithm for learning the coefficients of an $n$-qubit constant-local Lindbladian to $\varepsilon$ error with $O(g d^2 \log(n) / \varepsilon^2)$ total evolution time, where $g$ is the single-site energy and $d$ is the (approximate) degree of the interaction graph. Though Lindbladians present new challenges not present in the special case of Hamiltonians, our algorithm achieves the suite of desiderata attained by state-of-the-art Hamiltonian learning algorithms: (1) it uses non-adaptive, ancilla-free randomized Pauli measurement circuits with a time resolution of only $Θ(1/g)$; (2) it works without knowledge of the structure of the unknown Lindbladian; (3) it depends on a smooth form of degree, thereby supporting the learning of quasi-local and power-law Lindbladians.
  Our algorithm is a simple iterative method, where the objective function consists of Fourier coefficients of the Lindbladian restricted to few-site regions. Its analysis identifies the difficulty unique to open systems, which we call "confusing" terms. For settings where the "confusion" is limited, the performance of the algorithm improves. We demonstrate this for the case of structure learning of Hamiltonians from access to real-time evolution, where we obtain a new algorithm that is significantly simpler than previous work. In addition, using the same iterative method, we design the first efficient algorithm for structure learning Hamiltonians from high-temperature Gibbs states.

AI.tldr: An algorithm for learning constant-local Lindbladians with O(g d² log(n) / ε²) evolution time using non-adaptive, ancilla-free randomized Pauli measurements, without knowing the Lindbladian structure, and handling quasi-local/power-law interactions.
AI.motivation: To extend Hamiltonian learning techniques to open quantum systems (Lindbladians), addressing unique challenges like "confusing" terms that do not appear in closed-system Hamiltonian learning.
AI.method: A simple iterative method using Fourier coefficients of the Lindbladian restricted to few-site regions, with randomized Pauli measurement circuits at Θ(1/g) time resolution.
AI.result: Achieves O(g d² log(n) / ε²) total evolution time; works without prior knowledge of Lindbladian structure; supports quasi-local and power-law Lindbladians; yields simpler Hamiltonian structure learning from real-time evolution and first efficient algorithm for structure learning from high-temperature Gibbs states.
AI.conclusion: Open-system Lindbladian learning is feasible with similar efficiency to Hamiltonian learning, with performance improving when "confusion" is limited, enabling new applications in Hamiltonian structure learning from Gibbs states.

title: Blueprint for a fault-tolerant compound photon-atom quantum architecture
summary: Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires architectures that simultaneously address scalability, connectivity, and error correction under realistic noise constraints. We present a compound photonic-atomic quantum computing platform that uses cavity QED to realize near-deterministic entangling operations between flying photonic qubits and stationary atomic qubits. Photons provide long-range connectivity and scalability via measurement-based quantum computing (MBQC), while atoms supply reusable, near-deterministic resources for photon generation and entanglement, overcoming the inefficiency of purely photonic platforms. The core primitive is a symmetrized Duan-Kimble photon-atom controlled-phase (CZ) gate, robust to experimental imperfections and high-fidelity. Using single $^{87}$Rb atoms coupled to optical cavities, we give protocols for state preparation, measurement, photon generation, and entangling gates on tens-of-nanosecond timescales, and show how large-scale cluster states with effectively unrestricted connectivity and reduced overhead can be generated through atomic reuse. We analyze fault tolerance on the Raussendorf-Harrington-Goyal (RHG) lattice with a hardware-aware noise model capturing asymmetric loss and correlated photonic-atomic errors. Logical memory simulations yield a photon-loss threshold near $2.6\%$ per physical gate ($\sim$15\% total per trajectory). The full Clifford set -- Hadamard, phase, CNOT -- is implementable transversally or fold-transversally at thresholds matching the identity channel, and we propose two non-Clifford resource-state routes (code teleportation and magic state cultivation) within the foliated cluster-state architecture.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a hybrid photonic-atomic quantum computing platform using cavity QED, achieving near-deterministic entangling operations, large-scale cluster states via atomic reuse, and a photon-loss threshold of ~2.6% per gate on the RHG lattice with full Clifford implementability.
AI.motivation: To address the scalability, connectivity, and error correction challenges in fault-tolerant quantum computing by combining the strengths of photonic (long-range connectivity, scalability via MBQC) and atomic (near-deterministic resources, reusability) platforms, overcoming inefficiencies in purely photonic approaches.
AI.method: A compound photonic-atomic platform using cavity QED with a symmetrized Duan-Kimble photon-atom CZ gate, protocols for state preparation, measurement, photon generation, and entangling gates with single ⁸⁷Rb atoms in optical cavities. Large-scale cluster states are generated via atomic reuse. Fault tolerance is analyzed on the RHG lattice with a hardware-aware noise model capturing asymmetric loss and correlated errors.
AI.result: Photon-loss threshold near 2.6% per physical gate (~15% total per trajectory). Full Clifford set (Hadamard, phase, CNOT) implementable transversally or fold-transversally at thresholds matching the identity channel. Two non-Clifford resource-state routes proposed within the foliated cluster-state architecture.
AI.conclusion: The hybrid photonic-atomic architecture provides a viable path toward fault-tolerant quantum computing with realistic noise constraints, achieving competitive error thresholds and scalable connectivity.

title: Provable Quantum Advantage for Dynamical Phase Transition
summary: The universal scaling of critical behavior in phase transitions is a cornerstone of physics. Dynamical quantum phase transitions (DQPTs) are their nonequilibrium analogues: abrupt nonanalyticities that emerge as a quantum system evolves in time. Yet the hardness and cost of detecting this phenomenon remain largely unexplored. We prove that estimating DQPT to a certain precision is intractable even for quantum computers, whereas deciding a subsystem variant of DQPT is as hard as simulating generic quantum circuits, implying a provable exponential quantum advantage. Furthermore, to search for critical times of local DQPTs, we show a quadratically faster quantum algorithm that estimates observables of Hamiltonian dynamics at multiple time points with Heisenberg-limited precision and sublinear scaling in the number of time points. Moreover, through encoding classical evolution into quantum dynamics, our framework enables broader quantum speedups for detecting anomalous phenomena in classical systems.

AI.tldr: This paper proves that estimating dynamical quantum phase transitions (DQPTs) is intractable even for quantum computers, while deciding a subsystem variant offers provable exponential quantum advantage. It also presents a quadratic speedup quantum algorithm for finding DQPT critical times and extends quantum advantages to detecting anomalies in classical systems.
AI.motivation: The hardness and computational cost of detecting dynamical quantum phase transitions (DQPTs) remain largely unexplored, motivating a rigorous complexity-theoretic analysis of DQPT estimation and detection.
AI.method: The paper employs complexity theory to prove the intractability of estimating DQPTs, demonstrates equivalence between subsystem DQPT and simulating generic quantum circuits, and develops a quantum algorithm with Heisenberg-limited precision and sublinear time-point scaling for searching critical times.
AI.result: Estimating DQPT to certain precision is intractable for quantum computers; subsystem DQPT is as hard as simulating generic quantum circuits (exponential quantum advantage); a quadratically faster algorithm for critical time search with Heisenberg-limited precision and sublinear scaling is achieved.
AI.conclusion: DQPTs exhibit rich computational complexity, with provable quantum advantage for subsystem variants and practical algorithmic speedups, also extending to classical anomaly detection via quantum dynamics encoding.

title: Quantum Computations on Fusion Blanket Molten Salts
summary: Molten salts such as FLiBe (2LiF--BeF$_2$) are leading blanket materials for breeding and recovering tritium in fusion reactors. Predicting tritium speciation requires accurate electronic ground-state energies for representative molten-salt clusters, a demanding task for correlated electronic-structure methods. Here we report the first application of heterogeneous quantum--classical computing to tritium binding in FLiBe. Clusters drawn from ab initio molecular dynamics are partitioned by an embedded-wavefunction (EWF) method into atom-centered fragments, and the largest fragments are solved on IBM quantum hardware using extended sample-based quantum diagonalization (ext-SQD). Across nine clusters, the heterogeneous quantum--classical workflow reproduces fragment ground-state energies with agreement to full configuration interaction within 0.7~kcal/mol and a mean absolute deviation of 0.3~kcal/mol. In contrast, fragmented and unfragmented conformational energy differences and tritium binding energies differ by 12~kcal/mol and 110~kcal/mol on average, respectively, identifying fragment construction rather than fragment solution as the dominant source of algorithmic bias. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first such demonstration for a charged ionic system and in particular an inorganic molten salt, where electrostatic and polarization effects make the accurate treatment of electronic correlation particularly challenging. These results also identify areas of future research towards an accurate and scalable quantum--classical workflow to compute free-energy estimates of tritium speciation in fusion blankets.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates the first heterogeneous quantum-classical computing workflow for tritium binding in FLiBe molten salt, achieving fragment ground-state energies within 0.3 kcal/mol mean absolute deviation from full configuration interaction, while identifying fragment construction (not quantum solution) as the dominant error source.
AI.motivation: Accurate prediction of tritium speciation in fusion reactor blanket materials (FLiBe molten salt) is essential for breeding and recovering tritium, but requires computationally demanding correlated electronic-structure methods for representative molten-salt clusters.
AI.method: Clusters from ab initio molecular dynamics are partitioned via an embedded-wavefunction (EWF) method into atom-centered fragments; the largest fragments are solved on IBM quantum hardware using extended sample-based quantum diagonalization (ext-SQD).
AI.result: The quantum-classical workflow reproduces fragment ground-state energies with agreement to full configuration interaction within 0.7 kcal/mol (mean absolute deviation 0.3 kcal/mol). Fragmented vs. unfragmented conformational energy differences and tritium binding energies differ by 12 kcal/mol and 110 kcal/mol on average, respectively.
AI.conclusion: Fragment construction, not fragment solution on quantum hardware, is the dominant source of algorithmic bias; this is the first demonstration for a charged ionic system/inorganic molten salt, and future work should focus on improving free-energy estimates of tritium speciation.

title: Quantum-enhanced Monte Carlo Tree Search framework for combinatorial optimization problems
summary: Over the past decades, the operations research community has developed numerous effective optimization algorithms, yet quantum computing is emerging as a new computational paradigm with the potential to approach optimization problems more efficiently. Grover's algorithm offers a provable speedup for combinatorial optimization, but its circuit depth places it beyond current noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices. A more accessible alternative is to reformulate the optimization problem as a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) problem and apply quantum annealing; however, practical problem instances remain out of reach for existing hardware. We introduce AtomTreeSearch, a hybrid classical-quantum algorithm that integrates a quantum subroutine natively implementable on neutral-atom quantum computers within a Monte Carlo Tree Search framework. At each expansion step, a maximal weighted independent set of candidate actions provided by the quantum processor is selected, and these collective actions are performed to obtain a child node. We benchmark our method on the Traveling Salesman Problem, with instances of up to 60 cities on random Euclidean instances and up to 100 cities on TSPLIB instances. Our hybrid algorithm generally matches or outperforms both OR-Tools and simulated annealing on these instances, and we find that the quantum subroutine produces more diverse and higher-quality branches compared to classical alternate subroutines. These results suggest that carefully scoped quantum subroutines embedded in classical search frameworks represent a promising path toward near-term quantum utility in combinatorial optimization.

AI.tldr: AtomTreeSearch is a hybrid classical-quantum algorithm combining neutral-atom quantum computing with Monte Carlo Tree Search for combinatorial optimization, achieving competitive results on TSP instances (up to 100 cities) against OR-Tools and simulated annealing.
AI.motivation: Current quantum optimization approaches (Grover's algorithm, quantum annealing) are impractical for NISQ devices or real-world problem sizes; the authors aim to develop a near-term quantum utility by embedding a feasible quantum subroutine within a classical search framework.
AI.method: Integrates a native neutral-atom quantum subroutine for Maximal Weighted Independent Set into Monte Carlo Tree Search; at each expansion step, the quantum processor selects a maximal weighted independent set of candidate actions, and these collective actions are applied to generate child nodes.
AI.result: Matches or outperforms OR-Tools and simulated annealing on Euclidean TSP (up to 60 cities) and TSPLIB instances (up to 100 cities); the quantum subroutine produces more diverse and higher-quality branches than classical alternatives.
AI.conclusion: Embedding carefully scoped quantum subroutines in classical search frameworks is a promising path toward near-term quantum utility in combinatorial optimization.

title: Connecting Density Matrix Spectroscopy to Biexciton Entanglement Dynamics
summary: Quantum entanglement is one of the most intriguing features of quantum mechanics. To investigate the entanglement between two excitons in a biexciton, an experimental technique called density matrix spectroscopy (DMS) has recently been developed. DMS combines stimulated emission tomography and pump-probe techniques to obtain a time-resolved density matrix of the polarization state of a photon pair emitted from the biexciton. The reconstructed density matrix is expected to encode information about the biexciton state and its entanglement dynamics, but the precise nature of this connection has remained unclear. In this paper, we derive an analytical relationship between the density matrix obtained by DMS and the biexciton state. In addition, we perform numerical simulations to compare the entanglement dynamics obtained by DMS with the biexciton's entanglement dynamics in a two-dimensional electron-hole system using an extended ionic Hubbard model. We find that DMS can partially capture the entanglement in the biexciton, in particular, the dynamics of the difference $S_{\mathrm{bi}} - S_k$, where $S_{\mathrm{bi}}$ is the entanglement entropy of the biexciton and $S_k$ is the entanglement in terms of the wavevectors of the excitons that constitute the biexciton. These results demonstrate the validity of DMS for obtaining information about the entanglement dynamics of the biexciton.

AI.tldr: This paper derives an analytical relationship between density matrix spectroscopy (DMS) measurements and biexciton states, and shows through numerical simulations that DMS can partially capture biexciton entanglement dynamics, specifically the difference between biexciton entanglement entropy and wavevector-based entanglement.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to clarify the precise connection between the density matrix obtained by DMS and the biexciton state, as well as its entanglement dynamics, which had remained unclear despite DMS being a recently developed experimental technique.
AI.method: The authors derive an analytical relationship between the DMS-reconstructed density matrix and the biexciton state, and perform numerical simulations of entanglement dynamics in a two-dimensional electron-hole system using an extended ionic Hubbard model.
AI.result: DMS can partially capture biexciton entanglement, particularly the dynamics of the difference S_bi - S_k, where S_bi is the biexciton entanglement entropy and S_k is the wavevector-based entanglement of constituent excitons.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate the validity of DMS for obtaining information about biexciton entanglement dynamics.

title: Stable Qubit Readout and the Identifiability of Population Change
summary: Stable readout statistics are often taken as evidence for a well-defined physical response, but stability alone need not identify which state quantity has changed. We analyze this issue for finite collections of qubit states measured by binary readouts, focusing on changes in computational-basis population. The central question is when reproducible response data certify the sign or range of an underlying population change. We show that the answer is controlled by the calibrated measurement directions, not by loop consistency alone. For a fully calibrated finite readout family, we derive an exact closed-form interval of all compatible population changes. We also construct a same-record, jointly measurable example in which identical probabilities and accepted loop checks admit positive, zero, and negative population interpretations. When only a diagonal readout gain and a bound on coherence sensitivity are trusted, we obtain the sharp minimax interval and the necessary-and-sufficient sign condition $g>2χ$. These results separate implementation stability from population identifiability and provide analytic benchmarks for qubit readout calibration.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that stable qubit readout statistics alone do not guarantee identification of population changes; identifiability depends on calibrated measurement directions and specific conditions like g > 2χ, not just loop consistency.
AI.motivation: To challenge the assumption that stable, reproducible readout statistics (e.g., passing loop consistency checks) are sufficient to certify the sign or magnitude of an underlying population change in qubit systems, and to establish rigorous conditions under which such certification is possible.
AI.method: The authors derive exact closed-form intervals for compatible population changes given a fully calibrated finite readout family, and construct a counterexample with identical probabilities and accepted loop checks that admits multiple interpretations. They also derive minimax intervals and necessary-and-sufficient sign conditions (g > 2χ) under partial calibration (diagonal readout gain + coherence sensitivity bound).
AI.result: For fully calibrated readout families, an exact closed-form interval of all compatible population changes is derived. A same-record, jointly measurable example shows identical probabilities and passed loop checks can be consistent with positive, zero, or negative population changes. Under partial calibration, the sharp minimax interval is obtained, and the sign condition g > 2χ is necessary and sufficient.
AI.conclusion: Implementation stability (e.g., loop consistency) does not imply population identifiability; the key factor is the calibrated measurement directions. The results provide analytic benchmarks for qubit readout calibration and separate the concepts of stability from identifiability.

title: Demonstration of unpartible entanglement
summary: We report on the first experimental verification of mode-independent entanglement. Commonly, the entanglement of a state is firmly based on pre-defined parties that are correlated, and the state might be disentangled when the definition of the parties is changed. Exceeding this party-dependent concept, we realize a type of quantum entanglement that persists even if the parties, in our case modes, are transformed. This safeguards the performance of entanglement in real-world applications, such as quantum communication settings involving noise and untrusted parties. For the state generation, we present an experimental scheme based on a fully reconfigurable temporally multiplexed interferometer with measurement-induced nonlinearities, which generates heralded two-photon states in two modes that are entangled for all choices of orthonormal mode basis. For the certification process, we utilize a tailored quantum-state tomography, achieving fidelities that validate the presence of mode-independent entanglement as a resilient and operationally advantageous quantum correlation.

AI.tldr: First experimental demonstration of mode-independent entanglement, where quantum correlations persist across all mode basis choices, using a reconfigurable temporally multiplexed interferometer with heralded two-photon states.
AI.motivation: Standard entanglement depends on predefined parties/modes; entanglement can disappear when the party definition changes. The authors aim to realize entanglement that is robust against mode transformations, which is crucial for real-world quantum communication involving noise and untrusted parties.
AI.method: A fully reconfigurable temporally multiplexed interferometer with measurement-induced nonlinearities generates heralded two-photon states. Certification uses tailored quantum-state tomography to validate entanglement across all orthonormal mode bases.
AI.result: Achieved heralded two-photon states entangled for all choices of orthonormal mode basis, with fidelities confirming mode-independent entanglement.
AI.conclusion: Mode-independent entanglement is experimentally realizable and serves as a resilient, operationally advantageous quantum correlation, safeguarding performance in practical quantum communication settings.

title: Staged Hybridisation for Visual Quantum Reinforcement Learning via Knowledge Distillation
summary:
Visual environments are a demanding setting for quantum reinforcement learning (QRL): high-dimensional observations, unstable RL optimisation, and constrained variational quantum circuits (VQCs) are difficult to train jointly. This paper studies knowledge distillation (KD) as a staged hybridisation strategy for visual QRL. Instead of training a hybrid visual agent end-to-end from pixels, we first train a classical visual teacher, freeze its encoder as a feature interface, and distil the teacher's policy behaviour into compact downstream heads. These heads can be classical or VQC-based, enabling small quantum-compatible students to be evaluated under the same frozen representation as compact classical controls.
  We evaluate the pipeline on CartPole Pixels and Acrobot Pixels. The results show that staged KD enables shallow VQC heads to acquire non-trivial visual-control behaviour in settings where direct pixel-based training would be substantially more difficult. Angle-encoded VQC heads retain near-teacher performance, while amplitude-encoded heads push compactness to an extreme regime, at the cost of greater fragility, stronger budget sensitivity, and higher simulation time. Overall, staged KD reframes visual QRL as a compact-head learning problem, opening a practical route for training small quantum-compatible policies outside the standard end-to-end RL loop.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a staged knowledge distillation pipeline for visual quantum reinforcement learning, where a classical visual teacher is first trained, its encoder frozen, and its policy behaviour distilled into compact downstream heads (classical or VQC-based). This approach enables shallow VQC heads to achieve non-trivial visual-control performance on CartPole Pixels and Acrobot Pixels, with angle-encoded heads near teacher-level and amplitude-encoded heads offering extreme compactness at the cost of fragility.
AI.motivation: Visual environments pose challenges for quantum reinforcement learning due to high-dimensional observations, unstable RL optimisation, and constrained variational quantum circuits (VQCs) being difficult to train jointly in an end-to-end manner from pixels.
AI.method: Staged knowledge distillation: (1) train a classical visual teacher, (2) freeze its encoder as a feature interface, (3) distil the teacher's policy behaviour into compact downstream heads (either classical or VQC-based). This decouples representation learning from policy learning, enabling small quantum-compatible students to be evaluated under the same frozen representation.
AI.result: On CartPole Pixels and Acrobot Pixels, staged KD enables shallow VQC heads to acquire non-trivial visual-control behaviour where direct pixel-based training is substantially more difficult. Angle-encoded VQC heads achieve near-teacher performance; amplitude-encoded heads offer extreme compactness but with greater fragility, stronger budget sensitivity, and higher simulation time.
AI.conclusion: Staged KD reframes visual QRL as a compact-head learning problem, offering a practical route for training small quantum-compatible policies outside the standard end-to-end RL loop.

title: Working with measurement-based computations on qudits
summary:
Measurement-based quantum computing is a universal model of quantum computation in which successive product measurements of an entangled resource state drive the computation. The non-deterministic nature of measurements necessitates adaptivity to ensure an overall deterministic computation. Flow structures characterise cases in which such an adaptive correction procedure is possible. Recently, flow has been defined in a setting where the resource states are prime-dimensional qudit graph states rather than the usual qubit graph states. Yet, this qudit flow definition is more burdensome to work with than analogous definitions for qubits.
  Here, we give a simpler definition of qudit flow and consider various useful properties of this flow, drawing on results for the qubit case. In particular, we show how to focus qudit flow and argue that focused flow is canonical. We improve the previous algebraic formulation to capture focused flow and use it to obtain an $O(n^3)$ flow-finding algorithm (where $n$ is the number of qudits), matching the best known complexity for qubit flows and improving on the previous $O(n^4)$ result for qudits. Furthermore, we explore multiple flow-preserving transformations, thus opening a pathway to using flow for optimisation. These transformations include pivoting, removal and insertion of certain types of vertices, and reversibility of flow. Lastly, we propose an algorithmic approach to generating large qudit computations with flow, for testing or machine learning.

AI.tldr: This paper simplifies the definition of qudit flow in measurement-based quantum computing, establishes its canonical form (focused flow), develops an O(n³) flow-finding algorithm (improving from O(n⁴)), and explores flow-preserving transformations and generation of qudit computations with flow.
AI.motivation: The existing qudit flow definition for measurement-based quantum computation is more complex and burdensome than the qubit counterpart, and the best known algorithm for finding qudit flow had O(n⁴) complexity, lagging behind the O(n³) achievable for qubit flows.
AI.method: The authors provide a simpler definition of qudit flow, show focused flow is canonical, improve the algebraic formulation to capture focused flow, derive an O(n³) flow-finding algorithm, and explore flow-preserving transformations including pivoting, vertex insertion/removal, and flow reversibility. They also propose an algorithmic approach for generating large qudit computations with flow.
AI.result: A simpler definition of qudit flow; proof that focused qudit flow is canonical; an O(n³) flow-finding algorithm (matching qubit complexity); identification of multiple flow-preserving transformations; and a method for generating qudit computations with flow.
AI.conclusion: The simplified qudit flow definition and efficient algorithm lower barriers for working with qudit measurement-based quantum computing, and the flow-preserving transformations open pathways for optimization and synthesis of large-scale qudit computations.

title: Bridging the NISQ and Fault-Tolerant Regimes: Generative-ML-Assisted Quantum Selected CI for Molecular Simulations
summary: Calculation of binding energies for protein-ligand molecular systems requires accurate treatment of the electronic structure, a quantum chemistry problem that scales exponentially on classical hardware, while current quantum hardware remains too noisy for the required circuit depths. This report presents a hybrid quantum-classical workflow performed on the Fujitsu FX700 ideal state-vector simulator using QARP that addresses two structural inefficiencies in quantum-sampling-based diagonalization workflows. First, we integrate the Linear Scaling CNOT UCCSD (LCNot-UCCSD) ansatz into the QSCI framework, replacing the $\mathcal{O}(N^6)$ CCSD parameter initialization of the competing LUCJ ansatz approach with $\mathcal{O}(N^4)$ MP2-amplitude initialization. Second, we introduce QSCI-RBM, a variant that replaces the configuration recovery of the SQD framework with a Restricted Boltzmann Machine (RBM) acting as a compact generative subspace expansion model. Both are evaluated on eight different molecules in STO-3G across 14 controlled artificial error levels with 100 independent runs each, validated on potential energy surface scans of the N$_2$ molecule in cc-pVDZ, and embedded within DMET to treat the FDA-approved antiviral Amantadine (C$_{10}$H$_{17}$N, 11 DMET fragments) and the active region of the SARS-CoV-2 main protease complexed with its covalent inhibitor Carmofur (PDB: 7BUY, C$_{15}$H$_{28}$N$_4$O$_5$S, 10 fragments). To our knowledge, this is the first deployment of LCNot-UCCSD within QSCI on a quantum computing simulator, and the first DMET-QSCI(LCNot-UCCSD)-RBM application to an industry-relevant protein-ligand system. By utilizing a fraction of the classical computing resources required by the current state-of-the-art work by Cleveland Clinic, RIKEN, and IBM Quantum, this approach enables more efficient and economical drug discovery simulations for the industry.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a hybrid quantum-classical workflow combining LCNot-UCCSD ansatz with QSCI framework and RBM-based subspace expansion, achieving more efficient protein-ligand binding energy calculations on a quantum simulator. Tested on 8 molecules, N₂ scans, and two drug targets (Amantadine, SARS-CoV-2 Mpro with Carmofur), it reduces classical resource requirements compared to state-of-the-art methods.
AI.motivation: Protein-ligand binding energy calculations require accurate electronic structure treatment, which scales exponentially on classical hardware, while current quantum hardware is too noisy for deep circuits. The authors aim to develop a more efficient hybrid quantum-classical workflow that overcomes structural inefficiencies in existing quantum-sampling-based diagonalization methods.
AI.method: The workflow integrates LCNot-UCCSD ansatz into the QSCI framework (replacing O(N⁶) CCSD with O(N⁴) MP2-amplitude initialization) and introduces QSCI-RBM, replacing SQD configuration recovery with a Restricted Boltzmann Machine for compact generative subspace expansion. Evaluated on 8 molecules in STO-3G across 14 error levels (100 runs each), N₂ in cc-pVDZ, and embedded in DMET for Amantadine (11 fragments) and SARS-CoV-2 Mpro with Carmofur (10 fragments).
AI.result: First deployment of LCNot-UCCSD within QSCI on a quantum simulator, and first DMET-QSCI(LCNot-UCCSD)-RBM application to an industry-relevant protein-ligand system. Uses a fraction of classical computing resources compared to the state-of-the-art work by Cleveland Clinic, RIKEN, and IBM Quantum.
AI.conclusion: This hybrid quantum-classical approach enables more efficient and economical drug discovery simulations by reducing classical resource requirements, making it suitable for industry applications despite current quantum hardware limitations.

title: Revisiting crossed-correlated baths in open quantum systems simulated by HEOM or T-TEDOPA
summary: Excited-state dynamics of open quantum systems is analyzed by the hierarchical equations of motion (HEOM) or the thermalized time-evolving density operator with orthogonal polynomials algorithm (T-TEDOPA) method when a discrete $ab$ $initio$ linear vibronic model is parametrized by continuous temperature-dependent spectral densities leading to crossed correlation functions, i.e. correlated fluctuations of the energy gap collective modes. We focus on a conical intersection involving two collective modes tuning the energy of each excited state and we revisit the transformation of the initial correlated tuning baths to de-correlated shared baths in order to reduce the computational resources. While a completely frequency-dependent transformation poses problems for HEOM, we find that in some particular cases, an optimal approximate frequency-independent transformation may be derived. On the contrary, T-TEDOPA is very efficient and allows to use this frequency-dependent transformation at the price of managing long-range couplings in the tensor chain. An illustrative application is shown by using the linear vibronic coupling model of a planar symmetrical (phenylethynyl)benzene dimer.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes excited-state dynamics of open quantum systems using HEOM and T-TEDOPA methods, focusing on conical intersections with correlated tuning baths. It finds that T-TEDOPA efficiently handles frequency-dependent transformations that are problematic for HEOM, demonstrated on a phenylethynylbenzene dimer model.
AI.motivation: To analyze excited-state dynamics of open quantum systems with correlated fluctuations of energy gap collective modes at conical intersections, and to address computational challenges in transforming correlated tuning baths to de-correlated shared baths.
AI.method: The study compares HEOM and T-TEDOPA for handling continuous temperature-dependent spectral densities with crossed correlation functions. It examines frequency-independent versus frequency-dependent transformations of correlated tuning baths. A planar symmetrical (phenylethynyl)benzene dimer linear vibronic coupling model is used for illustration.
AI.result: A completely frequency-dependent transformation poses problems for HEOM, but an optimal approximate frequency-independent transformation can be derived in certain cases. T-TEDOPA efficiently handles the frequency-dependent transformation at the cost of managing long-range couplings in the tensor chain.
AI.conclusion: T-TEDOPA is more efficient than HEOM for treating correlated baths in conical intersection dynamics with frequency-dependent transformations, making it a preferable method for such open quantum system problems.

title: Untangling QLDPC Codes with Biased Noise Ancilla
summary: Remarkable technical progress has made high-rate, high-distance, quantum low-density parity-check codes (QLDPC) promising candidates for scalable quantum computing. However, it is hard to design low-depth syndrome extraction circuits that do not spread errors from ancilla qubits to multiple data qubits, also known as hook errors, for general QLDPC codes. Additionally, widely used decoders for these codes based on belief propagation are impaired due to short loops in the Tanner graph. Here, we investigate a hardware-aware approach to avoid these hooks and loops using biased noise ancillas. Using examples of bicycle bivariate codes and a cyclic hypergraph product code, which have been widely considered for practical application, we show that the effective fault-distance of the conventional syndrome extraction circuit can be significantly higher and the number of short loops can be significantly lower when the ancillas are subject to phase-flip errors only, compared to when they are also subject to bit-flip errors. This can result in almost an order of magnitude improvement in the logical error rate at circuit noise of $2\times 10^{-3}$ and when bit-flip errors in the ancilla are 50 times less likely than phase-flip errors. Our work demonstrates a significant and practical quantum error correction advantage with biased noise qubits in which full-bias cannot be maintained.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates a hardware-aware approach using biased noise ancillas to mitigate hook errors and short loops in QLDPC codes, achieving up to an order of magnitude improvement in logical error rate when ancilla bit-flip errors are suppressed relative to phase-flip errors.
AI.motivation: High-rate QLDPC codes are promising for scalable quantum computing, but designing low-depth syndrome extraction circuits that avoid hook errors (error spread from ancilla to data qubits) is difficult, and belief propagation decoders are impaired by short loops in Tanner graphs.
AI.method: The authors propose using biased noise ancillas (subject to phase-flip errors only or with suppressed bit-flip errors) in syndrome extraction circuits for bicycle bivariate codes and cyclic hypergraph product codes. They analyze effective fault-distance and short loop counts, comparing conventional circuits with biased-noise ancilla designs.
AI.result: Biased-noise ancillas yield significantly higher effective fault-distance and fewer short loops. At circuit noise of 2×10⁻³ and when ancilla bit-flip errors are 50× less likely than phase-flip errors, logical error rate improves by almost an order of magnitude.
AI.conclusion: A significant and practical quantum error correction advantage exists with biased noise qubits, even when full bias cannot be maintained, demonstrating a viable path for QLDPC code implementations.

title: Provably Efficient Learning of Fermionic Correlations under Particle-Number Symmetry
summary: Predicting local fermionic correlations is a central task in quantum many-body physics, as these correlations encode many physically relevant local observables. The ubiquitous particle-number symmetry imposes strong structural constraints on quantum states, suggesting that local correlations should be learned with fewer samples than by symmetry-agnostic approaches. However, it has remained unclear whether such a provable advantage exists in collective learning of local correlations. Here, we develop a framework of number-conserving fermionic-shadow tomography based on random orbital rotations. We prove that, for every given order $k$, we can simultaneously estimate {\it all} $k$-body fermionic correlations of an $N$-mode $η$-particle state with a given variance $\varepsilon^2$ using only $O_k(η^k/\varepsilon^2)$ samples, which are independent of the system size $N$. We further establish a matching information-theoretic lower bound $Ω_k(η^k/\varepsilon^2)$ for any adaptive protocol based on single-copy measurements, showing that the $(η^k,\varepsilon)$-dependence is optimal up to constants depending only on $k$. Furthermore, our numerical calculation shows that the proposal reduces the query count by roughly an order of magnitude compared with state-of-the-art methods for one-body correlation estimation in a system of $N=100$, $η=20$ at $\varepsilon=10^{-2}$. This work establishes a provably efficient advantage of particle-number symmetry for fermionic observables estimation.

AI.tldr: The paper develops number-conserving fermionic-shadow tomography based on random orbital rotations, proving that all k-body fermionic correlations of an N-mode η-particle state can be simultaneously estimated using only O_k(η^k/ε²) samples (independent of N), with matching lower bounds showing optimality, and numerical demonstrations of order-of-magnitude improvement over state-of-the-art methods.
AI.motivation: Predicting local fermionic correlations is central to quantum many-body physics, but it was unclear whether leveraging particle-number symmetry could provide a provable advantage in collective learning of local correlations compared to symmetry-agnostic approaches.
AI.method: The authors develop a framework of number-conserving fermionic-shadow tomography based on random orbital rotations, combined with information-theoretic lower bound analysis and numerical simulations comparing against state-of-the-art methods.
AI.result: All k-body fermionic correlations can be simultaneously estimated with O_k(η^k/ε²) samples (independent of system size N), a matching lower bound Ω_k(η^k/ε²) is established, and numerical results show approximately an order-of-magnitude reduction in query count for one-body correlation estimation in a system of N=100, η=20 at ε=10⁻².
AI.conclusion: This work establishes a provably efficient advantage of particle-number symmetry for fermionic observable estimation, with optimal sample complexity scaling with particle number η rather than system size N.

title: Repetition-code-based readout error detection and correction across hardware platforms and generations
summary: Readout errors are one of the dominant sources of noise in current quantum processors, limiting both expectation-value estimation and sampling-based applications. Since they affect only the classical measurement outcomes, they can be addressed using classical coding techniques: immediately before measurement, each data qubit is redundantly encoded with ancilla qubits, and the resulting bit string is decoded either by post-selection or by majority voting. Unlike conventional readout error mitigation, which corrects only aggregate quantities such as expectation values, this approach operates on individual measurement shots and can therefore produce approximately corrected samples. We present a systematic cross-platform and cross-generation experimental evaluation of repetition-code readout error detection and correction. We benchmark the same protocol on IBM Heron r1-r3 superconducting processors and Quantinuum H1 and H2 trapped-ion processors while independently varying the code distance, hardware generation, and encoding layout. We find that both error detection and correction improve readout fidelity on every device and generation tested, even as the unencoded baseline improves substantially across successive hardware releases. At the same time, the value of additional redundancy depends strongly on the underlying hardware. On superconducting processors, the extra gate errors introduced by the encoding rapidly offset its benefits, whereas on trapped-ion processors the much lower gate error rates allow larger code distances to remain advantageous.

AI.tldr: This paper experimentally evaluates repetition-code readout error detection and correction across IBM superconducting (Heron r1-r3) and Quantinuum trapped-ion (H1, H2) processors, finding that while both methods improve readout fidelity across all devices, the benefit of increased code distance is limited on superconducting processors due to encoding-induced gate errors, whereas trapped-ion processors sustain gains at larger code distances due to lower gate error rates.
AI.motivation: Readout errors are a dominant noise source in quantum processors, limiting both expectation-value estimation and sampling-based applications. Unlike conventional readout error mitigation (which corrects only aggregate quantities), the authors aim to correct individual measurement shots using classical repetition coding, enabling approximately corrected samples.
AI.method: The method encodes each data qubit redundantly with ancilla qubits immediately before measurement, using repetition codes decoded by post-selection or majority voting. The protocol is benchmarked systematically across IBM Heron r1-r3 (superconducting) and Quantinuum H1, H2 (trapped-ion) processors, varying code distance, hardware generation, and encoding layout.
AI.result: Error detection and correction improved readout fidelity on every device and generation. On superconducting processors, extra gate errors from encoding rapidly offset benefits, limiting useful code distance. On trapped-ion processors, lower gate error rates allowed larger code distances to remain advantageous.
AI.conclusion: Repetition-code readout error correction is effective cross-platform but hardware-dependent; trapped-ion processors benefit more from increased redundancy due to lower gate errors, while superconducting processors see diminishing returns at larger code distances.

title: Cavity-mediated probabilistic magic $T$-gate injection
summary: Non-Clifford gates are a necessary resource for universal quantum computation, yet their fault-tolerant implementation typically relies on magic-state distillation, which incurs significant overhead in qubit count and circuit depth. In this work, we propose a probabilistic cavity-based magic-state injection protocol. Our scheme exploits controlled atom-cavity interactions and conditional measurements to probabilistically prepare an effective magic state encoded in the first two level Fock subspace of a single cavity mode, achieving a success probability of $0.74$ per attempt, independent of the target magic phase. The cavity-encoded magic state is subsequently injected into a computational atom via a teleportation-based protocol mediated by dressed-state transitions, requiring only Clifford operations and a single auxiliary atom for readout. We show that all required operations -- state preparation, two-qubit exchange gates, and projective measurement -- can be implemented with experimentally available techniques in Rydberg atom-cavity platforms. We further discuss how the scheme can in principle be adapted to operate at the logical level, where collective Rydberg interactions and optical nonlinearities provide a route toward cavity-mediated $T$-gate injection directly into code-encoded qubits.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a probabilistic cavity-based magic-state injection protocol using controlled atom-cavity interactions and conditional measurements to prepare a magic state in a cavity mode with 74% success probability, then inject it into a computational atom via Clifford operations and teleportation, all implementable in Rydberg atom-cavity platforms.
